courses.title: Math — Kindergarten
courses.description: Numbers, operations, geometry & more. Grade level: Kindergarten.

lessons.title: Counting & Cardinality
lessons.content:
Counting & Cardinality

Learning Objectives

  • • Count 5 apples: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
  • • Show 3 fingers
  • • Count 15 blocks
  • • Write the number 18
  • • 5 is more than 3
  • • 4 is equal to 4
Kindergarten
🔢 Math
Module 1

Counting & Cardinality

Learn to count objects, recognize numbers, and understand how many.

Learning Objectives

Count to 100 by ones and tens

Write numbers 0–20

Compare two groups of objects

Lessons

1. Counting to 10

Practice counting objects from 1 to 10 using pictures and manipulatives.

Examples:

  • • Count 5 apples: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5
  • • Show 3 fingers

2. Counting to 20

Extend counting skills up to 20.

Examples:

  • • Count 15 blocks
  • • Write the number 18

3. Comparing Numbers

Learn to compare groups using more, fewer, and equal.

Examples:

  • • 5 is more than 3
  • • 4 is equal to 4

lessons.title: Shapes & Geometry
lessons.content:

Shapes & Geometry

Examples:

lessons.title: Addition & Subtraction Basics
lessons.content:
Addition & Subtraction Basics

Learning Objectives

  • • 2 cats + 1 cat = 3 cats
  • • 3 + 2 = 5
  • • 5 apples - 2 apples = 3 apples
  • • 4 - 1 = 3
Kindergarten
🔢 Math
Module 3

Addition & Subtraction Basics

Understand addition as putting together and subtraction as taking apart.

Learning Objectives

Add within 5

Subtract within 5

Use objects to solve problems

Lessons

1. Putting Together

Learn what it means to add by combining groups.

Examples:

  • • 2 cats + 1 cat = 3 cats
  • • 3 + 2 = 5

2. Taking Apart

Learn subtraction by removing objects from a group.

Examples:

  • • 5 apples - 2 apples = 3 apples
  • • 4 - 1 = 3

lessons.title: Measurement
lessons.content:
Measurement

Learning Objectives

  • • The pencil is longer than the crayon
  • • The book is shorter than the desk
  • • A rock is heavier than a feather
  • • A pillow is lighter than a backpack

🔢 Math
Module 4

Measurement

Compare lengths, weights, and capacities using direct comparison.

Learning Objectives

Compare lengths using longer/shorter

Compare weights using heavier/lighter

Lessons

Examples:

  • • The pencil is longer than the crayon
  • • The book is shorter than the desk

2. Comparing Weights

Hold objects to compare which is heavier or lighter.

Examples:

  • • A rock is heavier than a feather
  • • A pillow is lighter than a backpack

lessons.title: Numbers to 100
lessons.content:
Numbers to 100

lessons.title: Patterns & Sorting
lessons.content:
Patterns & Sorting

Learning Objectives

  • • Red, blue, red, blue, ___ (red)

  • • Sort shapes by number of sides

Extend a pattern

Find what comes next in a pattern.

Examples:

  • • Red, blue, red, blue, ___ (red)
  • • Circle, square, triangle, circle, square, ___ (triangle)

Examples:

  • • Sort shapes by number of sides

lessons.title: Addition to 10
lessons.content:
Addition to 10

Learning Objectives

  • • 🐱🐱 + 🐱 = 3 cats
  • • 4 + 3 = 7
  • • 1+9, 2+8, 3+7, 4+6, 5+5
  • • 10 is a special number in math!
Kindergarten
🔢 Math
Module 7

Addition to 10

Use pictures, objects, and drawings to add within 10.

Learning Objectives

Add within 10

Understand the + and = symbols

Examples:

  • • 4 + 3 = 7

lessons.title: Subtraction from 10
lessons.content:
Subtraction from 10

Learning Objectives

  • • 🍎🍎🍎🍎 − 🍎 = 3
  • • 8 - 3 = 5
  • • 10 - ___ = 6 (answer: 4)
  • • 7 - ___ = 2 (answer: 5)
Kindergarten
🔢 Math
Module 8

Subtraction from 10

Use pictures and objects to subtract within 10.

Learning Objectives

Subtract within 10

Understand the − symbol

Relate addition and subtraction

Lessons

1. Taking Away

Cross out objects to show subtraction.

Examples:

  • • 🍎🍎🍎🍎 − 🍎 = 3
  • • 8 - 3 = 5

2. Missing Numbers

Find what was taken away.

Examples:

  • • 10 - ___ = 6 (answer: 4)
  • • 7 - ___ = 2 (answer: 5)

lessons.title: Addition & Subtraction to 20
lessons.content:
Addition & Subtraction to 20

Learning Objectives

  • • 7 + 3 = 10
  • • 6 + 2 = 8
  • • 9 + 5 = 14
  • • 8 + 7 = 15
  • • 15 - 7 = 8 because 8 + 7 = 15
  • • 12 - 5 = 7
1st Grade
🔢 Math
Module 1

Addition & Subtraction to 20

Master addition and subtraction facts within 20.

Learning Objectives

Add within 20

Subtract within 20

Understand fact families

Lessons

1. Adding to 10

Use number bonds and ten frames to add numbers up to 10.

Examples:

  • • 7 + 3 = 10
  • • 6 + 2 = 8

2. Adding to 20

Examples:

  • • 9 + 5 = 14
  • • 8 + 7 = 15

3. Subtraction Strategies

Count back and use related addition facts.

Examples:

  • • 15 - 7 = 8 because 8 + 7 = 15
  • • 12 - 5 = 7

lessons.title: Fractions — Halves & Fourths
lessons.content:
Fractions — Halves & Fourths

Learning Objectives

  • • A pizza cut in 2 equal parts — each is ½
  • • ½ + ½ = 1 whole
  • • A square cut into 4 equal parts — each is ¼
  • • 4 fourths = 1 whole
1st Grade
🔢 Math
Module 6

Fractions — Halves & Fourths

Partition circles and rectangles into equal shares.

Learning Objectives

Divide shapes into halves

Divide shapes into fourths

Use vocabulary: half, quarter, whole

Lessons

1. Halves

A half is one of 2 equal parts of a whole.

Examples:

  • • A pizza cut in 2 equal parts — each is ½
  • • ½ + ½ = 1 whole

2. Fourths

A fourth is one of 4 equal parts of a whole.

Examples:

  • • A square cut into 4 equal parts — each is ¼
  • • 4 fourths = 1 whole

lessons.title: Word Problems
lessons.content:
Word Problems

Word Problems

2. Subtract to Find the Difference

Examples:

  • • There were 15 birds. 7 flew away. How many left? 15−7=8

  • • Find the total: 4 1/2 + 4 3/4 + 4 1/2 + 5 + 4 3/4 = 23 1/2

2. Mean, Median, Mode

Three measures of center describe typical data values.

Examples:

  • • Data: 3, 5, 7, 7, 8. Mean = 30/5 = 6. Median = 7. Mode = 7.

lessons.title: Introduction to Ratios
lessons.content:
Introduction to Ratios

Learning Objectives

  • • 3 red apples to 5 green apples: 3:5
  • • 10 boys and 12 girls: boys to girls = 10:12 = 5:6
  • • 2:3 = 4:6 = 6:9 = 8:12
  • • 12:16 simplified: ÷4 = 3:4
5th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 10

Introduction to Ratios

Introduce ratio concepts as a foundation for 6th-grade ratio reasoning.

Learning Objectives

Understand a ratio as a comparison

Write ratios in multiple forms

Find equivalent ratios

Lessons

1. What is a Ratio?

A ratio compares two quantities. It can be written as a:b, a/b, or 'a to b'.

Examples:

  • • 3 red apples to 5 green apples: 3:5
  • • 10 boys and 12 girls: boys to girls = 10:12 = 5:6

2. Equivalent Ratios

Multiply or divide both parts of a ratio by the same number.

Examples:

  • • 2:3 = 4:6 = 6:9 = 8:12
  • • 12:16 simplified: ÷4 = 3:4

courses.title: Math — 6th Grade
courses.description: Numbers, operations, geometry & more. Grade level: 6th Grade.

lessons.title: Ratios and Proportional Relationships
lessons.content:
Ratios and Proportional Relationships

Learning Objectives

  • • 60 miles in 2 hours = 30 miles per hour
  • • $7.50 for 5 apples = $1.50 per apple
  • • 3/4 = x/12 → 3 × 12 = 4x → x = 9
  • • If 5 notebooks cost $8.75, how much do 8 cost? 5/8.75 = 8/x → x = $14
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 1

Ratios and Proportional Relationships

Understand ratios and unit rates; use them to solve problems.

Learning Objectives

Write and simplify ratios

Calculate unit rates

Solve proportion problems

Lessons

1. Ratios and Unit Rates

A unit rate has a denominator of 1 and is useful for comparisons.

Examples:

  • • 60 miles in 2 hours = 30 miles per hour
  • • $7.50 for 5 apples = $1.50 per apple

2. Solving Proportions

Set up equal ratios and solve using cross-multiplication.

Examples:

  • • 3/4 = x/12 → 3 × 12 = 4x → x = 9
  • • If 5 notebooks cost $8.75, how much do 8 cost? 5/8.75 = 8/x → x = $14

lessons.title: Percent
lessons.content:
Percent

Learning Objectives

  • • 75% = 0.75 = 3/4
  • • 0.4 = 40%
  • • 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%
  • • 20% of 50 = 0.20 × 50 = 10
  • • 15% tip on $40 = 0.15 × 40 = $6
  • • 30% off $80: 0.30 × 80 = $24 discount; final price = $56
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 2

Percent

Understand percent as a ratio out of 100; apply to real-world problems.

Learning Objectives

Convert between fractions, decimals, and percents

Calculate percent of a number

Find percent increase and decrease

Lessons

1. Percent Conversions

Percent means 'per hundred'. Convert by moving the decimal or dividing by 100.

Examples:

  • • 75% = 0.75 = 3/4
  • • 0.4 = 40%
  • • 3/5 = 0.6 = 60%

2. Percent of a Number

Multiply the decimal form of the percent by the number.

Examples:

  • • 20% of 50 = 0.20 × 50 = 10
  • • 15% tip on $40 = 0.15 × 40 = $6
  • • 30% off $80: 0.30 × 80 = $24 discount; final price = $56

lessons.title: Integers and the Number Line
lessons.content:
Integers and the Number Line

Learning Objectives

  • • −5 < −2 < 0 < 3 < 7
  • • Temperature −10°F is colder than −3°F
  • • Elevation: Death Valley is −282 ft below sea level
  • • |−7| = 7
  • • |5| = 5
  • • |−12| = 12; 12 > |-9| = 9
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 3

Integers and the Number Line

Understand negative numbers; compare, order, and use absolute value.

Learning Objectives

Represent integers on a number line

Compare and order integers

Find and apply absolute value

Lessons

1. Negative Numbers

Integers extend the number line below zero.

Examples:

  • • −5 < −2 < 0 < 3 < 7
  • • Temperature −10°F is colder than −3°F
  • • Elevation: Death Valley is −282 ft below sea level

2. Absolute Value

Absolute value is the distance from zero; it is always positive.

Examples:

  • • |−7| = 7
  • • |5| = 5
  • • |−12| = 12; 12 > |-9| = 9

lessons.title: Operations with Integers
lessons.content:
Operations with Integers

Learning Objectives

  • • −4 + (−3) = −7
  • • −8 + 5 = −3
  • • 6 − (−4) = 6 + 4 = 10
  • • (−3)(−4) = 12
  • • (−6)(5) = −30
  • • (−20) ÷ (−4) = 5
  • • 18 ÷ (−3) = −6
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 4

Operations with Integers

Add, subtract, multiply, and divide positive and negative integers.

Learning Objectives

Add and subtract integers using rules

Multiply and divide integers

Solve real-world problems with integers

Lessons

1. Adding and Subtracting Integers

Same signs: add and keep the sign. Different signs: subtract and take the sign of the larger absolute value.

Examples:

  • • −4 + (−3) = −7
  • • −8 + 5 = −3
  • • 6 − (−4) = 6 + 4 = 10

2. Multiplying and Dividing Integers

Same signs give positive; different signs give negative.

Examples:

  • • (−3)(−4) = 12
  • • (−6)(5) = −30
  • • (−20) ÷ (−4) = 5
  • • 18 ÷ (−3) = −6

lessons.title: Expressions and Variables
lessons.content:
Expressions and Variables

Learning Objectives

  • • '5 more than a number n' = n + 5
  • • '3 times a number decreased by 2' = 3n − 2
  • • 'Half of x plus 7' = x/2 + 7
  • • 3n + 2n − 4 = 5n − 4
  • • Evaluate 2x² − 3x for x = 4: 2(16) − 12 = 20
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 5

Expressions and Variables

Write, evaluate, and simplify algebraic expressions.

Learning Objectives

Write expressions from word problems

Evaluate expressions by substituting values

Simplify by combining like terms

Lessons

1. Writing Expressions

Use variables to represent unknown quantities.

Examples:

  • • '5 more than a number n' = n + 5
  • • '3 times a number decreased by 2' = 3n − 2
  • • 'Half of x plus 7' = x/2 + 7

2. Evaluating and Simplifying

Substitute values to evaluate; combine like terms to simplify.

Examples:

  • • 3n + 2n − 4 = 5n − 4
  • • Evaluate 2x² − 3x for x = 4: 2(16) − 12 = 20

lessons.title: Equations and Inequalities
lessons.content:
Equations and Inequalities

Learning Objectives

  • • x + 7 = 15 → x = 8
  • • 3n = 27 → n = 9
  • • y ÷ 4 = 6 → y = 24
  • • x > 3: open circle at 3, arrow right
  • • x ≤ −2: closed circle at −2, arrow left
  • • 2x < 10 → x < 5
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 6

Equations and Inequalities

Write and solve one-step equations and inequalities.

Learning Objectives

Write equations from problem situations

Solve one-step equations

Graph and interpret inequalities on a number line

Lessons

1. One-Step Equations

Use inverse operations to isolate the variable.

Examples:

  • • x + 7 = 15 → x = 8
  • • 3n = 27 → n = 9
  • • y ÷ 4 = 6 → y = 24

2. Inequalities

An inequality has a range of solutions; graph with an open or closed circle.

Examples:

  • • x > 3: open circle at 3, arrow right
  • • x ≤ −2: closed circle at −2, arrow left
  • • 2x < 10 → x < 5

lessons.title: Area, Surface Area, and Volume
lessons.content:
Area, Surface Area, and Volume

Learning Objectives

  • • Triangle: A = ½bh
  • • Parallelogram: A = bh
  • • Trapezoid: A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h
  • • Rectangular prism: SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)
  • • V = lwh: a box 4×3×2 has V = 24 units³
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 7

Area, Surface Area, and Volume

Calculate area of complex shapes; find surface area and volume of 3D figures.

Learning Objectives

Find area of triangles, parallelograms, and trapezoids

Calculate surface area of prisms

Calculate volume of prisms

Lessons

1. Area Formulas

Different shapes have specific area formulas.

Examples:

  • • Triangle: A = ½bh
  • • Parallelogram: A = bh
  • • Trapezoid: A = ½(b₁ + b₂)h

2. Surface Area and Volume

Surface area is the total area of all faces; volume is interior space.

Examples:

  • • Rectangular prism: SA = 2(lw + lh + wh)
  • • V = lwh: a box 4×3×2 has V = 24 units³

lessons.title: Statistics — Distributions
lessons.content:
Statistics — Distributions

Learning Objectives

  • • Data: 4,5,5,7,9. Mean=6, Median=5, Mode=5, Range=5
  • • Box plot: shows minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum
  • • Data: 2,4,6,8,10. Mean=6. Distances: 4,2,0,2,4. MAD = 12/5 = 2.4
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 8

Statistics — Distributions

Summarize data using measures of center and variability.

Learning Objectives

Find mean, median, mode, and range

Understand mean absolute deviation (MAD)

Create and interpret box plots and histograms

Lessons

1. Measures of Center and Spread

Summarize a data set with one typical value and a measure of how spread out it is.

Examples:

  • • Data: 4,5,5,7,9. Mean=6, Median=5, Mode=5, Range=5
  • • Box plot: shows minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum

2. Mean Absolute Deviation

MAD measures the average distance of each data point from the mean.

Examples:

  • • Data: 2,4,6,8,10. Mean=6. Distances: 4,2,0,2,4. MAD = 12/5 = 2.4

lessons.title: Geometry — Coordinate Plane
lessons.content:
Geometry — Coordinate Plane

Learning Objectives

  • • Q1: (+,+), Q2: (−,+), Q3: (−,−), Q4: (+,−)
  • • Plot (−3, 4) and (3, 4): they are reflections across the y-axis
  • • Distance from (−2, 5) to (4, 5) = |−2−4| = 6
  • • Distance from (3,−1) to (3, 7) = |−1−7| = 8
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 9

Geometry — Coordinate Plane

Use all four quadrants of the coordinate plane to solve problems.

Learning Objectives

Plot points in all four quadrants

Find distances between points

Reflect points across axes

Lessons

1. Four Quadrants

The axes divide the coordinate plane into four quadrants.

Examples:

  • • Q1: (+,+), Q2: (−,+), Q3: (−,−), Q4: (+,−)
  • • Plot (−3, 4) and (3, 4): they are reflections across the y-axis

2. Distance Between Points

Find horizontal or vertical distance by taking the absolute difference of the same coordinate.

Examples:

  • • Distance from (−2, 5) to (4, 5) = |−2−4| = 6
  • • Distance from (3,−1) to (3, 7) = |−1−7| = 8

lessons.title: Probability — Introduction
lessons.content:
Probability — Introduction

Learning Objectives

  • • P(rolling a 3 on a die) = 1/6
  • • P(flipping heads) = 1/2
  • • P(drawing a red card) = 26/52 = 1/2
  • • P(not rolling 3) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6
  • • P(not raining) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65
6th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 10

Probability — Introduction

Understand basic probability concepts and calculate simple probabilities.

Learning Objectives

Define probability as a number from 0 to 1

Calculate theoretical probability

Find the complement of an event

Lessons

1. Theoretical Probability

P(event) = (favorable outcomes) ÷ (total outcomes)

Examples:

  • • P(rolling a 3 on a die) = 1/6
  • • P(flipping heads) = 1/2
  • • P(drawing a red card) = 26/52 = 1/2

2. Complement

The complement is everything that is NOT the event. P(not A) = 1 − P(A)

Examples:

  • • P(not rolling 3) = 1 − 1/6 = 5/6
  • • P(not raining) = 1 − 0.35 = 0.65

courses.title: Math — 7th Grade
courses.description: Numbers, operations, geometry & more. Grade level: 7th Grade.

lessons.title: Proportional Relationships
lessons.content:
Proportional Relationships

Learning Objectives

  • • y = 3x is proportional; unit rate = 3
  • • y = 3x + 2 is NOT proportional (doesn't pass through origin)
  • • Table: (1,4),(2,8),(3,12) — ratios all equal 4 → proportional
  • • If a car travels 55 mph: d = 55t
  • • Graph is a straight line through (0,0)
7th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 1

Proportional Relationships

Recognize and represent proportional relationships between quantities.

Learning Objectives

Determine if a relationship is proportional

Write equations for proportional relationships

Interpret graphs of proportional relationships

Lessons

1. Proportional vs Non-Proportional

A proportional relationship has a constant ratio (unit rate) and passes through the origin.

Examples:

  • • y = 3x is proportional; unit rate = 3
  • • y = 3x + 2 is NOT proportional (doesn't pass through origin)
  • • Table: (1,4),(2,8),(3,12) — ratios all equal 4 → proportional

2. Equations and Graphs

Write y = kx where k is the constant of proportionality.

Examples:

  • • If a car travels 55 mph: d = 55t
  • • Graph is a straight line through (0,0)

lessons.title: Rational Number Operations
lessons.content:
Rational Number Operations

Learning Objectives

  • • −2/3 + 1/4 = −8/12 + 3/12 = −5/12
  • • (−3/4)(−2/3) = 6/12 = 1/2
  • • −5 ÷ 2/3 = −5 × 3/2 = −15/2 = −7.5
  • • A temperature drops 3/2 degrees per hour for 4 hours: −3/2 × 4 = −6°
  • • Balance: $50, spend $12.75, earn $8.50, spend $22: 50 − 12.75 + 8.50 − 22 = $23.75
7th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 2

Rational Number Operations

Add, subtract, multiply, and divide rational numbers including fractions and negatives.

Learning Objectives

Apply rules for operations with rational numbers

Solve multi-step problems with rational numbers

Convert between fractions, decimals, and percents

Lessons

1. Operations with Rational Numbers

Combine integer rules with fraction rules.

Examples:

  • • −2/3 + 1/4 = −8/12 + 3/12 = −5/12
  • • (−3/4)(−2/3) = 6/12 = 1/2
  • • −5 ÷ 2/3 = −5 × 3/2 = −15/2 = −7.5

2. Multi-Step Problems

Apply multiple operations in the correct order.

Examples:

  • • A temperature drops 3/2 degrees per hour for 4 hours: −3/2 × 4 = −6°
  • • Balance: $50, spend $12.75, earn $8.50, spend $22: 50 − 12.75 + 8.50 − 22 = $23.75

lessons.title: Expressions and the Distributive Property
lessons.content:
Expressions and the Distributive Property

Learning Objectives

  • • 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15
  • • −2(x − 4) = −2x + 8
  • • (x + 3)(2) = 2x + 6
  • • 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)
  • • 4x − 12 = 4(x − 3)
  • • 15x² + 10x = 5x(3x + 2)
7th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 3

Expressions and the Distributive Property

Expand and factor expressions using the distributive property.

Learning Objectives

Apply the distributive property

Combine like terms to simplify

Factor expressions by finding GCF

Lessons

1. Distributive Property

a(b + c) = ab + ac

Examples:

  • • 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15
  • • −2(x − 4) = −2x + 8
  • • (x + 3)(2) = 2x + 6

2. Factoring

Reverse the distributive property by pulling out the GCF.

Examples:

  • • 6x + 9 = 3(2x + 3)
  • • 4x − 12 = 4(x − 3)
  • • 15x² + 10x = 5x(3x + 2)

lessons.title: Equations and Inequalities — Multi-Step
lessons.content:
Equations and Inequalities — Multi-Step

Learning Objectives

  • • 2x + 7 = 19 → 2x = 12 → x = 6
  • • 3(x − 2) = 15 → 3x − 6 = 15 → x = 7
  • • −4x + 3 = −9 → x = 3
  • • 2x − 5 > 11 → x > 8
  • • −3x ≤ 12 → x ≥ −4 (flip sign!)
7th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 4

Equations and Inequalities — Multi-Step

Solve multi-step equations and inequalities with rational numbers.

Learning Objectives

Solve two-step and multi-step equations

Solve inequalities and graph solutions

Write equations and inequalities for word problems

Lessons

1. Multi-Step Equations

Use inverse operations and the distributive property to solve.

Examples:

  • • 2x + 7 = 19 → 2x = 12 → x = 6
  • • 3(x − 2) = 15 → 3x − 6 = 15 → x = 7
  • • −4x + 3 = −9 → x = 3

2. Inequalities

Solving is like equations, but flip the inequality sign when multiplying/dividing by negatives.

Examples:

  • • 2x − 5 > 11 → x > 8
  • • −3x ≤ 12 → x ≥ −4 (flip sign!)

lessons.title: Geometry — Scale Drawings
lessons.content:
Geometry — Scale Drawings

Learning Objectives

  • • Scale 1:100 means 1 cm on drawing = 100 cm in reality
  • • A room 4 cm on map with scale 1:50 is 200 cm = 2 m real
  • • Floor plan: bedroom 6 cm × 4 cm at 1:24 scale → 144 cm × 96 cm real
7th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 5

Geometry — Scale Drawings

Use scale factors to create and interpret scale drawings and models.

Learning Objectives

Understand scale factor

Find actual dimensions from scale drawings

Create scale drawings

Lessons

1. Scale Factor

A scale factor is the ratio of a drawing length to actual length.

Examples:

  • • Scale 1:100 means 1 cm on drawing = 100 cm in reality
  • • A room 4 cm on map with scale 1:50 is 200 cm = 2 m real
  • • Floor plan: bedroom 6 cm × 4 cm at 1:24 scale → 144 cm × 96 cm real

lessons.title: Geometry — Circles
lessons.content:
Geometry — Circles

Learning Objectives

  • • d = 10 cm: C = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm
  • • r = 7 m: C = 14π ≈ 44.0 m
  • • r = 5: A = 25π ≈ 78.5 square units
  • • r = 3: A = 9π ≈ 28.3 square units
  • • Semicircle area = πr²/2
7th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 6

Geometry — Circles

Understand the parts of a circle; calculate circumference and area.

Learning Objectives

Identify radius, diameter, chord, arc

Calculate circumference using C = πd

Calculate area using A = πr²

Lessons

1. Circumference

The perimeter of a circle is called circumference: C = πd = 2πr.

Examples:

  • • d = 10 cm: C = 10π ≈ 31.4 cm
  • • r = 7 m: C = 14π ≈ 44.0 m

2. Area of a Circle

A = πr²

Examples:

  • • r = 5: A = 25π ≈ 78.5 square units
  • • r = 3: A = 9π ≈ 28.3 square units
  • • Semicircle area = πr²/2

lessons.title: Statistics — Comparing Populations
lessons.content:
Statistics — Comparing Populations

Learning Objectives

  • • Class A median = 78, IQR = 12; Class B median = 72, IQR = 20 → A has higher center and less spread
  • • Use double box plots for visual comparison
  • • Survey 30 randomly selected students to estimate school opinion
  • • Larger samples give more reliable estimates
7th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 7

Statistics — Comparing Populations

Use measures of center and variability to compare two data sets.

Learning Objectives

Calculate and compare medians and means

Compare variability using IQR and MAD

Draw inferences from samples

Lessons

1. Comparing Data Sets

Use box plots and statistics to compare two populations.

Examples:

  • • Class A median = 78, IQR = 12; Class B median = 72, IQR = 20 → A has higher center and less spread
  • • Use double box plots for visual comparison

2. Sampling

A random sample is used to make inferences about a population.

Examples:

  • • Survey 30 randomly selected students to estimate school opinion
  • • Larger samples give more reliable estimates

lessons.title: Probability — Compound Events
lessons.content:
Probability — Compound Events

Learning Objectives

  • • Flipping 2 coins: HH, HT, TH, TT → 4 outcomes
  • • Rolling a die and flipping a coin: 6 × 2 = 12 outcomes
  • • P(heads and rolling 6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12
  • • P(drawing 2 aces with replacement) = 4/52 × 4/52 = 1/169
7th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 8

Probability — Compound Events

Calculate probabilities of compound events using lists, trees, and tables.

Learning Objectives

List all outcomes in a sample space

Find probability of compound events

Distinguish independent from dependent events

Lessons

1. Sample Space

All possible outcomes can be organized in a table or tree diagram.

Examples:

  • • Flipping 2 coins: HH, HT, TH, TT → 4 outcomes
  • • Rolling a die and flipping a coin: 6 × 2 = 12 outcomes

2. Independent Events

P(A and B) = P(A) × P(B) for independent events.

Examples:

  • • P(heads and rolling 6) = 1/2 × 1/6 = 1/12
  • • P(drawing 2 aces with replacement) = 4/52 × 4/52 = 1/169

lessons.title: Percent Applications
lessons.content:
Percent Applications

Learning Objectives

  • • 8% tax on $45: 0.08 × 45 = $3.60 → total $48.60
  • • 20% tip on $60: 0.20 × 60 = $12
  • • 30% off $120: 0.30 × 120 = $36 off → $84
  • • $500 at 4% for 3 years: I = 500 × 0.04 × 3 = $60
  • • Final amount = $500 + $60 = $560
7th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 9

Percent Applications

Apply percent to tax, tip, discount, markup, and interest.

Learning Objectives

Calculate sales tax and tip

Find discounts and markups

Calculate simple interest

Lessons

1. Tax, Tip, and Discount

Multiply the percent (as decimal) by the original price.

Examples:

  • • 8% tax on $45: 0.08 × 45 = $3.60 → total $48.60
  • • 20% tip on $60: 0.20 × 60 = $12
  • • 30% off $120: 0.30 × 120 = $36 off → $84

2. Simple Interest

I = Prt where P = principal, r = rate, t = time in years.

Examples:

  • • $500 at 4% for 3 years: I = 500 × 0.04 × 3 = $60
  • • Final amount = $500 + $60 = $560

lessons.title: Geometry — 3D Figures
lessons.content:
Geometry — 3D Figures

Learning Objectives

  • • Triangular prism: 2 triangles + 3 rectangles

🔢 Math
Module 10

Geometry — 3D Figures

Find surface area and volume of prisms, pyramids, and cylinders.

Learning Objectives

Calculate surface area of prisms and pyramids

Calculate volume of prisms and cylinders

Solve real-world geometry problems

1. Surface Area

Sum of the areas of all faces.

Examples:

  • • Triangular prism: 2 triangles + 3 rectangles
  • • Square pyramid: 1 square base + 4 triangular faces

2. Volume of Cylinders

V = πr²h

Examples:

  • • r = 3, h = 10: V = 9π × 10 = 90π ≈ 282.7 cubic units
  • • Soup can r = 4 cm, h = 12 cm: V ≈ 603.2 cm³

courses.title: Math — 8th Grade
courses.description: Numbers, operations, geometry & more. Grade level: 8th Grade.

lessons.title: Linear Equations — One Variable
lessons.content:
Linear Equations — One Variable

Learning Objectives

  • • 2(3x − 1) + 4 = 18 → 6x − 2 + 4 = 18 → 6x = 16 → x = 8/3
  • • 5x + 3 = 3x + 11 → 2x = 8 → x = 4
  • • 3x + 5 = 3x + 9 → 5 = 9 (impossible) → no solution
  • • 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 → 0 = 0 (always true) → infinitely many solutions
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 1

Linear Equations — One Variable

Solve linear equations with one variable, including those requiring multiple steps.

Learning Objectives

Solve multi-step equations

Recognize equations with one, no, or infinitely many solutions

Apply equations to real-world problems

Lessons

1. Multi-Step Equations

Combine like terms, distribute, then isolate the variable.

Examples:

  • • 2(3x − 1) + 4 = 18 → 6x − 2 + 4 = 18 → 6x = 16 → x = 8/3
  • • 5x + 3 = 3x + 11 → 2x = 8 → x = 4

2. Special Cases

Some equations have no solution or infinitely many solutions.

Examples:

  • • 3x + 5 = 3x + 9 → 5 = 9 (impossible) → no solution
  • • 2(x + 3) = 2x + 6 → 0 = 0 (always true) → infinitely many solutions

lessons.title: Linear Equations — Two Variables
lessons.content:
Linear Equations — Two Variables

Learning Objectives

  • • y = 2x + 3: slope = 2, y-intercept = 3
  • • y = −x + 5: falls 1 for every 1 moved right
  • • Rewrite 2x + y = 7 → y = −2x + 7
  • • Points (1,3) and (4,9): slope = (9−3)/(4−1) = 6/3 = 2
  • • A line through (0,0) and (5,−10): slope = −2
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 2

Linear Equations — Two Variables

Graph and interpret linear equations in two variables.

Learning Objectives

Graph a line using slope and y-intercept

Rewrite equations in slope-intercept form

Interpret slope as rate of change

Lessons

1. Slope-Intercept Form

y = mx + b, where m is slope and b is y-intercept.

Examples:

  • • y = 2x + 3: slope = 2, y-intercept = 3
  • • y = −x + 5: falls 1 for every 1 moved right
  • • Rewrite 2x + y = 7 → y = −2x + 7

2. Slope as Rate of Change

Slope = rise/run = (y₂−y₁)/(x₂−x₁)

Examples:

  • • Points (1,3) and (4,9): slope = (9−3)/(4−1) = 6/3 = 2
  • • A line through (0,0) and (5,−10): slope = −2

lessons.title: Systems of Equations
lessons.content:
Systems of Equations

Learning Objectives

  • • y = 2x and y = −x + 6 intersect at (2, 4)
  • • Parallel lines: no solution; same line: infinitely many solutions
  • • y = x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 → x + 1 = 2x − 3 → x = 4, y = 5
  • • 3x + 2y = 12 and x − 2y = 0 → add: 4x = 12 → x = 3, y = 3/2
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 3

Systems of Equations

Solve systems of two linear equations by graphing, substitution, and elimination.

Learning Objectives

Solve systems by graphing

Solve by substitution

Solve by elimination

Lessons

1. Graphing Method

Graph both lines; the intersection is the solution.

Examples:

  • • y = 2x and y = −x + 6 intersect at (2, 4)
  • • Parallel lines: no solution; same line: infinitely many solutions

2. Substitution and Elimination

Algebraic methods give exact solutions.

Examples:

  • • y = x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 → x + 1 = 2x − 3 → x = 4, y = 5
  • • 3x + 2y = 12 and x − 2y = 0 → add: 4x = 12 → x = 3, y = 3/2

lessons.title: Functions
lessons.content:
Functions

Learning Objectives

  • • (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) → function
  • • (1,2),(1,5),(2,3) → NOT a function (1 maps to two outputs)
  • • Vertical line test: if a vertical line crosses the graph twice, not a function
  • • y = 3x − 2: linear (constant slope)
  • • y = x²: nonlinear (parabola)
  • • y = 2^x: nonlinear (exponential)
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 4

Functions

Understand functions as input-output rules; compare linear and nonlinear functions.

Learning Objectives

Define a function; identify from tables and graphs

Compare linear and nonlinear functions

Write functions to model relationships

Lessons

1. What is a Function?

A function assigns exactly one output to each input.

Examples:

  • • (1,2),(2,4),(3,6) → function
  • • (1,2),(1,5),(2,3) → NOT a function (1 maps to two outputs)
  • • Vertical line test: if a vertical line crosses the graph twice, not a function

2. Linear vs. Nonlinear

Linear functions form straight lines; nonlinear do not.

Examples:

  • • y = 3x − 2: linear (constant slope)
  • • y = x²: nonlinear (parabola)
  • • y = 2^x: nonlinear (exponential)

lessons.title: Exponents and Scientific Notation
lessons.content:
Exponents and Scientific Notation

Learning Objectives

  • • xᵃ · xᵇ = xᵃ⁺ᵇ: x³ · x⁴ = x⁷
  • • xᵃ ÷ xᵇ = xᵃ⁻ᵇ: x⁶ ÷ x² = x⁴
  • • (xᵃ)ᵇ = xᵃᵇ: (x²)³ = x⁶
  • • x⁰ = 1; x⁻² = 1/x²
  • • 93,000,000 = 9.3 × 10⁷
  • • 0.000045 = 4.5 × 10⁻⁵
  • • (3 × 10⁴)(2 × 10³) = 6 × 10⁷
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 5

Exponents and Scientific Notation

Apply properties of exponents; express very large/small numbers in scientific notation.

Learning Objectives

Apply product, quotient, and power rules for exponents

Convert to and from scientific notation

Compute with scientific notation

Lessons

1. Exponent Rules

Laws of exponents simplify expressions.

Examples:

  • • xᵃ · xᵇ = xᵃ⁺ᵇ: x³ · x⁴ = x⁷
  • • xᵃ ÷ xᵇ = xᵃ⁻ᵇ: x⁶ ÷ x² = x⁴
  • • (xᵃ)ᵇ = xᵃᵇ: (x²)³ = x⁶
  • • x⁰ = 1; x⁻² = 1/x²

2. Scientific Notation

Write as a × 10ⁿ where 1 ≤ a < 10.

Examples:

  • • 93,000,000 = 9.3 × 10⁷
  • • 0.000045 = 4.5 × 10⁻⁵
  • • (3 × 10⁴)(2 × 10³) = 6 × 10⁷

lessons.title: Geometry — Transformations
lessons.content:
Geometry — Transformations

Learning Objectives

  • • Translate (3,2) by vector (−1,4) → (2,6)
  • • Reflect (3,−2) over x-axis → (3, 2)
  • • Rotate (2,0) 90° counterclockwise → (0,2)
  • • Triangle (1,1),(3,1),(2,3) scaled by factor 2 → (2,2),(6,2),(4,6)
  • • Scale factor > 1: enlargement; between 0 and 1: reduction
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 6

Geometry — Transformations

Perform and describe transformations: translations, rotations, reflections, dilations.

Learning Objectives

Translate, rotate, and reflect figures on the coordinate plane

Identify congruence and similarity through transformations

Perform dilations using scale factors

Lessons

1. Rigid Transformations

Congruence-preserving transformations: translations, rotations, reflections.

Examples:

  • • Translate (3,2) by vector (−1,4) → (2,6)
  • • Reflect (3,−2) over x-axis → (3, 2)
  • • Rotate (2,0) 90° counterclockwise → (0,2)

2. Dilations

Dilations change size but not shape (similarity transformation).

Examples:

  • • Triangle (1,1),(3,1),(2,3) scaled by factor 2 → (2,2),(6,2),(4,6)
  • • Scale factor > 1: enlargement; between 0 and 1: reduction

lessons.title: Pythagorean Theorem
lessons.content:
Pythagorean Theorem

Learning Objectives

  • • 3² + 4² = 5² → 9 + 16 = 25 ✓
  • • Find c: 5² + 12² = c² → c = 13
  • • Find b: 10² + b² = 26² → b = 24
  • • Distance from (1,2) to (4,6) = √(9+16) = √25 = 5
  • • Distance from (0,0) to (3,4) = 5
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 7

Pythagorean Theorem

Understand and apply the Pythagorean Theorem in 2D and 3D.

Learning Objectives

State and prove the Pythagorean Theorem

Find missing side lengths

Apply to distance and 3D problems

Lessons

1. The Theorem

In a right triangle: a² + b² = c² (c is the hypotenuse).

Examples:

  • • 3² + 4² = 5² → 9 + 16 = 25 ✓
  • • Find c: 5² + 12² = c² → c = 13
  • • Find b: 10² + b² = 26² → b = 24

2. Distance Formula

Distance between two points = √((x₂−x₁)² + (y₂−y₁)²)

Examples:

  • • Distance from (1,2) to (4,6) = √(9+16) = √25 = 5
  • • Distance from (0,0) to (3,4) = 5

lessons.title: Volume of Curved Solids
lessons.content:
Volume of Curved Solids

Learning Objectives

  • • Cylinder r=4, h=9: V = 144π ≈ 452
  • • Cone r=3, h=8: V = ⅓(9π)(8) = 24π ≈ 75.4
  • • r = 6: V = (4/3)π(216) = 288π ≈ 904
  • • Basketball r ≈ 12 cm: V ≈ 7,238 cm³
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 8

Volume of Curved Solids

Calculate volume of cylinders, cones, and spheres.

Learning Objectives

Use volume formulas for cylinders, cones, and spheres

Compare volumes

Solve real-world problems

Lessons

1. Cylinder and Cone

Cylinder: V = πr²h. Cone: V = ⅓πr²h (one-third of cylinder).

Examples:

  • • Cylinder r=4, h=9: V = 144π ≈ 452
  • • Cone r=3, h=8: V = ⅓(9π)(8) = 24π ≈ 75.4

2. Sphere

V = (4/3)πr³

Examples:

  • • r = 6: V = (4/3)π(216) = 288π ≈ 904
  • • Basketball r ≈ 12 cm: V ≈ 7,238 cm³

lessons.title: Statistics — Bivariate Data
lessons.content:
Statistics — Bivariate Data

Learning Objectives

  • • Hours studied vs. test score: positive correlation
  • • Temperature vs. hot chocolate sales: negative correlation
  • • No pattern: positive correlation, negative correlation, or no correlation
  • • Line: y = 5x + 60; predict score for 8 hours: y = 5(8) + 60 = 100
  • • Extrapolation (predicting beyond data range) can be unreliable
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 9

Statistics — Bivariate Data

Analyze relationships between two variables using scatter plots and linear models.

Learning Objectives

Construct and interpret scatter plots

Identify correlation and trend lines

Predict using a line of best fit

Lessons

1. Scatter Plots

Plot paired data (x, y); look for patterns.

Examples:

  • • Hours studied vs. test score: positive correlation
  • • Temperature vs. hot chocolate sales: negative correlation
  • • No pattern: positive correlation, negative correlation, or no correlation

2. Line of Best Fit

A trend line models the relationship; use it to predict.

Examples:

  • • Line: y = 5x + 60; predict score for 8 hours: y = 5(8) + 60 = 100
  • • Extrapolation (predicting beyond data range) can be unreliable

lessons.title: Introduction to Algebra — Quadratics Preview
lessons.content:
Introduction to Algebra — Quadratics Preview

Learning Objectives

  • • y = x²: (0,0),(1,1),(2,4),(3,9),(4,16)
  • • Compare linear y=2x to quadratic y=x²: quadratic overtakes linear quickly
  • • y = x² − 3x + 2, x=4: 16−12+2 = 6
  • • y = 2x² + x for x=−1: 2(1)+(−1) = 1
8th Grade
🔢 Math
Module 10

Introduction to Algebra — Quadratics Preview

Explore quadratic patterns and prepare for high school algebra.

Learning Objectives

Recognize quadratic patterns from tables and graphs

Understand the shape of a parabola

Evaluate quadratic expressions

Lessons

1. Quadratic Patterns

Quadratic functions grow faster than linear; their graphs are parabolas.

Examples:

  • • y = x²: (0,0),(1,1),(2,4),(3,9),(4,16)
  • • Compare linear y=2x to quadratic y=x²: quadratic overtakes linear quickly

2. Evaluating Quadratics

Substitute x values to find y values for y = ax² + bx + c.

Examples:

  • • y = x² − 3x + 2, x=4: 16−12+2 = 6
  • • y = 2x² + x for x=−1: 2(1)+(−1) = 1

lessons.title: Phonological Awareness
lessons.content:
Phonological Awareness

Learning Objectives

  • • cat – hat – bat – mat
  • • dog – log – frog
  • • el-e-phant = 3 claps
  • • but-ter-fly = 3 claps
  • • dog = 1 clap
Kindergarten
📖 ELA
Module 2

Phonological Awareness

Hear and play with sounds in spoken language — rhymes, syllables, and individual sounds.

Learning Objectives

Clap syllables in words

Blend and segment onset and rime

1. Rhyming Words

Rhyming words share the same ending sound.

Examples:

  • • cat – hat – bat – mat
  • • dog – log – frog

Clap once for each syllable (word chunk).

Examples:

  • • but-ter-fly = 3 claps
  • • dog = 1 clap

lessons.title: Phonics — Letters & Sounds
lessons.content:
Phonics — Letters & Sounds

  • • Short E: egg, elephant

  • • B says /b/ — ball, bat
  • • C says /k/ — cat, cup

Learning Objectives

Name all 26 letters

Produce the sound for each letter

The 5 vowels are A, E, I, O, U. They each have a short and long sound.

Examples:

  • • Short A: apple, ant
  • • Short E: egg, elephant
  • • Short I: igloo, insect

2. Consonants

All other letters are consonants. Learn their most common sounds.

Examples:

  • • B says /b/ — ball, bat
  • • C says /k/ — cat, cup
  • • D says /d/ — dog, duck

lessons.title: Reading Literature
lessons.content:
Reading Literature

Learning Objectives

  • • In 'The Three Bears', the characters are Goldilocks and three bears
  • • The setting is a house in the forest
  • • First… Then… Finally…
  • • Beginning: Goldilocks finds the cottage. Middle: She tries the porridge. End: She runs away.
Kindergarten
📖 ELA
Module 4

Reading Literature

Listen to and discuss stories, identifying characters, setting, and key events.

Learning Objectives

Identify the main characters

Describe the setting

Retell key events in order

Lessons

1. Characters & Setting

The characters are who the story is about. The setting is where and when it happens.

Examples:

  • • In 'The Three Bears', the characters are Goldilocks and three bears
  • • The setting is a house in the forest

2. Retelling a Story

Use beginning, middle, and end to retell.

Examples:

  • • First… Then… Finally…
  • • Beginning: Goldilocks finds the cottage. Middle: She tries the porridge. End: She runs away.

lessons.title: Reading Informational Text
lessons.content:
Reading Informational Text

Learning Objectives

  • • Topic: Frogs. Detail: Frogs lay eggs in water.

  • • A caption explains what a photo shows
  • • A label points to a part of a diagram

📖 ELA

Reading Informational Text

Explore nonfiction books to learn about the world.

Identify the topic of an informational text

Find key details that support the topic

Use text features like photos and captions

1. Topic & Details

The topic is what the book is mostly about. Details give more information.

Examples:

  • • Topic: Frogs. Detail: Frogs lay eggs in water.
  • • Topic: Rain. Detail: Rain comes from clouds.

2. Text Features

Photos, captions, and labels help us understand nonfiction.

Examples:

  • • A caption explains what a photo shows
  • • A label points to a part of a diagram

lessons.title: Writing — Drawing & Labeling
lessons.content:
Writing — Drawing & Labeling

Writing — Drawing & Labeling

Express ideas by drawing pictures and adding labels or words.

Learning Objectives

Draw to communicate an idea

Add a label or sentence to a drawing

Use invented spelling to write

Add details to your drawing to tell more.

Examples:

Write the first letter or whole word next to parts of your drawing.

Examples:

  • • Draw a dog, label: nose, tail, paw
  • • Draw a flower, label: petal, stem, leaf

lessons.title: Sight Words — Set 1

Sight Words — Set 1

Vocabulary & Word Meaning

  • • Animals: cat, dog, bird, fish
  • • Foods: apple, bread, milk, rice

📖 ELA
Module 8

Vocabulary & Word Meaning

Build vocabulary by learning new words from stories and conversations.

Learning Objectives

Learn new words from read-alouds

Use context clues to figure out word meaning

Sort words into categories

Use the words and pictures around an unknown word to figure out its meaning.

Group words that belong together.

Examples:

lessons.title: Speaking & Listening
lessons.content:
Speaking & Listening

Speaking & Listening

Good conversations have rules that help everyone participate.

lessons.title: Writing Sentences
lessons.content:
Writing Sentences

Writing Sentences

A sentence expresses a complete thought and has a subject and verb.

Every sentence starts with a capital and ends with punctuation.

Examples:

1st Grade

Module 7

Writing — Opinion

State an opinion clearly

Give two or more reasons

Use opinion words like 'I think' and 'because'

Lessons

1. Stating an Opinion

An opinion tells what you think or believe.

Examples:

  • • I think dogs are the best pets.
  • • In my opinion, summer is better than winter.

2. Supporting with Reasons

Give reasons that explain why you have that opinion.

Examples:

  • • I think dogs are the best pets because they are loyal and fun to play with.

lessons.title: Grammar — Nouns & Verbs
lessons.content:
Grammar — Nouns & Verbs

Learning Objectives

  • • Person: teacher, student
  • • Place: school, park
  • • Thing: book, pencil
  • • Animal: cat, dolphin
  • • Action: run, jump, write, eat
  • • Being: is, are, was, were
1st Grade
📖 ELA
Module 8

Grammar — Nouns & Verbs

Identify and use nouns, verbs, and adjectives in sentences.

Learning Objectives

Define and identify nouns

Define and identify verbs

Use adjectives to describe nouns

Lessons

1. Nouns

A noun names a person, place, thing, or animal.

Examples:

  • • Person: teacher, student
  • • Place: school, park
  • • Thing: book, pencil
  • • Animal: cat, dolphin

2. Verbs

A verb shows action or state of being.

Examples:

  • • Action: run, jump, write, eat
  • • Being: is, are, was, were

lessons.title: Vocabulary — Context Clues
lessons.content:
Vocabulary — Context Clues

Learning Objectives

  • • 'The pup, a tiny puppy, barked all night.' — pup means puppy
  • • 'She was ecstatic — the happiest she'd ever been.' — ecstatic means very happy
  • • play → playing, played, player, playful
  • • help → helpful, helpless, helper, helping
1st Grade
📖 ELA
Module 9

Vocabulary — Context Clues

Use context clues and word parts to figure out unknown words.

Learning Objectives

Use surrounding words to define unfamiliar words

Identify root words

Sort words by category

Lessons

1. Using Clues in a Sentence

Look at the other words in the sentence to figure out a new word.

Examples:

  • • 'The pup, a tiny puppy, barked all night.' — pup means puppy
  • • 'She was ecstatic — the happiest she'd ever been.' — ecstatic means very happy

2. Root Words

Many words are built on a base root word.

Examples:

  • • play → playing, played, player, playful
  • • help → helpful, helpless, helper, helping

lessons.title: Fluency & Comprehension
lessons.content:
Fluency & Comprehension

Learning Objectives

  • • Read excited parts faster and louder
  • • Read sad parts slower and quieter
  • • Give each character a different voice
  • • Before: What do I think this book is about?
  • • During: Why did the character do that?
  • • After: What was the most important part?
1st Grade
📖 ELA
Module 10

Fluency & Comprehension

Read aloud with accuracy, appropriate rate, and expression. Demonstrate understanding.

Learning Objectives

Read grade-level text with fluency

Answer who, what, where, when, why, how questions

Retell what was read

Lessons

1. Reading with Expression

Change your voice to match what is happening in the story.

Examples:

  • • Read excited parts faster and louder
  • • Read sad parts slower and quieter
  • • Give each character a different voice

2. Asking & Answering Questions

Good readers ask questions before, during, and after reading.

Examples:

  • • Before: What do I think this book is about?
  • • During: Why did the character do that?
  • • After: What was the most important part?

courses.title: ELA — 2nd Grade
courses.description: Reading, writing, grammar & vocabulary. Grade level: 2nd Grade.

lessons.title: Phonics — Long Vowels
lessons.content:
Phonics — Long Vowels

Learning Objectives

  • • cap → cape
  • • hop → hope
  • • fin → fine
  • • cut → cute
  • • ai/ay: rain, day, train, play
  • • ee/ea: see, read, feet, bean
  • • oa: boat, coat, road
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 1

Phonics — Long Vowels

Read and spell words with long vowel patterns (VCe, vowel teams).

Learning Objectives

Read VCe words (silent e)

Read vowel team words (ai, ay, ee, ea, oa...)

Distinguish long and short vowel sounds

Lessons

1. Silent E (VCe)

Adding a silent e at the end makes the vowel say its name.

Examples:

  • • cap → cape
  • • hop → hope
  • • fin → fine
  • • cut → cute

2. Vowel Teams

Two vowels together often make the long sound of the first vowel.

Examples:

  • • ai/ay: rain, day, train, play
  • • ee/ea: see, read, feet, bean
  • • oa: boat, coat, road

lessons.title: Phonics — R-Controlled Vowels & Diphthongs
lessons.content:
Phonics — R-Controlled Vowels & Diphthongs

Learning Objectives

  • • ar: car, star, farm
  • • er/ir/ur: her, bird, turn
  • • or: corn, fort, storm
  • • oi/oy: coin, boy, oil, joy
  • • ou/ow: cloud, cow, house, flower
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 2

Phonics — R-Controlled Vowels & Diphthongs

Read words where the vowel is changed by R, and words with diphthong sounds.

Learning Objectives

Read ar, er, ir, or, ur words

Read diphthong words (oi, oy, ou, ow)

Spell r-controlled and diphthong words

Lessons

1. R-Controlled Vowels

When R follows a vowel, it changes the vowel's sound.

Examples:

  • • ar: car, star, farm
  • • er/ir/ur: her, bird, turn
  • • or: corn, fort, storm

2. Diphthongs

Diphthongs are vowel sounds that glide from one sound to another.

Examples:

  • • oi/oy: coin, boy, oil, joy
  • • ou/ow: cloud, cow, house, flower

lessons.title: Reading Literature
lessons.content:
Reading Literature

Learning Objectives

  • • When the wolf blew down the house, the pig ran to his brother's house — he was smart and brave
  • • How would you have reacted?
  • • 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf' — moral: Don't lie, or no one will believe you when you tell the truth
  • • 'The Ant and the Grasshopper' — moral: Work hard and prepare for the future
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 3

Reading Literature

Read and respond to stories, fables, and poetry — analyzing characters and themes.

Learning Objectives

Describe how characters respond to challenges

Identify the moral of a fable

Compare and contrast two versions of a story

Lessons

1. Character Responses

Think about how a character acts when something difficult happens.

Examples:

  • • When the wolf blew down the house, the pig ran to his brother's house — he was smart and brave
  • • How would you have reacted?

2. Fables & Morals

A fable is a short story with a moral — a lesson about how to live.

Examples:

  • • 'The Boy Who Cried Wolf' — moral: Don't lie, or no one will believe you when you tell the truth
  • • 'The Ant and the Grasshopper' — moral: Work hard and prepare for the future

lessons.title: Reading Informational Text
lessons.content:
Reading Informational Text

Learning Objectives

  • • Topic: Bees. Main idea: Bees are important because they pollinate plants.
  • • Details: Bees carry pollen. Without bees, many plants can't reproduce.
  • • Main idea: Exercise is good for you. Detail: It strengthens your heart. Detail: It improves your mood.
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 4

Reading Informational Text

Identify main idea and supporting details in nonfiction texts.

Learning Objectives

State the main idea of a text

Find key supporting details

Explain how details support the main idea

Lessons

1. Main Idea vs. Topic

The topic is the subject. The main idea is the most important point about the topic.

Examples:

  • • Topic: Bees. Main idea: Bees are important because they pollinate plants.
  • • Details: Bees carry pollen. Without bees, many plants can't reproduce.

2. Supporting Details

Details give evidence, examples, or explanations for the main idea.

Examples:

  • • Main idea: Exercise is good for you. Detail: It strengthens your heart. Detail: It improves your mood.

lessons.title: Writing — Informational
lessons.content:
Writing — Informational

Learning Objectives

  • • Did you know that dolphins are some of the smartest animals on Earth?
  • • Butterflies go through four amazing stages of life.
  • • A dolphin can recognize itself in a mirror.
  • • A butterfly starts as an egg, then a caterpillar, then a chrysalis, then a butterfly.
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 5

Writing — Informational

Write an informational piece about a topic using facts and text features.

Learning Objectives

Introduce a topic

Include several facts

Use linking words (also, another, because)

Lessons

1. Introducing a Topic

Start your informational piece with a strong opening sentence.

Examples:

  • • Did you know that dolphins are some of the smartest animals on Earth?
  • • Butterflies go through four amazing stages of life.

2. Adding Facts

Research and include real facts about your topic.

Examples:

  • • A dolphin can recognize itself in a mirror.
  • • A butterfly starts as an egg, then a caterpillar, then a chrysalis, then a butterfly.

lessons.title: Writing — Narrative
lessons.content:
Writing — Narrative

Learning Objectives

  • • On a rainy Tuesday, I discovered something amazing in our backyard.
  • • Last summer, my family took a road trip I will never forget.
  • • That was the day I learned that trying new things can be scary but worth it.
  • • From that moment on, the forest felt like our own secret world.
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 6

Writing — Narrative

Write a narrative with a clear event sequence, details, and a conclusion.

Learning Objectives

Establish a situation and narrator

Use descriptive details

Write a satisfying conclusion

Lessons

1. Setting the Scene

Use the opening lines to tell who, where, and when.

Examples:

  • • On a rainy Tuesday, I discovered something amazing in our backyard.
  • • Last summer, my family took a road trip I will never forget.

2. Concluding Sentence

End your story by wrapping up the events.

Examples:

  • • That was the day I learned that trying new things can be scary but worth it.
  • • From that moment on, the forest felt like our own secret world.

lessons.title: Grammar — Sentences & Punctuation
lessons.content:
Grammar — Sentences & Punctuation

Learning Objectives

  • • Statement: The sky is blue.
  • • Question: Is the sky blue?
  • • Exclamation: Wow, the sky is so blue!
  • • Command: Look at the blue sky.
  • • I like dogs, cats, and fish.
  • • She bought apples, bananas, grapes, and oranges.
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 7

Grammar — Sentences & Punctuation

Write complete sentences, use proper punctuation, and identify sentence types.

Learning Objectives

Write statements, questions, exclamations, and commands

Use commas in a series

Use apostrophes for contractions and possessives

Lessons

1. Four Types of Sentences

Sentences do different jobs depending on their purpose.

Examples:

  • • Statement: The sky is blue.
  • • Question: Is the sky blue?
  • • Exclamation: Wow, the sky is so blue!
  • • Command: Look at the blue sky.

2. Commas in a Series

Use commas to separate three or more items in a list.

Examples:

  • • I like dogs, cats, and fish.
  • • She bought apples, bananas, grapes, and oranges.

lessons.title: Vocabulary — Prefixes & Suffixes
lessons.content:
Vocabulary — Prefixes & Suffixes

Learning Objectives

  • • un- means not: unhappy, unkind, unsafe
  • • re- means again: redo, replay, rewrite
  • • pre- means before: preview, preschool, preheat
  • • -ful means full of: helpful, joyful, colorful
  • • -less means without: helpless, careless, fearless
  • • -er/-est: taller/tallest, faster/fastest
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 8

Vocabulary — Prefixes & Suffixes

Use common prefixes and suffixes to determine word meanings.

Learning Objectives

Recognize common prefixes (un-, re-, pre-)

Recognize common suffixes (-ful, -less, -er, -est)

Use affixes to figure out new word meanings

Lessons

1. Prefixes

A prefix is added to the beginning of a word to change its meaning.

Examples:

  • • un- means not: unhappy, unkind, unsafe
  • • re- means again: redo, replay, rewrite
  • • pre- means before: preview, preschool, preheat

2. Suffixes

A suffix is added to the end of a word to change its meaning or part of speech.

Examples:

  • • -ful means full of: helpful, joyful, colorful
  • • -less means without: helpless, careless, fearless
  • • -er/-est: taller/tallest, faster/fastest

lessons.title: Poetry & Figurative Language
lessons.content:
Poetry & Figurative Language

Learning Objectives

  • • Roses are red, violets are blue — 'red' and 'blue' don't rhyme, but 'blue' and 'true' do!
  • • Clap the beat of a poem as you read it aloud
  • • Simile: The clouds were like fluffy white pillows.
  • • Alliteration: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 9

Poetry & Figurative Language

Read and appreciate poetry, understanding rhythm, rhyme, and basic figurative language.

Learning Objectives

Identify rhyme scheme and rhythm

Understand simile and alliteration

Write a simple poem

Lessons

1. Rhyme & Rhythm

Poems often have a beat and words that sound the same at the end of lines.

Examples:

  • • Roses are red, violets are blue — 'red' and 'blue' don't rhyme, but 'blue' and 'true' do!
  • • Clap the beat of a poem as you read it aloud

2. Simile & Alliteration

Poets use comparisons and repeated sounds to make language beautiful.

Examples:

  • • Simile: The clouds were like fluffy white pillows.
  • • Alliteration: Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers.

lessons.title: Research & Speaking
lessons.content:
Research & Speaking

Learning Objectives

  • • Look in the table of contents or index to find your topic
  • • A search engine can help you find kid-friendly websites
  • • Speak clearly and make eye contact
  • • Use pictures or drawings to help explain your topic
2nd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 10

Research & Speaking

Research a topic using multiple sources and present findings to the class.

Learning Objectives

Find information from books and digital sources

Take simple notes

Present information in an organized way

Lessons

1. Finding Information

Use books, encyclopedias, and trusted websites to research.

Examples:

  • • Look in the table of contents or index to find your topic
  • • A search engine can help you find kid-friendly websites

2. Presenting Your Research

Organize your facts and share them clearly with your audience.

Examples:

  • • Speak clearly and make eye contact
  • • Use pictures or drawings to help explain your topic

courses.title: ELA — 3rd Grade
courses.description: Reading, writing, grammar & vocabulary. Grade level: 3rd Grade.

lessons.title: Reading Literature — Story Analysis
lessons.content:
Reading Literature — Story Analysis

Learning Objectives

  • • Charlotte weaves words in her web because she wants to save Wilbur — she is selfless and clever
  • • What does the character want? What is standing in their way?
  • • Theme of Charlotte's Web: True friendship means sacrifice.
  • • Theme of Because of Winn-Dixie: Loneliness can be healed by connection and community.
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 1

Reading Literature — Story Analysis

Analyze characters, plot, theme, and craft in grade-level fiction.

Learning Objectives

Describe characters in depth using traits and motivations

Identify theme and distinguish from topic

Explain how a character's actions drive the plot

Lessons

1. Character Traits & Motivations

Think about why a character does what they do.

Examples:

  • • Charlotte weaves words in her web because she wants to save Wilbur — she is selfless and clever
  • • What does the character want? What is standing in their way?

2. Theme

The theme is the big life lesson the author wants you to take away.

Examples:

  • • Theme of Charlotte's Web: True friendship means sacrifice.
  • • Theme of Because of Winn-Dixie: Loneliness can be healed by connection and community.

lessons.title: Reading Informational Text — Text Structure
lessons.content:
Reading Informational Text — Text Structure

Learning Objectives

  • • Sequence: first, next, then, finally, after, before
  • • Compare/Contrast: however, on the other hand, similarly, both
  • • Cause/Effect: because, as a result, therefore, so
  • • A passage about how volcanoes erupt might use cause/effect
  • • A passage about two types of sharks might use compare/contrast
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 2

Reading Informational Text — Text Structure

Identify text structures: description, sequence, compare/contrast, cause/effect, problem/solution.

Learning Objectives

Identify the text structure of a passage

Use signal words to recognize each structure

Explain how structure helps convey information

Lessons

1. Signal Words

Each text structure uses specific signal words.

Examples:

  • • Sequence: first, next, then, finally, after, before
  • • Compare/Contrast: however, on the other hand, similarly, both
  • • Cause/Effect: because, as a result, therefore, so

2. Identifying Structure

Read a passage and identify its structure by looking for signal words and the author's purpose.

Examples:

  • • A passage about how volcanoes erupt might use cause/effect
  • • A passage about two types of sharks might use compare/contrast

lessons.title: Writing — Opinion Paragraphs
lessons.content:
Writing — Opinion Paragraphs

Learning Objectives

  • • Claim: Recess should be longer.
  • • Reason 1: Students need exercise to stay healthy.
  • • Reason 2: Taking a break helps kids focus better in class.
  • • Conclusion: For these reasons, longer recess benefits everyone.
  • • First, ... In addition, ... Furthermore, ... Most importantly, ... For these reasons, ...
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 3

Writing — Opinion Paragraphs

Write a well-organized opinion paragraph with a clear claim, reasons, and a conclusion.

Learning Objectives

Write a clear opinion statement

Provide two or more reasons with evidence

Use linking words and a concluding statement

Lessons

1. The Opinion Sandwich

Think of an opinion paragraph like a sandwich: claim on top, reasons in the middle, conclusion at the bottom.

Examples:

  • • Claim: Recess should be longer.
  • • Reason 1: Students need exercise to stay healthy.
  • • Reason 2: Taking a break helps kids focus better in class.
  • • Conclusion: For these reasons, longer recess benefits everyone.

2. Linking Words

Use these words to connect your reasons smoothly.

Examples:

  • • First, ... In addition, ... Furthermore, ... Most importantly, ... For these reasons, ...

lessons.title: Writing — Informational Essays
lessons.content:
Writing — Informational Essays

Learning Objectives

  • • Question hook: Have you ever wondered how rainbows form?
  • • Fact hook: Every day, over 1 billion people are affected by water shortages.
  • • Topic sentence → 2–3 supporting facts → concluding sentence for that paragraph
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 4

Writing — Informational Essays

Write a multi-paragraph informational essay with an introduction, body, and conclusion.

Learning Objectives

Write an introductory paragraph

Develop two or more body paragraphs with facts

Write a concluding paragraph

Lessons

1. The Introduction

Hook the reader and introduce your topic clearly.

Examples:

  • • Question hook: Have you ever wondered how rainbows form?
  • • Fact hook: Every day, over 1 billion people are affected by water shortages.

2. Body Paragraphs

Each body paragraph covers one main point with supporting details.

Examples:

  • • Topic sentence → 2–3 supporting facts → concluding sentence for that paragraph

lessons.title: Grammar — Parts of Speech
lessons.content:
Grammar — Parts of Speech

Learning Objectives

  • • Concrete: chair, river, teacher
  • • Abstract: love, courage, freedom
  • • Irregular plural: child→children, mouse→mice, tooth→teeth
  • • Adjective: The tall, graceful giraffe ate the tender leaves.
  • • Adverb: She sang beautifully. He ran extremely fast.
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 5

Grammar — Parts of Speech

Identify and use nouns, pronouns, verbs, adjectives, and adverbs correctly.

Learning Objectives

Identify all major parts of speech

Use regular and irregular plural nouns

Use abstract nouns and collective nouns

Lessons

1. Nouns: Regular, Irregular, Abstract

Nouns can be concrete (things you see) or abstract (ideas you feel).

Examples:

  • • Concrete: chair, river, teacher
  • • Abstract: love, courage, freedom
  • • Irregular plural: child→children, mouse→mice, tooth→teeth

2. Adjectives & Adverbs

Adjectives describe nouns. Adverbs describe verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs.

Examples:

  • • Adjective: The tall, graceful giraffe ate the tender leaves.
  • • Adverb: She sang beautifully. He ran extremely fast.

lessons.title: Vocabulary — Context & Reference
lessons.content:
Vocabulary — Context & Reference

Learning Objectives

  • • Definition: The arid, or extremely dry, desert stretched for miles.
  • • Example: She loved citrus fruits such as oranges, lemons, and grapefruits.
  • • Contrast: Unlike her timid brother, Mia was bold.
  • • Synonyms: happy / joyful / elated
  • • Antonyms: hot / cold, brave / cowardly
  • • Homophones: their / there / they're ; to / two / too
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 6

Vocabulary — Context & Reference

Use context clues, reference materials, and word relationships to determine word meanings.

Learning Objectives

Use context clues (definition, example, contrast)

Use a dictionary and thesaurus

Understand synonyms, antonyms, and homophones

Lessons

1. Types of Context Clues

Authors often provide clues within the text to help you understand difficult words.

Examples:

  • • Definition: The arid, or extremely dry, desert stretched for miles.
  • • Example: She loved citrus fruits such as oranges, lemons, and grapefruits.
  • • Contrast: Unlike her timid brother, Mia was bold.

2. Synonyms, Antonyms & Homophones

Understanding word relationships expands your vocabulary.

Examples:

  • • Synonyms: happy / joyful / elated
  • • Antonyms: hot / cold, brave / cowardly
  • • Homophones: their / there / they're ; to / two / too

lessons.title: Writing — Narrative Stories
lessons.content:
Writing — Narrative Stories

Learning Objectives

  • • Instead of: 'Mia was brave.' Try: Mia took a deep breath and stepped into the dark hallway anyway.
  • • Give your character a clear want and a clear obstacle
  • • 'I can do this,' Maya whispered to herself.
  • • 'You'll never make it in time!' shouted Raj.
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 7

Writing — Narrative Stories

Write a narrative with a well-developed character, problem, and resolution.

Learning Objectives

Develop a character with traits and feelings

Build a clear problem and resolution

Use dialogue and descriptive details

Lessons

1. Developing Your Character

Show who your character is through actions, dialogue, and feelings — not just description.

Examples:

  • • Instead of: 'Mia was brave.' Try: Mia took a deep breath and stepped into the dark hallway anyway.
  • • Give your character a clear want and a clear obstacle

2. Using Dialogue

Dialogue makes characters come alive. Use it to show personality.

Examples:

  • • 'I can do this,' Maya whispered to herself.
  • • 'You'll never make it in time!' shouted Raj.

lessons.title: Research Writing
lessons.content:
Research Writing

Learning Objectives

  • • Instead of copying: 'Cheetahs are the fastest land animals, reaching up to 75 mph.'
  • • Your note: Cheetahs — fastest land animal — up to 75 mph
  • • Paragraph 1: What cheetahs look like
  • • Paragraph 2: What they eat and how they hunt
  • • Paragraph 3: Where they live and conservation
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 8

Research Writing

Conduct a short research project using multiple sources and present findings in writing.

Learning Objectives

Gather information from two or more sources

Take notes without copying directly

Write an organized research report

Lessons

1. Note-Taking

Write ideas in your own words using bullets or key phrases.

Examples:

  • • Instead of copying: 'Cheetahs are the fastest land animals, reaching up to 75 mph.'
  • • Your note: Cheetahs — fastest land animal — up to 75 mph

2. Organizing Your Report

Group your notes by subtopic to create your paragraphs.

Examples:

  • • Paragraph 1: What cheetahs look like
  • • Paragraph 2: What they eat and how they hunt
  • • Paragraph 3: Where they live and conservation

lessons.title: Poetry & Figurative Language
lessons.content:
Poetry & Figurative Language

Learning Objectives

  • • Simile: Her smile was like sunshine.
  • • Metaphor: Her smile was sunshine.
  • • Simile: He was as quiet as a mouse.
  • • Metaphor: He was a silent ghost.
  • • The wind whispered through the trees.
  • • The stars danced in the night sky.
  • • The old car groaned and shuddered.
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 9

Poetry & Figurative Language

Read and write poetry; understand metaphor, personification, simile, and imagery.

Learning Objectives

Identify and explain simile and metaphor

Identify personification

Write a poem using at least two figurative language techniques

Lessons

1. Simile vs. Metaphor

Both compare two unlike things, but similes use 'like' or 'as'.

Examples:

  • • Simile: Her smile was like sunshine.
  • • Metaphor: Her smile was sunshine.
  • • Simile: He was as quiet as a mouse.
  • • Metaphor: He was a silent ghost.

2. Personification

Giving human qualities to non-human things.

Examples:

  • • The wind whispered through the trees.
  • • The stars danced in the night sky.
  • • The old car groaned and shuddered.

lessons.title: Speaking, Listening & Presentation
lessons.content:
Speaking, Listening & Presentation

Learning Objectives

  • • Build on others' ideas: 'I agree with what you said about… and I'd like to add…'
  • • Ask questions: 'Can you explain what you mean by…?'
  • • Speak at an appropriate pace — not too fast or too slow
  • • Use eye contact and gestures to engage your audience
  • • Include a poster, diagram, or picture to support your points
3rd Grade
📖 ELA
Module 10

Speaking, Listening & Presentation

Engage in collaborative discussions and deliver a short informational presentation.

Learning Objectives

Follow agreed-upon rules for discussion

Ask clarifying questions

Deliver a 2–3 minute presentation with visual support

Lessons

1. Collaborative Discussion

Prepare for discussions by reading the material and noting ideas.

Examples:

  • • Build on others' ideas: 'I agree with what you said about… and I'd like to add…'
  • • Ask questions: 'Can you explain what you mean by…?'

2. Delivering a Presentation

Organize your ideas and present them clearly to your audience.

Examples:

  • • Speak at an appropriate pace — not too fast or too slow
  • • Use eye contact and gestures to engage your audience
  • • Include a poster, diagram, or picture to support your points

courses.title: ELA — 4th Grade
courses.description: Reading, writing, grammar & vocabulary. Grade level: 4th Grade.

lessons.title: Reading Literature — Theme & Craft
lessons.content:
Reading Literature — Theme & Craft

Learning Objectives

  • • Theme of Hatchet: Resilience and self-reliance can help you survive any challenge.
  • • How do details about Brian's struggle support this theme?
  • • First person: I walked into the dark cave, my heart pounding.
  • • Third person limited: Brian was afraid as he entered the cave.
  • • Third person omniscient: Brian was afraid; little did he know, the cave held his greatest challenge yet.
4th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 1

Reading Literature — Theme & Craft

Analyze theme, point of view, and author's craft in complex grade-level texts.

Learning Objectives

Determine theme from key story details

Compare first- and third-person point of view

Analyze word choice and its effect on tone

Lessons

1. Theme vs. Main Idea

Theme is the big life lesson in fiction. Main idea is the key point in nonfiction.

Examples:

  • • Theme of Hatchet: Resilience and self-reliance can help you survive any challenge.
  • • How do details about Brian's struggle support this theme?

2. Point of View

Who is telling the story affects what the reader knows and feels.

Examples:

  • • First person: I walked into the dark cave, my heart pounding.
  • • Third person limited: Brian was afraid as he entered the cave.
  • • Third person omniscient: Brian was afraid; little did he know, the cave held his greatest challenge yet.

lessons.title: Writing — Opinion Essays
lessons.content:
Writing — Opinion Essays

Learning Objectives

  • • Some people believe school starts too early. While they argue students need more sleep, research shows that structured schedules improve academic performance.
  • • According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, children need 9–11 hours of sleep.
  • • In a survey of 500 students, 78% said they felt more focused after recess.
4th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 3

Writing — Opinion Essays

Write a multi-paragraph opinion essay with a strong claim, organized reasons, and evidence.

Learning Objectives

Write a compelling opinion with clear claim

Organize reasons logically with evidence

Address a counterargument

Write a strong concluding paragraph

Lessons

1. Acknowledging the Counterargument

A strong opinion writer considers opposing views and explains why their position is still stronger.

Examples:

  • • Some people believe school starts too early. While they argue students need more sleep, research shows that structured schedules improve academic performance.

2. Evidence

Back up each reason with a fact, statistic, example, or quote.

Examples:

  • • According to the American Academy of Pediatrics, children need 9–11 hours of sleep.
  • • In a survey of 500 students, 78% said they felt more focused after recess.

lessons.title: Writing — Informational Reports
lessons.content:
Writing — Informational Reports

  • • Science: ecosystem, photosynthesis, organism

Use domain-specific vocabulary

Include text features: headings, captions, glossary

Synthesize information from multiple sources

Use precise, technical words that belong to your topic.

Examples:

Text features make informational writing easier to navigate and understand.

lessons.title: Writing — Narrative with Craft
lessons.content:
Writing — Narrative with Craft

Learning Objectives

  • • TELL: Lily was nervous.
  • • SHOW: Lily's hands wouldn't stop shaking. She read the sentence three times and still couldn't make sense of it.
  • • Sight: The sky burned orange and pink as the sun dipped below the mountains.
  • • Sound: The floorboards groaned beneath her feet.
  • • Smell: The sharp smell of pine needles filled the air.
4th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 5

Writing — Narrative with Craft

Write a polished narrative using advanced craft techniques.

Learning Objectives

Use show-don't-tell to develop character emotion

Vary sentence structure for effect

Use precise language and sensory details

Lessons

1. Show Don't Tell

Instead of telling the reader how a character feels, show it through actions, thoughts, and sensory details.

Examples:

  • • TELL: Lily was nervous.
  • • SHOW: Lily's hands wouldn't stop shaking. She read the sentence three times and still couldn't make sense of it.

2. Sensory Details

Use all five senses to bring your writing to life.

Examples:

  • • Sight: The sky burned orange and pink as the sun dipped below the mountains.
  • • Sound: The floorboards groaned beneath her feet.
  • • Smell: The sharp smell of pine needles filled the air.

lessons.title: Grammar — Advanced Sentence Structure
lessons.content:
Grammar — Advanced Sentence Structure

Learning Objectives

  • • Although she was tired, she finished her homework.
  • • Because the storm was coming, we went inside.
  • • After the game ended, they celebrated.
  • • The book that I borrowed was fascinating.
  • • My neighbor, who is a firefighter, rescued the cat.
  • • The river, which runs through the town, flooded last spring.
4th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 6

Grammar — Advanced Sentence Structure

Write complex sentences using conjunctions, relative clauses, and correct mechanics.

Learning Objectives

Use coordinating and subordinating conjunctions

Form and use relative clauses

Use commas with conjunctions and introductory phrases

Lessons

1. Subordinating Conjunctions

Use these words to connect a dependent clause to an independent clause.

Examples:

  • • Although she was tired, she finished her homework.
  • • Because the storm was coming, we went inside.
  • • After the game ended, they celebrated.

2. Relative Clauses

A relative clause adds detail about a noun using who, which, or that.

Examples:

  • • The book that I borrowed was fascinating.
  • • My neighbor, who is a firefighter, rescued the cat.
  • • The river, which runs through the town, flooded last spring.

lessons.title: Vocabulary — Greek & Latin Roots
lessons.content:
Vocabulary — Greek & Latin Roots

Examples:

Examples:

  • • scrib/script = write: describe, manuscript, prescribe

lessons.title: Figurative Language & Word Choice
lessons.content:
Figurative Language & Word Choice

Learning Objectives

  • • Hyperbole: I've told you a million times!
  • • Hyperbole: My backpack weighs a ton.
  • • Idiom: Break a leg! (Good luck!)
  • • Idiom: It's raining cats and dogs. (It's raining very hard.)
  • • He faced his Goliath moment when he stepped onto the field for the first time.
  • • She was a modern-day Cinderella — hardworking, kind, and overlooked.
4th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 8

Figurative Language & Word Choice

Identify and use advanced figurative language — hyperbole, idiom, metaphor, allusion.

Learning Objectives

Identify and explain hyperbole

Understand common idioms

Recognize allusion in literature

Lessons

1. Hyperbole & Idiom

Hyperbole is a huge exaggeration. An idiom is a phrase with a non-literal meaning.

Examples:

  • • Hyperbole: I've told you a million times!
  • • Hyperbole: My backpack weighs a ton.
  • • Idiom: Break a leg! (Good luck!)
  • • Idiom: It's raining cats and dogs. (It's raining very hard.)

2. Allusion

An allusion is a reference to a well-known person, place, event, or text.

Examples:

  • • He faced his Goliath moment when he stepped onto the field for the first time.
  • • She was a modern-day Cinderella — hardworking, kind, and overlooked.

lessons.title: Research & Synthesis
lessons.content:
Research & Synthesis

Learning Objectives

  • • Reliable: encyclopedias, educational websites (.edu, .gov), published books
  • • Less reliable: random blogs, social media posts, anonymous websites
  • • Original: Sharks have been on Earth for more than 400 million years.
  • • Paraphrase: Sharks are ancient animals that have existed for over 400 million years. (Source: Ocean Encyclopedia, p. 45)
4th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 9

Research & Synthesis

Conduct an extended research project, synthesizing information from multiple sources.

Learning Objectives

Identify credible sources

Synthesize information across texts

Avoid plagiarism by paraphrasing and citing sources

Lessons

1. Evaluating Sources

Not all sources are equally reliable. Look for accuracy, authority, and currency.

Examples:

  • • Reliable: encyclopedias, educational websites (.edu, .gov), published books
  • • Less reliable: random blogs, social media posts, anonymous websites

2. Paraphrasing & Citing

Paraphrase by restating information in your own words, then note where it came from.

Examples:

  • • Original: Sharks have been on Earth for more than 400 million years.
  • • Paraphrase: Sharks are ancient animals that have existed for over 400 million years. (Source: Ocean Encyclopedia, p. 45)

lessons.title: Speaking, Listening & Debate
lessons.content:
Speaking, Listening & Debate

Learning Objectives

  • • 'I agree with ___ because…'
  • • 'I respectfully disagree because the evidence shows…'
  • • 'Can you clarify what you mean by…?'
  • • 'Building on what ___ said, I think…'
  • • Structure: Hook → Claim → 3 Reasons with Evidence → Address Counterargument → Call to Action
  • • Use a strong voice, eye contact, and visual aids to persuade your audience
4th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 10

Speaking, Listening & Debate

Engage in structured academic discussions and deliver persuasive presentations.

Learning Objectives

Engage in academic discussion using evidence

Build on and question others' ideas

Deliver a persuasive presentation with clear structure

Lessons

1. Structured Academic Discussion

Use sentence starters to engage thoughtfully with classmates' ideas.

Examples:

  • • 'I agree with ___ because…'
  • • 'I respectfully disagree because the evidence shows…'
  • • 'Can you clarify what you mean by…?'
  • • 'Building on what ___ said, I think…'

2. Persuasive Presentation

Organize your argument clearly and deliver it with confidence.

Examples:

  • • Structure: Hook → Claim → 3 Reasons with Evidence → Address Counterargument → Call to Action
  • • Use a strong voice, eye contact, and visual aids to persuade your audience

lessons.title: Reading Literature — Theme and Summary
lessons.content:
Reading Literature — Theme and Summary

Learning Objectives

  • • Topic: friendship. Theme: True friends support each other even when it's hard.
  • • Look for what the main character learns or how they change
  • • Include: main character, conflict, key events, resolution
  • • Exclude: minor details, personal reactions
5th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 1

Reading Literature — Theme and Summary

Determine themes and summarize literary texts.

Learning Objectives

Determine theme from details

Summarize without personal opinion

Compare themes across texts

Lessons

1. Finding Theme

Theme is the central message the author wants to convey; it is not the topic.

Examples:

  • • Topic: friendship. Theme: True friends support each other even when it's hard.
  • • Look for what the main character learns or how they change

2. Summarizing

A summary captures the most important events without retelling every detail.

Examples:

  • • Include: main character, conflict, key events, resolution
  • • Exclude: minor details, personal reactions

lessons.title: Reading Informational Text — Main Idea
lessons.content:
Reading Informational Text — Main Idea

Reading Informational Text — Main Idea

Identify main idea of a passage

Explain how details support the main idea

Summarize informational text
