1. Main Idea vs. Topic

The topic is the subject; the main idea is the author's point about it.

Examples:

  • • Topic: volcanoes. Main idea: Volcanic eruptions are destructive but also create new land.
  • • Ask: What does the author want me to understand?

2. Supporting Details

Details provide evidence, examples, or explanations for the main idea.

Examples:

  • • Quote relevant sentences that directly support the main idea
  • • Distinguish relevant details from interesting but tangential information

Authors organize informational text in specific patterns.

Respond to others' ideas respectfully

Analyzing Literary Texts

lessons.title: Argument and Evidence
lessons.content:
Argument and Evidence

Identify claims, reasons, and evidence

Distinguish facts from opinions

lessons.title: Vocabulary in Context

  • • 'She was obstinate — no matter what we said, she refused to change' → obstinate = stubborn

Use context clues to infer word meaning

Recognize denotation vs. connotation

Understand word relationships (synonyms, antonyms, analogies)

1. Context Clues

Words and sentences surrounding an unknown word can help you infer its meaning.

Examples:

2. Connotation

Words have literal meanings (denotation) and emotional associations (connotation).

Examples:

  • • Slender (positive) vs. scrawny (negative) — both mean thin

lessons.title: Informational Writing — Research Essay

Module 7

Reading Poetry — Analyzing Sound and Meaning

Analyze how sound devices and structure contribute to a poem's meaning.

Learning Objectives

Identify alliteration, assonance, consonance

Analyze the effect of rhyme and rhythm

Interpret the meaning of a poem

Lessons

1. Sound Devices

Poets use sound to create mood and reinforce meaning.

Examples:

  • • Alliteration: 'Peter Piper picked a peck of pickled peppers'
  • • Assonance: 'The rain in Spain stays mainly in the plain' (long 'a' sounds)
  • • Consonance: 'the luck of the duck in the muck'

2. Close Reading of Poetry

Read a poem multiple times; each reading reveals more.

Examples:

  • • First read: overall impression
  • • Second read: identify structure, rhyme, sound devices
  • • Third read: connect structure to meaning

lessons.title: Media Literacy
lessons.content:
Media Literacy

Learning Objectives

  • • News article: inform (ideally objective)
  • • Advertisement: persuade and sell
  • • Satirical news: entertain while commenting on current events
  • • Stop before sharing — check if it's credible
  • • Investigate the source: who created it and why?
  • • Find other sources covering the same story
  • • Trace quotes to originals to check context
6th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 8

Media Literacy

Analyze how media presents information and shapes perception.

Learning Objectives

Identify purpose and audience of media

Recognize bias and persuasive techniques

Evaluate credibility of online sources

Lessons

1. Media Purpose

Every media message has a purpose: inform, persuade, entertain, or sell.

Examples:

  • • News article: inform (ideally objective)
  • • Advertisement: persuade and sell
  • • Satirical news: entertain while commenting on current events

2. Evaluating Sources — SIFT

SIFT method: Stop, Investigate, Find better coverage, Trace claims.

Examples:

  • • Stop before sharing — check if it's credible
  • • Investigate the source: who created it and why?
  • • Find other sources covering the same story
  • • Trace quotes to originals to check context

lessons.title: Shakespeare Introduction
lessons.content:
Shakespeare Introduction

Learning Objectives

  • • Born in Stratford-upon-Avon, 1564; died 1616
  • • Wrote 37 plays and 154 sonnets
  • • The Globe Theatre: outdoor amphitheater; audiences stood or sat around the stage
  • • 'Thou' = you (informal), 'thee' = you (object)
  • • 'Dost' = do/does: 'What dost thou think?' = 'What do you think?'
  • • Read for meaning first, then worry about every word
6th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 9

Shakespeare Introduction

Introduction to Shakespeare's language, themes, and historical context.

Learning Objectives

Understand basic facts about Shakespeare and his era

Read and interpret Elizabethan language

Analyze a scene for character and theme

Lessons

1. Shakespeare's World

Shakespeare wrote in Elizabethan England during a cultural golden age.

Examples:

  • • Born in Stratford-upon-Avon, 1564; died 1616
  • • Wrote 37 plays and 154 sonnets
  • • The Globe Theatre: outdoor amphitheater; audiences stood or sat around the stage

2. Reading Shakespeare

Break down thee/thou/dost language; use the context to infer meaning.

Examples:

  • • 'Thou' = you (informal), 'thee' = you (object)
  • • 'Dost' = do/does: 'What dost thou think?' = 'What do you think?'
  • • Read for meaning first, then worry about every word

lessons.title: Speaking and Listening — Presentations
lessons.content:
Speaking and Listening — Presentations

Learning Objectives

  • • Opening hook: striking statistic, question, or story
  • • Each slide should have one main idea with minimal text
  • • End with a memorable takeaway or call to action
  • • Maintain eye contact with the audience (not the screen)
  • • Vary pace and volume for emphasis
  • • Practice enough times that you don't need to read from notes
6th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 10

Speaking and Listening — Presentations

Plan and deliver an organized oral presentation with visual support.

Learning Objectives

Organize a presentation with a clear structure

Use evidence and visual aids effectively

Practice effective speaking techniques

Lessons

1. Organizing a Presentation

Structure: hook → main points (2-3) → conclusion. Each point needs evidence.

Examples:

  • • Opening hook: striking statistic, question, or story
  • • Each slide should have one main idea with minimal text
  • • End with a memorable takeaway or call to action

2. Delivery Techniques

How you say it matters as much as what you say.

Examples:

  • • Maintain eye contact with the audience (not the screen)
  • • Vary pace and volume for emphasis
  • • Practice enough times that you don't need to read from notes

courses.title: ELA — 7th Grade
courses.description: Reading, writing, grammar & vocabulary. Grade level: 7th Grade.

lessons.title: Literary Analysis — Craft and Structure
lessons.content:
Literary Analysis — Craft and Structure

Learning Objectives

  • • Foreshadowing: early hints that create suspense ('Little did she know that...')
  • • Flashback: moves back in time to reveal background
  • • Unreliable narrator: the narrator's perspective is limited or distorted
  • • The Outsiders: themes of class conflict, loyalty, and identity all intersect
  • • One event can develop multiple themes simultaneously
7th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 1

Literary Analysis — Craft and Structure

Analyze how authors develop plot, character, and theme through craft choices.

Learning Objectives

Analyze plot structure with precision

Explain how an author's word choices shape meaning

Evaluate how multiple themes interact

Lessons

1. Analyzing Author's Craft

Every word choice, structural decision, and narrative technique is intentional.

Examples:

  • • Foreshadowing: early hints that create suspense ('Little did she know that...')
  • • Flashback: moves back in time to reveal background
  • • Unreliable narrator: the narrator's perspective is limited or distorted

2. Multiple Themes

Complex literary works often have several interrelated themes.

Examples:

  • • The Outsiders: themes of class conflict, loyalty, and identity all intersect
  • • One event can develop multiple themes simultaneously

lessons.title: Argumentative Writing
lessons.content:
Argumentative Writing

Learning Objectives

  • • Weak: 'Homework has pros and cons'
  • • Strong: 'Nightly homework should be eliminated for middle schoolers because it increases stress, reduces family time, and fails to improve academic achievement'
  • • 'Some argue that homework builds responsibility; however, research indicates that self-directed reading is more effective for developing independent learners'
7th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 2

Argumentative Writing

Plan and write a formal argumentative essay with claim, evidence, and counterargument.

Learning Objectives

Write a debatable thesis/claim

Use relevant evidence from credible sources

Effectively address counterarguments

Lessons

1. Thesis and Structure

A strong thesis is specific, debatable, and previews main reasons.

Examples:

  • • Weak: 'Homework has pros and cons'
  • • Strong: 'Nightly homework should be eliminated for middle schoolers because it increases stress, reduces family time, and fails to improve academic achievement'

2. Counterargument and Rebuttal

Acknowledge opposing views, then refute them with evidence.

Examples:

  • • 'Some argue that homework builds responsibility; however, research indicates that self-directed reading is more effective for developing independent learners'

lessons.title: Reading Nonfiction — Rhetorical Analysis
lessons.content:
Reading Nonfiction — Rhetorical Analysis

Learning Objectives

  • • Ethos: 'As a doctor with 20 years of experience...' (credibility)
  • • Pathos: a story about a child suffering from pollution (emotion)
  • • Logos: statistics showing 80% of scientists agree on climate change (logic)
  • • 'Militants' vs. 'freedom fighters' — same people, very different connotation
  • • Formal, objective language builds credibility; passionate language builds emotion
7th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 3

Reading Nonfiction — Rhetorical Analysis

Analyze the rhetorical strategies authors use to persuade in nonfiction texts.

Learning Objectives

Identify ethos, pathos, and logos

Analyze how word choice and structure support the argument

Evaluate the effectiveness of persuasion

Lessons

1. Rhetorical Appeals

Persuasive writers appeal to credibility, emotion, and logic.

Examples:

  • • Ethos: 'As a doctor with 20 years of experience...' (credibility)
  • • Pathos: a story about a child suffering from pollution (emotion)
  • • Logos: statistics showing 80% of scientists agree on climate change (logic)

2. Analyzing Language

Word choice (diction) and tone shape how readers feel about the argument.

Examples:

  • • 'Militants' vs. 'freedom fighters' — same people, very different connotation
  • • Formal, objective language builds credibility; passionate language builds emotion

lessons.title: Grammar — Phrases and Clauses
lessons.content:
Grammar — Phrases and Clauses

Learning Objectives

  • • Prepositional phrase: 'under the old bridge'
  • • Participial phrase: 'Running through the rain, she finally reached home'
  • • Infinitive phrase: 'To win the championship was her goal'
  • • Simple: 'She ran.'
  • • Compound: 'She ran, but she was too late.'
  • • Complex: 'Although she ran as fast as she could, she missed the train.'
7th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 4

Grammar — Phrases and Clauses

Identify and correctly use phrases and clauses to add variety and precision.

Learning Objectives

Identify noun, verb, adjective, and adverb phrases

Use participial and infinitive phrases

Write sentences with varied clause structures

Lessons

1. Phrases

A phrase lacks a subject-verb pair and cannot stand alone.

Examples:

  • • Prepositional phrase: 'under the old bridge'
  • • Participial phrase: 'Running through the rain, she finally reached home'
  • • Infinitive phrase: 'To win the championship was her goal'

2. Varied Sentence Structure

Varying sentences keeps writing engaging.

Examples:

  • • Simple: 'She ran.'
  • • Compound: 'She ran, but she was too late.'
  • • Complex: 'Although she ran as fast as she could, she missed the train.'

lessons.title: Research — Synthesis Writing
lessons.content:
Research — Synthesis Writing

Learning Objectives

  • • Summary: 'Source A says X. Source B says Y.'
  • • Synthesis: 'Multiple experts agree that X (Source A; Source B), while Source C offers the counterpoint that Y'
7th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 5

Research — Synthesis Writing

Synthesize information from multiple sources into a coherent research essay.

Learning Objectives

Integrate evidence from 4+ sources

Write without plagiarism; cite correctly

Synthesize rather than simply summarize sources

Lessons

1. Synthesis vs. Summary

Synthesis weaves ideas from multiple sources together around YOUR argument.

Examples:

  • • Summary: 'Source A says X. Source B says Y.'
  • • Synthesis: 'Multiple experts agree that X (Source A; Source B), while Source C offers the counterpoint that Y'

lessons.title: Reading Across Genres — Comparing Texts
lessons.content:
Reading Across Genres — Comparing Texts

Learning Objectives

  • • Topic: war. Compare: a war poem (Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est'), a novel excerpt (All Quiet on the Western Front), a news article
  • • Each form uses different techniques to create impact
7th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 6

Reading Across Genres — Comparing Texts

Compare how different genres handle the same topic or theme.

Learning Objectives

Compare a poem, story, and nonfiction text on the same theme

Analyze what each genre can and cannot do

Evaluate which treatment is most effective

Lessons

1. Genre Comparison

The same subject can be explored through different lenses.

Examples:

  • • Topic: war. Compare: a war poem (Owen's 'Dulce et Decorum Est'), a novel excerpt (All Quiet on the Western Front), a news article
  • • Each form uses different techniques to create impact

lessons.title: Vocabulary — Academic Language

Vocabulary — Academic Language

Learning Objectives

Build academic vocabulary for reading, writing, and discussion across subjects.

Use context and morphology to infer meaning

Apply academic vocabulary in writing

Academic words appear across subjects and in formal writing.

lessons.title: Drama — Reading and Performance
lessons.content:
Drama — Reading and Performance

Learning Objectives

  • • Stage directions give clues about setting, mood, and character
  • • Subtext: what characters mean beyond what they literally say
  • • Cast plays strategically when reading aloud in class
  • • Some dialogue is cut in films; scenes may be added
  • • Consider: what can film do that a stage cannot? What can a stage do that film cannot?

📖 ELA
Module 8

Drama — Reading and Performance

Read, analyze, and perform dramatic texts.

Learning Objectives

Analyze dialogue and stage directions

Compare a dramatic text to its film adaptation

Perform a scene with attention to character and tone

Lessons

1. Reading Drama

Drama is meant to be performed; read with performance in mind.

Examples:

  • • Stage directions give clues about setting, mood, and character
  • • Subtext: what characters mean beyond what they literally say
  • • Cast plays strategically when reading aloud in class

2. Adaptation Analysis

Compare a play to its film adaptation — what changes and why?

Examples:

  • • Some dialogue is cut in films; scenes may be added
  • • Consider: what can film do that a stage cannot? What can a stage do that film cannot?

lessons.title: Personal Narrative
lessons.content:
Personal Narrative

Learning Objectives

  • • Start in the middle of action (in medias res)
  • • Use sensory details: sight, sound, smell, taste, touch
  • • 'I remember the exact smell of rain on hot pavement that afternoon...'
  • • Move beyond description to meaning: 'That moment taught me...'
  • • Connect the personal to the universal: how does your experience relate to larger human experiences?
7th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 9

Personal Narrative

Write a personal narrative that conveys a meaningful experience with reflection.

Learning Objectives

Choose a meaningful event

Use literary techniques in personal writing

Reflect on significance — not just what happened but why it mattered

Lessons

1. Crafting the Narrative

Great personal narratives use literary techniques to create meaning.

Examples:

  • • Start in the middle of action (in medias res)
  • • Use sensory details: sight, sound, smell, taste, touch
  • • 'I remember the exact smell of rain on hot pavement that afternoon...'

2. Reflection

The reflection is the most important part — it shows what you learned or how you changed.

Examples:

  • • Move beyond description to meaning: 'That moment taught me...'
  • • Connect the personal to the universal: how does your experience relate to larger human experiences?

lessons.title: Independent Reading and Book Clubs
lessons.content:
Independent Reading and Book Clubs

Learning Objectives

  • • Personal: 'This character reminded me of...because...'
  • • Analytical: 'The author uses foreshadowing in chapter 3 when...'
  • • Evaluative: 'I think the ending was unsatisfying because...'
  • • Ask genuine questions you don't know the answer to
  • • 'I was confused by... Can anyone explain...?'
  • • 'What I found most interesting was... Does anyone disagree?'
7th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 10

Independent Reading and Book Clubs

Develop as independent readers through choice reading and collaborative discussion.

Learning Objectives

Read independently for sustained periods

Discuss books in a small-group book club format

Write reader's response and book review

Lessons

1. Reader's Response

Respond personally and analytically to what you read.

Examples:

  • • Personal: 'This character reminded me of...because...'
  • • Analytical: 'The author uses foreshadowing in chapter 3 when...'
  • • Evaluative: 'I think the ending was unsatisfying because...'

2. Book Club Discussion

Book clubs thrive on genuine questions and diverse perspectives.

Examples:

  • • Ask genuine questions you don't know the answer to
  • • 'I was confused by... Can anyone explain...?'
  • • 'What I found most interesting was... Does anyone disagree?'

courses.title: ELA — 8th Grade
courses.description: Reading, writing, grammar & vocabulary. Grade level: 8th Grade.

lessons.title: Reading Complex Texts
lessons.content:
Reading Complex Texts

Learning Objectives

  • • Annotate as you read: underline key passages, circle unfamiliar words, mark patterns
  • • First read: what happens? Second read: how is it written? Third read: what does it mean?
  • • Find the 'moments of friction' — places where the text surprises or confuses you
  • • Strong: 'Holden Caulfield's repeated use of the word 'phony' reveals his disillusionment with adult society (Salinger, 2)','Weak: 'The character seems unhappy'
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 1

Reading Complex Texts

Read and analyze complex literary and informational texts with close reading strategies.

Learning Objectives

Apply close reading strategies

Analyze complex syntax and diction

Draw inferences supported by textual evidence

Lessons

1. Close Reading

Close reading involves careful, repeated analysis of how a text creates meaning.

Examples:

  • • Annotate as you read: underline key passages, circle unfamiliar words, mark patterns
  • • First read: what happens? Second read: how is it written? Third read: what does it mean?
  • • Find the 'moments of friction' — places where the text surprises or confuses you

2. Textual Evidence

All claims about a text must be supported with specific evidence.

Examples:

  • • Strong: 'Holden Caulfield's repeated use of the word 'phony' reveals his disillusionment with adult society (Salinger, 2)','Weak: 'The character seems unhappy'

lessons.title: Literary Analysis Essay
lessons.content:
Literary Analysis Essay

Learning Objectives

  • • Weak: 'In Lord of the Flies, the boys become savage'
  • • Strong: 'Golding uses the conch shell as a symbol of democratic order to show how quickly civilization collapses when authority is no longer enforced by force'
  • • Introduce: 'Golding emphasizes this collapse when...'
  • • Cite: '...the conch shattered into a thousand white fragments' (181)
  • • Explain: 'The physical destruction of the conch symbolizes the final dissolution of democratic order on the island'
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 2

Literary Analysis Essay

Write a formal literary analysis essay with a thesis, textual evidence, and analysis.

Learning Objectives

Write a sophisticated, arguable thesis

Integrate quotations smoothly (ICE: introduce, cite, explain)

Develop analysis beyond plot summary

Lessons

1. The Literary Analysis Thesis

A literary analysis thesis makes a specific, arguable claim about how a text works.

Examples:

  • • Weak: 'In Lord of the Flies, the boys become savage'
  • • Strong: 'Golding uses the conch shell as a symbol of democratic order to show how quickly civilization collapses when authority is no longer enforced by force'

2. ICE — Integrate Evidence

Quote integration: Introduce the quote, Cite it, then Explain its significance.

Examples:

  • • Introduce: 'Golding emphasizes this collapse when...'
  • • Cite: '...the conch shattered into a thousand white fragments' (181)
  • • Explain: 'The physical destruction of the conch symbolizes the final dissolution of democratic order on the island'

lessons.title: Informational Reading — Multiple Perspectives
lessons.content:
Informational Reading — Multiple Perspectives

Learning Objectives

  • • Two historians may interpret the same event differently based on their sources
  • • Identify: What evidence does each author use? What are their assumptions?
  • • Neither text need be 'wrong' — complexity is normal in real inquiry
  • • Check: Who funded this study?
  • • Are counterarguments addressed honestly?
  • • Does the author have relevant expertise?
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 3

Informational Reading — Multiple Perspectives

Analyze how different authors treat the same topic; evaluate conflicting evidence.

Learning Objectives

Compare accounts with different perspectives

Evaluate credibility and bias

Synthesize conflicting information

Lessons

1. Multiple Perspectives

On any complex topic, credible sources may reach different conclusions.

Examples:

  • • Two historians may interpret the same event differently based on their sources
  • • Identify: What evidence does each author use? What are their assumptions?
  • • Neither text need be 'wrong' — complexity is normal in real inquiry

2. Evaluating Bias

All texts have a perspective; bias isn't always intentional.

Examples:

  • • Check: Who funded this study?
  • • Are counterarguments addressed honestly?
  • • Does the author have relevant expertise?

lessons.title: Research — Extended Project
lessons.content:
Research — Extended Project

Learning Objectives

  • • Too broad: 'Is climate change real?'
  • • Too narrow: 'What is the average temperature in Phoenix in July 2019?'
  • • Just right: 'How has climate change affected wildfire frequency in California over the past 30 years?'
  • • Summary: What does this source argue or show?
  • • Evaluation: How credible is it? What is its potential bias?
  • • Usefulness: How does it relate to your research question?
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 4

Research — Extended Project

Complete an extended research project with annotated bibliography and formal paper.

Learning Objectives

Develop an original research question

Create an annotated bibliography

Write a well-organized research paper with proper MLA citations

Lessons

1. The Research Question

A great research question is specific, debatable, and researchable.

Examples:

  • • Too broad: 'Is climate change real?'
  • • Too narrow: 'What is the average temperature in Phoenix in July 2019?'
  • • Just right: 'How has climate change affected wildfire frequency in California over the past 30 years?'

2. Annotated Bibliography

Each source gets a citation plus a paragraph summarizing and evaluating it.

Examples:

  • • Summary: What does this source argue or show?
  • • Evaluation: How credible is it? What is its potential bias?
  • • Usefulness: How does it relate to your research question?

lessons.title: Grammar — Advanced Usage and Style
lessons.content:
Grammar — Advanced Usage and Style

Learning Objectives

  • • Passive: 'The ball was kicked by John.'
  • • Active: 'John kicked the ball.' (clearer, more direct)
  • • Appropriate passive: 'Mistakes were made' (when actor is unknown or irrelevant)
  • • Wrong: 'She liked reading, to swim, and dances'
  • • Correct: 'She liked reading, swimming, and dancing'
  • • Wrong: 'He is talented, hardworking, and has a lot of patience'
  • • Correct: 'He is talented, hardworking, and patient'
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 5

Grammar — Advanced Usage and Style

Master advanced grammar for precise, effective writing.

Learning Objectives

Use active vs. passive voice appropriately

Avoid common errors: dangling modifiers, faulty parallelism

Vary sentence structure for rhetorical effect

Lessons

1. Active vs. Passive Voice

Active voice is direct and clear; passive has its uses but can obscure meaning.

Examples:

  • • Passive: 'The ball was kicked by John.'
  • • Active: 'John kicked the ball.' (clearer, more direct)
  • • Appropriate passive: 'Mistakes were made' (when actor is unknown or irrelevant)

2. Parallel Structure

Items in a series must have the same grammatical form.

Examples:

  • • Wrong: 'She liked reading, to swim, and dances'
  • • Correct: 'She liked reading, swimming, and dancing'
  • • Wrong: 'He is talented, hardworking, and has a lot of patience'
  • • Correct: 'He is talented, hardworking, and patient'

lessons.title: Dystopian Literature
lessons.content:
Dystopian Literature

Learning Objectives

  • • Total government control (1984, The Giver)
  • • Loss of individual freedom, enforced conformity
  • • Technology used to oppress (surveillance, propaganda)
  • • Often features a protagonist who begins to question the system
  • • 1984 (1949): critiques Stalinist totalitarianism and surveillance
  • • The Hunger Games: critiques media exploitation and wealth inequality
  • • Handmaid's Tale: critiques patriarchy and religious extremism
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 6

Dystopian Literature

Analyze the dystopian genre through major works and the social critiques they encode.

Learning Objectives

Define dystopian fiction and its conventions

Analyze how dystopias critique real societies

Compare two dystopian texts

Lessons

1. Dystopia Conventions

Dystopian fiction presents a nightmarish future society to critique present trends.

Examples:

  • • Total government control (1984, The Giver)
  • • Loss of individual freedom, enforced conformity
  • • Technology used to oppress (surveillance, propaganda)
  • • Often features a protagonist who begins to question the system

2. Social Critique

Dystopias always comment on real fears and tendencies in contemporary society.

Examples:

  • • 1984 (1949): critiques Stalinist totalitarianism and surveillance
  • • The Hunger Games: critiques media exploitation and wealth inequality
  • • Handmaid's Tale: critiques patriarchy and religious extremism

lessons.title: Speeches and Rhetoric
lessons.content:
Speeches and Rhetoric

Learning Objectives

  • • MLK's 'I Have a Dream': anaphora ('I have a dream that...'), vivid metaphor, emotional appeal
  • • Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: parallel structure, elevated diction, emotional pathos
  • • Malala's UN Speech: ethos (personal experience), logos (statistics), pathos (urgency)
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 7

Speeches and Rhetoric

Analyze great speeches for rhetorical strategies and craft; write and deliver a speech.

Learning Objectives

Analyze rhetorical strategies in historic speeches

Write a persuasive speech with ethos, pathos, logos

Deliver a speech with effective techniques

Lessons

1. Analyzing Great Speeches

Great speeches combine rhetorical appeals with powerful language.

Examples:

  • • MLK's 'I Have a Dream': anaphora ('I have a dream that...'), vivid metaphor, emotional appeal
  • • Lincoln's Gettysburg Address: parallel structure, elevated diction, emotional pathos
  • • Malala's UN Speech: ethos (personal experience), logos (statistics), pathos (urgency)

lessons.title: Vocabulary — Figurative and Connotative Language
lessons.content:
Vocabulary — Figurative and Connotative Language

Learning Objectives

  • • 'Hope is the thing with feathers' (Emily Dickinson) — hope is compared to a bird throughout
  • • 'All the world's a stage' (Shakespeare) — people as actors, life as a play
  • • The green light in Gatsby: the American Dream, unattainable hope
  • • The conch in Lord of the Flies: democratic order and civilization
  • • The mockingbird in To Kill a Mockingbird: innocence destroyed by evil
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 8

Vocabulary — Figurative and Connotative Language

Analyze how figurative and connotative language shapes meaning and tone.

Learning Objectives

Analyze extended metaphors

Interpret symbolism in literary texts

Evaluate how word choice creates tone

Lessons

1. Extended Metaphors

A metaphor sustained across a text creates layered meaning.

Examples:

  • • 'Hope is the thing with feathers' (Emily Dickinson) — hope is compared to a bird throughout
  • • 'All the world's a stage' (Shakespeare) — people as actors, life as a play

2. Symbolism

Symbols are objects, characters, or events that represent larger ideas.

Examples:

  • • The green light in Gatsby: the American Dream, unattainable hope
  • • The conch in Lord of the Flies: democratic order and civilization
  • • The mockingbird in To Kill a Mockingbird: innocence destroyed by evil

lessons.title: Multimedia and Digital Literacy
lessons.content:
Multimedia and Digital Literacy

Learning Objectives

  • • A documentary uses interview, narration, b-roll footage, and music together
  • • Websites layer text, images, hyperlinks, and interactive elements
  • • Analyze each element: What does the image add that words don't? How does music shape emotional response?
  • • Understand copyright: you can't use others' images/music without permission
  • • Cite digital sources; use Creative Commons-licensed images
  • • Think before posting: digital footprints are permanent
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 9

Multimedia and Digital Literacy

Create and analyze multimodal texts; evaluate digital information critically.

Learning Objectives

Analyze how visuals and text work together

Create a multimedia presentation or documentary

Evaluate digital sources using advanced criteria

Lessons

1. Multimodal Texts

Modern communication combines words, images, sound, and video.

Examples:

  • • A documentary uses interview, narration, b-roll footage, and music together
  • • Websites layer text, images, hyperlinks, and interactive elements
  • • Analyze each element: What does the image add that words don't? How does music shape emotional response?

2. Digital Citizenship

Responsible digital citizenship includes creating and sharing responsibly.

Examples:

  • • Understand copyright: you can't use others' images/music without permission
  • • Cite digital sources; use Creative Commons-licensed images
  • • Think before posting: digital footprints are permanent

lessons.title: Independent Reading and Reflection
lessons.content:
Independent Reading and Reflection

Learning Objectives

  • • Choose books that push you: unfamiliar settings, complex characters, challenging ideas
  • • A little struggle is productive — if you understand every sentence immediately, the book may not be challenging enough
  • • How did reading this book change how you see the world?
  • • What question did it leave you with?
  • • Connect ideas from the book to other texts, courses, or your own experience
8th Grade
📖 ELA
Module 10

Independent Reading and Reflection

Synthesize learning through sustained independent reading and reflective writing.

Learning Objectives

Read a self-selected challenging text

Write a reflective reader's essay

Connect reading to personal growth and worldview

Lessons

1. Choosing Challenging Texts

Reading above your comfort level builds skills and expands worldview.

Examples:

  • • Choose books that push you: unfamiliar settings, complex characters, challenging ideas
  • • A little struggle is productive — if you understand every sentence immediately, the book may not be challenging enough

2. Reflective Reading Essay

A reflective essay connects the text to your own thinking and growth.

Examples:

  • • How did reading this book change how you see the world?
  • • What question did it leave you with?
  • • Connect ideas from the book to other texts, courses, or your own experience

courses.title: Science — Kindergarten
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: Kindergarten.

lessons.title: My Five Senses
lessons.content:
My Five Senses

Learning Objectives

  • • Sight — eyes: We see colors, shapes, and sizes
  • • Hearing — ears: We hear loud, soft, high, and low sounds
  • • Smell — nose: We smell flowers, food, and rain
  • • Touch — skin: rough, smooth, bumpy, hot, cold
  • • Taste — tongue: sweet, salty, sour, bitter
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 1

My Five Senses

Explore the world using sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch.

Learning Objectives

Name and describe the five senses

Identify the body part used for each sense

Observe objects using multiple senses

Lessons

1. What Are the Senses?

We use our five senses to learn about the world around us.

Examples:

  • • Sight — eyes: We see colors, shapes, and sizes
  • • Hearing — ears: We hear loud, soft, high, and low sounds
  • • Smell — nose: We smell flowers, food, and rain

2. Touch and Taste

Touch and taste give us even more information.

Examples:

  • • Touch — skin: rough, smooth, bumpy, hot, cold
  • • Taste — tongue: sweet, salty, sour, bitter

lessons.title: Living and Non-Living Things
lessons.content:
Living and Non-Living Things

Learning Objectives

  • • Living: plants, animals, people, insects
  • • Non-living: rocks, water, clouds, chairs
  • • Plants need sunlight, water, and air
  • • Animals need food, water, shelter, and air
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 2

Living and Non-Living Things

Distinguish between living things and non-living things.

Learning Objectives

Define what makes something living

Sort objects into living and non-living

Explain that living things need food, water, and air

Lessons

1. What is Living?

Living things grow, breathe, eat, and reproduce.

Examples:

  • • Living: plants, animals, people, insects
  • • Non-living: rocks, water, clouds, chairs

2. What Living Things Need

All living things need certain things to survive.

Examples:

  • • Plants need sunlight, water, and air
  • • Animals need food, water, shelter, and air

lessons.title: Plants Around Us
lessons.content:
Plants Around Us

Learning Objectives

  • • Roots: soak up water from the soil
  • • Stem: carries water up to the leaves
  • • Leaves: make food using sunlight
  • • Flower: makes seeds for new plants
  • • Plant a bean seed and watch it sprout over days
  • • Seed → sprout → seedling → plant
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 3

Plants Around Us

Learn about the parts of a plant and how plants grow.

Learning Objectives

Identify roots, stem, leaves, and flower

Explain what plants need to grow

Observe how a seed becomes a plant

Lessons

1. Parts of a Plant

Every plant has parts that do special jobs.

Examples:

  • • Roots: soak up water from the soil
  • • Stem: carries water up to the leaves
  • • Leaves: make food using sunlight
  • • Flower: makes seeds for new plants

2. How Seeds Grow

Seeds need water, warmth, and soil to sprout.

Examples:

  • • Plant a bean seed and watch it sprout over days
  • • Seed → sprout → seedling → plant

lessons.title: Animals and Their Needs
lessons.content:
Animals and Their Needs

Learning Objectives

  • • Mammals: dogs, cats, whales — have fur and feed babies milk
  • • Birds: eagles, penguins — have feathers and beaks
  • • Fish: salmon, goldfish — live in water, have gills
  • • A fish lives in water
  • • A polar bear lives in the Arctic
  • • A monkey lives in the rainforest
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 4

Animals and Their Needs

Discover different types of animals and what they need to survive.

Learning Objectives

Name basic animal groups (mammals, birds, fish, insects, reptiles)

Describe what animals need to survive

Match animals to their habitats

Lessons

1. Animal Groups

Scientists group animals by their features.

Examples:

  • • Mammals: dogs, cats, whales — have fur and feed babies milk
  • • Birds: eagles, penguins — have feathers and beaks
  • • Fish: salmon, goldfish — live in water, have gills

2. Animal Homes

Animals live in habitats that meet their needs.

Examples:

  • • A fish lives in water
  • • A polar bear lives in the Arctic
  • • A monkey lives in the rainforest

lessons.title: Weather and Seasons
lessons.content:
Weather and Seasons

Learning Objectives

  • • Sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy, windy, foggy
  • • We measure temperature to tell if it's hot or cold
  • • Spring: warm, flowers bloom
  • • Summer: hot, long days
  • • Fall: cool, leaves change color
  • • Winter: cold, some places get snow
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 5

Weather and Seasons

Observe and describe daily weather and how it changes with the seasons.

Learning Objectives

Describe different types of weather

Explain the four seasons

Connect weather to what we wear and do

Lessons

1. Types of Weather

Weather describes what the sky and air are like outside.

Examples:

  • • Sunny, cloudy, rainy, snowy, windy, foggy
  • • We measure temperature to tell if it's hot or cold

2. The Four Seasons

Earth has four seasons that bring different weather.

Examples:

  • • Spring: warm, flowers bloom
  • • Summer: hot, long days
  • • Fall: cool, leaves change color
  • • Winter: cold, some places get snow

lessons.title: The Sun, Moon, and Stars
lessons.content:
The Sun, Moon, and Stars

Learning Objectives

  • • The sun rises in the morning and sets at night
  • • Without the sun, Earth would be dark and cold
  • • New moon: we can't see it
  • • Full moon: we see a full circle
  • • Stars look tiny because they are very far away
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 6

The Sun, Moon, and Stars

Observe patterns in the sky — the sun, moon, and stars.

Learning Objectives

Describe the sun as our nearest star

Identify that the moon changes shape over time

Observe that stars are visible at night

Lessons

1. Our Sun

The sun is a star that gives us light and warmth.

Examples:

  • • The sun rises in the morning and sets at night
  • • Without the sun, Earth would be dark and cold

2. The Moon and Stars

The moon reflects sunlight and changes shape (phases) over about a month.

Examples:

  • • New moon: we can't see it
  • • Full moon: we see a full circle
  • • Stars look tiny because they are very far away

lessons.title: Push and Pull — Forces
lessons.content:
Push and Pull — Forces

Learning Objectives

  • • Pushing a shopping cart makes it go forward
  • • Pulling a door opens it
  • • Kicking a ball is a push
  • • A gentle push makes a ball roll slowly
  • • A hard kick makes a ball fly fast
  • • Heavy objects need stronger forces to move
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 7

Push and Pull — Forces

Understand how pushes and pulls change the way objects move.

Learning Objectives

Define push and pull

Predict how a push or pull changes motion

Compare the effect of strong vs. gentle forces

Lessons

1. Pushes and Pulls

A force is a push or a pull that can move objects.

Examples:

  • • Pushing a shopping cart makes it go forward
  • • Pulling a door opens it
  • • Kicking a ball is a push

2. Strength of Force

A stronger push or pull causes more change in motion.

Examples:

  • • A gentle push makes a ball roll slowly
  • • A hard kick makes a ball fly fast
  • • Heavy objects need stronger forces to move

lessons.title: Materials and Their Properties
lessons.content:
Materials and Their Properties

Learning Objectives

  • • A rock is hard, heavy, and rough
  • • Cotton is soft, light, and smooth
  • • Metal is shiny, hard, and cold to touch
  • • Sort buttons by color, size, or shape
  • • Sort blocks by material: wood, plastic, or foam
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 8

Materials and Their Properties

Observe and sort objects by their physical properties.

Learning Objectives

Describe objects using size, shape, color, weight, and texture

Sort objects by properties

Identify materials: wood, metal, plastic, fabric

Lessons

1. Describing Materials

We use properties to describe and compare materials.

Examples:

  • • A rock is hard, heavy, and rough
  • • Cotton is soft, light, and smooth
  • • Metal is shiny, hard, and cold to touch

2. Sorting by Properties

We can sort objects into groups based on what they have in common.

Examples:

  • • Sort buttons by color, size, or shape
  • • Sort blocks by material: wood, plastic, or foam

lessons.title: Water: Liquid, Solid, Gas
lessons.content:
Water: Liquid, Solid, Gas

Learning Objectives

  • • Liquid: water in a glass or river
  • • Solid: ice, snow, icicles
  • • Gas: steam rising from hot soup
  • • Ice cube left in the sun melts into water
  • • Water put in a freezer becomes ice
  • • Puddles dry up as water turns to invisible gas (evaporation)
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 9

Water: Liquid, Solid, Gas

Observe how water changes between liquid, solid (ice), and gas (steam).

Learning Objectives

Identify three states of water

Describe melting and freezing

Connect water changes to temperature

Lessons

1. Three States of Water

Water can be a liquid, solid, or gas depending on temperature.

Examples:

  • • Liquid: water in a glass or river
  • • Solid: ice, snow, icicles
  • • Gas: steam rising from hot soup

2. Melting and Freezing

Heat melts ice into liquid. Cold freezes liquid into ice.

Examples:

  • • Ice cube left in the sun melts into water
  • • Water put in a freezer becomes ice
  • • Puddles dry up as water turns to invisible gas (evaporation)

lessons.title: Taking Care of Our Earth
lessons.content:
Taking Care of Our Earth

Learning Objectives

  • • Harm: littering, cutting down forests, wasting water
  • • Help: planting trees, cleaning up trash, saving energy
  • • Reduce: use less — turn off the tap while brushing
  • • Reuse: use again — bring a reusable bag
  • • Recycle: turn old things into new — paper, cans, plastic
Kindergarten
🔬 Science
Module 10

Taking Care of Our Earth

Learn how humans affect the environment and how to protect it.

Learning Objectives

Identify ways humans help and harm the environment

Practice reduce, reuse, and recycle

Describe simple conservation actions

Lessons

1. Helping and Harming

Our actions can help or hurt the Earth.

Examples:

  • • Harm: littering, cutting down forests, wasting water
  • • Help: planting trees, cleaning up trash, saving energy

2. Reduce, Reuse, Recycle

The 3 R's help us make less waste.

Examples:

  • • Reduce: use less — turn off the tap while brushing
  • • Reuse: use again — bring a reusable bag
  • • Recycle: turn old things into new — paper, cans, plastic

courses.title: Science — 1st Grade
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 1st Grade.

lessons.title: Structure and Function of Plants
lessons.content: Structure and Function of Plants

lessons.title: Animal Structures and Survival
lessons.content:
Animal Structures and Survival

Learning Objectives

  • • Duck's webbed feet: perfect for swimming
  • • Giraffe's long neck: reach leaves high up in trees
  • • Eagle's sharp beak and talons: catch and hold prey
  • • Porcupine: sharp quills keep predators away
  • • Chameleon: changes color to blend in (camouflage)
  • • Skunk: sprays a bad smell
1st Grade
🔬 Science
Module 2

Animal Structures and Survival

Discover how animals' bodies are built to help them survive.

Learning Objectives

Describe how body parts help animals survive

Give examples of how animals protect themselves

Explain how animals get food using their structures

Lessons

1. Body Parts for Survival

Animals have special body parts designed for where they live.

Examples:

  • • Duck's webbed feet: perfect for swimming
  • • Giraffe's long neck: reach leaves high up in trees
  • • Eagle's sharp beak and talons: catch and hold prey

2. Defense Structures

Animals protect themselves using special features.

Examples:

  • • Porcupine: sharp quills keep predators away
  • • Chameleon: changes color to blend in (camouflage)
  • • Skunk: sprays a bad smell

lessons.title: Light and Sound
lessons.content:
Light and Sound

Learning Objectives

  • • A flashlight beam shows light traveling straight
  • • Transparent objects let light through (clear glass)
  • • Opaque objects block light and create shadows
  • • Pluck a rubber band — it vibrates and makes a sound
  • • Drums vibrate when hit
  • • Loud sounds have big vibrations; soft sounds have small vibrations
1st Grade
🔬 Science
Module 3

Light and Sound

Investigate the properties of light and sound.

Learning Objectives

Explain that light travels in straight lines

Describe how objects can block, reflect, or absorb light

Explain that sound is made by vibration

Lessons

1. How Light Travels

Light travels in straight lines from a source.

Examples:

  • • A flashlight beam shows light traveling straight
  • • Transparent objects let light through (clear glass)
  • • Opaque objects block light and create shadows

2. Sound and Vibration

Sound is made when something vibrates and travels through the air.

Examples:

  • • Pluck a rubber band — it vibrates and makes a sound
  • • Drums vibrate when hit
  • • Loud sounds have big vibrations; soft sounds have small vibrations

lessons.title: Properties of Matter
lessons.content:
Properties of Matter

Learning Objectives

  • • Solid: keeps its shape — ice, rock, wood
  • • Liquid: takes the shape of its container — water, juice, honey
  • • Gas: spreads out to fill space — air, steam, helium in a balloon
  • • Sand and water: the sand doesn't disappear, it mixes
  • • Salt dissolved in water: the salt seems to disappear but is still there
  • • Baking soda + vinegar: produces a gas (bubbles!)
1st Grade
🔬 Science
Module 4

Properties of Matter

Observe and describe matter using physical properties.

Learning Objectives

Describe matter using measurable properties

Compare solids, liquids, and gases

Investigate how mixing materials can create new substances

Lessons

1. Solids, Liquids, and Gases

All matter is made of particles in one of three states.

Examples:

  • • Solid: keeps its shape — ice, rock, wood
  • • Liquid: takes the shape of its container — water, juice, honey
  • • Gas: spreads out to fill space — air, steam, helium in a balloon

2. Mixing Materials

When we mix materials, we can make something new.

Examples:

  • • Sand and water: the sand doesn't disappear, it mixes
  • • Salt dissolved in water: the salt seems to disappear but is still there
  • • Baking soda + vinegar: produces a gas (bubbles!)

lessons.title: Earth's Surface
lessons.content:
Earth's Surface

Learning Objectives

  • • Mountain: tall, rocky land rising high above the surroundings
  • • Valley: low area between mountains
  • • Plain: flat, wide stretch of land
  • • Island: land completely surrounded by water
  • • Ocean: the largest body of salt water
  • • River: fresh water flowing from mountains to the sea
  • • Lake: body of fresh water surrounded by land
1st Grade
🔬 Science
Module 5

Earth's Surface

Explore the features of Earth's land and water.

Learning Objectives

Identify major landforms (mountains, valleys, plains, islands)

Identify major bodies of water (ocean, river, lake)

Explain that most of Earth's surface is covered by water

Lessons

1. Landforms

Earth's surface has many different shapes called landforms.

Examples:

  • • Mountain: tall, rocky land rising high above the surroundings
  • • Valley: low area between mountains
  • • Plain: flat, wide stretch of land
  • • Island: land completely surrounded by water

2. Bodies of Water

Water covers about 71% of Earth's surface.

Examples:

  • • Ocean: the largest body of salt water
  • • River: fresh water flowing from mountains to the sea
  • • Lake: body of fresh water surrounded by land

lessons.title: Weather Patterns
lessons.content:
Weather Patterns

Learning Objectives

  • • Record temperature, precipitation, and cloud cover daily
  • • Graph the data: how many sunny, cloudy, and rainy days this month?
  • • Evaporation: water from oceans rises as vapor
  • • Condensation: vapor cools and forms clouds
  • • Precipitation: water falls as rain or snow
  • • Collection: water gathers in rivers, lakes, and oceans
1st Grade
🔬 Science
Module 6

Weather Patterns

Collect weather data and identify patterns over time.

Learning Objectives

Record daily weather observations

Identify weather patterns across weeks and seasons

Describe the water cycle simply

Lessons

1. Observing and Recording Weather

Scientists track weather every day to find patterns.

Examples:

  • • Record temperature, precipitation, and cloud cover daily
  • • Graph the data: how many sunny, cloudy, and rainy days this month?

2. The Water Cycle

Water moves from Earth to the sky and back again.

Examples:

  • • Evaporation: water from oceans rises as vapor
  • • Condensation: vapor cools and forms clouds
  • • Precipitation: water falls as rain or snow
  • • Collection: water gathers in rivers, lakes, and oceans

lessons.title: The Moon's Changing Shape
lessons.content:
The Moon's Changing Shape

Learning Objectives

  • • New Moon: dark side faces us — moon invisible
  • • First Quarter: half of the moon is lit
  • • Full Moon: entire face is lit
  • • Last Quarter: opposite half is lit
  • • Draw the moon shape you see each night for 28 days
  • • The cycle repeats approximately every 29.5 days
1st Grade
🔬 Science
Module 7

The Moon's Changing Shape

Observe and track the phases of the moon over a month.

Learning Objectives

Name the major phases of the moon

Explain that the moon does not make its own light

Track and predict moon phases

Lessons

1. Why the Moon Changes Shape

The moon reflects sunlight. As it orbits Earth, we see different portions lit up.

Examples:

  • • New Moon: dark side faces us — moon invisible
  • • First Quarter: half of the moon is lit
  • • Full Moon: entire face is lit
  • • Last Quarter: opposite half is lit

2. Moon Phase Calendar

Track the moon each night to see how it changes.

Examples:

  • • Draw the moon shape you see each night for 28 days
  • • The cycle repeats approximately every 29.5 days

lessons.title: Habitats and Ecosystems
lessons.content:
Habitats and Ecosystems

Learning Objectives

  • • Desert: hot, dry — camels, cacti, scorpions are adapted here
  • • Ocean: salty water — fish, whales, coral, kelp
  • • Forest: trees and shade — deer, owls, foxes, mushrooms
  • • A forest fire destroys shelter and food for animals
  • • Draining a wetland removes habitat for frogs and birds
  • • People can help by creating wildlife reserves
1st Grade
🔬 Science
Module 8

Habitats and Ecosystems

Explore how living things depend on their habitat for survival.

Learning Objectives

Define habitat and ecosystem

Give examples of animals matched to their habitats

Explain how changes to a habitat affect living things

Lessons

1. What is a Habitat?

A habitat provides everything a living thing needs: food, water, shelter, and space.

Examples:

  • • Desert: hot, dry — camels, cacti, scorpions are adapted here
  • • Ocean: salty water — fish, whales, coral, kelp
  • • Forest: trees and shade — deer, owls, foxes, mushrooms

2. Habitat Disruption

When a habitat changes, living things can be affected.

Examples:

  • • A forest fire destroys shelter and food for animals
  • • Draining a wetland removes habitat for frogs and birds
  • • People can help by creating wildlife reserves

lessons.title: Simple Machines
lessons.content:
Simple Machines

Learning Objectives

  • • Lever: seesaw, bottle opener
  • • Wheel and axle: bicycle wheel, doorknob
  • • Pulley: flagpole, blinds
  • • Inclined plane: ramp, slide
  • • Wedge: knife, doorstop
  • • Screw: bolt, jar lid
  • • Scissors = two levers + two wedges
  • • Stairs = inclined plane
  • • Pencil sharpener = wheel and axle + wedge
1st Grade
🔬 Science
Module 9

Simple Machines

Identify simple machines and explain how they make work easier.

Learning Objectives

Name six simple machines

Give everyday examples of each

Explain how simple machines reduce effort

Lessons

1. Six Simple Machines

Simple machines help us do work with less force.

Examples:

  • • Lever: seesaw, bottle opener
  • • Wheel and axle: bicycle wheel, doorknob
  • • Pulley: flagpole, blinds
  • • Inclined plane: ramp, slide
  • • Wedge: knife, doorstop
  • • Screw: bolt, jar lid

2. Machines Around Us

Simple machines are everywhere — look for them in your daily life.

Examples:

  • • Scissors = two levers + two wedges
  • • Stairs = inclined plane
  • • Pencil sharpener = wheel and axle + wedge

lessons.title: Recycling and Natural Resources
lessons.content:
Recycling and Natural Resources

Learning Objectives

  • • Renewable: sunlight, wind, water, trees (can be replaced)
  • • Non-renewable: coal, oil, natural gas (take millions of years to form)
  • • Recycling aluminum uses 95% less energy than making new aluminum
  • • Recycling 1 ton of paper saves 17 trees
  • • Glass can be recycled endlessly without losing quality
1st Grade
🔬 Science
Module 10

Recycling and Natural Resources

Identify natural resources and learn how to conserve them.

Learning Objectives

Define natural resources

Distinguish renewable from non-renewable resources

Explain how recycling conserves resources

Lessons

1. Natural Resources

Natural resources come from nature and are used by people.

Examples:

  • • Renewable: sunlight, wind, water, trees (can be replaced)
  • • Non-renewable: coal, oil, natural gas (take millions of years to form)

2. Why Recycle?

Recycling turns old materials into new products, saving natural resources.

Examples:

  • • Recycling aluminum uses 95% less energy than making new aluminum
  • • Recycling 1 ton of paper saves 17 trees
  • • Glass can be recycled endlessly without losing quality

courses.title: Science — 2nd Grade
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 2nd Grade.

lessons.title: Life Cycles
lessons.content:
Life Cycles

Learning Objectives

  • • Seed → germination → seedling → mature plant → flower → seed
  • • An oak tree takes decades to mature but produces thousands of acorns
  • • Complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult (butterfly, beetle)
  • • Incomplete metamorphosis: egg → nymph → adult (grasshopper, dragonfly)
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 1

Life Cycles

Compare the life cycles of plants, insects, frogs, and mammals.

Learning Objectives

Describe the stages of a plant life cycle

Compare complete vs. incomplete metamorphosis

Explain how life cycles repeat

Lessons

1. Plant Life Cycle

Plants grow from seeds and produce new seeds to start the cycle again.

Examples:

  • • Seed → germination → seedling → mature plant → flower → seed
  • • An oak tree takes decades to mature but produces thousands of acorns

2. Insect Metamorphosis

Many insects change dramatically as they grow.

Examples:

  • • Complete metamorphosis: egg → larva → pupa → adult (butterfly, beetle)
  • • Incomplete metamorphosis: egg → nymph → adult (grasshopper, dragonfly)

lessons.title: Ecosystems and Food Chains
lessons.content:
Ecosystems and Food Chains

Learning Objectives

  • • Producer: grass (makes its own food via sunlight)
  • • Primary consumer: rabbit (eats grass)
  • • Secondary consumer: fox (eats rabbit)
  • • Decomposer: mushroom (breaks down dead matter)
  • • If rabbits disappear, foxes lose a food source
  • • If grass disappears, all animals that eat it are affected
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 2

Ecosystems and Food Chains

Explore how energy flows through a food chain.

Learning Objectives

Define producer, consumer, and decomposer

Build a simple food chain

Explain what happens when one part of a food chain is removed

Lessons

1. Producers and Consumers

Energy flows from the sun through plants to animals.

Examples:

  • • Producer: grass (makes its own food via sunlight)
  • • Primary consumer: rabbit (eats grass)
  • • Secondary consumer: fox (eats rabbit)
  • • Decomposer: mushroom (breaks down dead matter)

2. Food Web Connections

A food web shows how many food chains overlap and connect.

Examples:

  • • If rabbits disappear, foxes lose a food source
  • • If grass disappears, all animals that eat it are affected

lessons.title: Properties of Matter
lessons.content:
Properties of Matter

Learning Objectives

  • • Mass: measured with a balance scale (grams/kilograms)
  • • Volume: measured with a graduated cylinder (liters/milliliters)
  • • Temperature: measured with a thermometer (°C or °F)
  • • Physical: cutting paper, melting ice, breaking glass
  • • Chemical: burning wood, rusting iron, baking a cake (new substances form)
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 3

Properties of Matter

Investigate the physical and chemical properties of materials.

Learning Objectives

Measure mass, volume, and temperature

Identify physical properties of materials

Distinguish physical changes from chemical changes

Lessons

1. Measuring Matter

We use tools to measure properties of matter.

Examples:

  • • Mass: measured with a balance scale (grams/kilograms)
  • • Volume: measured with a graduated cylinder (liters/milliliters)
  • • Temperature: measured with a thermometer (°C or °F)

2. Physical vs. Chemical Change

Physical changes don't create new substances. Chemical changes do.

Examples:

  • • Physical: cutting paper, melting ice, breaking glass
  • • Chemical: burning wood, rusting iron, baking a cake (new substances form)

lessons.title: States of Matter and Changes
lessons.content:
States of Matter and Changes

Learning Objectives

  • • Melting: solid → liquid (ice → water)
  • • Freezing: liquid → solid (water → ice)
  • • Evaporation: liquid → gas (water → water vapor)
  • • Condensation: gas → liquid (steam → water droplets on a mirror)
  • • Butter melts in a hot pan
  • • Chocolate hardens in the freezer
  • • Dew forms on cold grass in the morning (condensation)
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 4

States of Matter and Changes

Investigate how matter changes state and what causes those changes.

Learning Objectives

Explain melting, freezing, evaporation, and condensation

Connect state changes to temperature

Investigate how heating and cooling changes materials

Lessons

1. Four Key Changes

Matter changes state when energy (heat) is added or removed.

Examples:

  • • Melting: solid → liquid (ice → water)
  • • Freezing: liquid → solid (water → ice)
  • • Evaporation: liquid → gas (water → water vapor)
  • • Condensation: gas → liquid (steam → water droplets on a mirror)

2. Heating and Cooling

Adding heat gives particles more energy; removing heat slows them down.

Examples:

  • • Butter melts in a hot pan
  • • Chocolate hardens in the freezer
  • • Dew forms on cold grass in the morning (condensation)

lessons.title: Earth's Materials
lessons.content:
Earth's Materials

Learning Objectives

  • • Granite: coarse, speckled, very hard
  • • Limestone: light-colored, can contain fossils
  • • Quartz: glassy, hard, often clear or white
  • • Sandy soil drains quickly; clay soil holds water
  • • A fossil fern tells us forests once grew where there is now desert
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 5

Earth's Materials

Investigate rocks, minerals, soil, and fossils.

Learning Objectives

Classify rocks by observable properties

Describe how soil is formed

Explain what fossils tell us about the past

Lessons

1. Rocks and Minerals

Rocks are made of minerals. We identify them by color, hardness, and texture.

Examples:

  • • Granite: coarse, speckled, very hard
  • • Limestone: light-colored, can contain fossils
  • • Quartz: glassy, hard, often clear or white

2. Soil and Fossils

Soil contains broken rocks, minerals, and organic matter. Fossils preserve ancient life.

Examples:

  • • Sandy soil drains quickly; clay soil holds water
  • • A fossil fern tells us forests once grew where there is now desert

lessons.title: Weather and Climate
lessons.content:
Weather and Climate

Learning Objectives

  • • Weather: It's raining today in Seattle.
  • • Climate: Seattle has a rainy climate.
  • • The Sahara has a desert climate — very hot and dry year-round
  • • Hurricane: spinning storm with very strong winds and heavy rain
  • • Tornado: fast-spinning column of air reaching the ground
  • • Blizzard: heavy snowstorm with strong winds
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 6

Weather and Climate

Distinguish between weather and climate, and explore extreme weather.

Learning Objectives

Explain the difference between weather and climate

Describe causes of extreme weather events

Explain how scientists forecast weather

Lessons

1. Weather vs. Climate

Weather is what's happening outside today. Climate is the usual pattern over many years.

Examples:

  • • Weather: It's raining today in Seattle.
  • • Climate: Seattle has a rainy climate.
  • • The Sahara has a desert climate — very hot and dry year-round

2. Extreme Weather

Some weather events are powerful and dangerous.

Examples:

  • • Hurricane: spinning storm with very strong winds and heavy rain
  • • Tornado: fast-spinning column of air reaching the ground
  • • Blizzard: heavy snowstorm with strong winds

lessons.title: Forces and Motion
lessons.content:
Forces and Motion

Learning Objectives

  • • Hitting a baseball changes its direction
  • • A brake applies friction to slow a bicycle
  • • Pushing a toy car along carpet is harder than on a smooth floor (more friction)
  • • A ball thrown up always falls back down
  • • Everything has weight because gravity pulls it
  • • On the Moon, gravity is weaker — you'd weigh 6x less
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 7

Forces and Motion

Investigate how forces cause objects to move and change direction.

Learning Objectives

Define force, speed, and direction

Explain how friction affects motion

Investigate how gravity pulls objects down

Lessons

1. Speed and Direction

A force can make objects start, stop, speed up, slow down, or change direction.

Examples:

  • • Hitting a baseball changes its direction
  • • A brake applies friction to slow a bicycle
  • • Pushing a toy car along carpet is harder than on a smooth floor (more friction)

2. Gravity

Gravity is a force that pulls all objects toward Earth.

Examples:

  • • A ball thrown up always falls back down
  • • Everything has weight because gravity pulls it
  • • On the Moon, gravity is weaker — you'd weigh 6x less

lessons.title: Magnets
lessons.content:
Magnets

Learning Objectives

  • • N + S = attract (pull together)
  • • N + N = repel (push apart)
  • • Earth is like a giant magnet with north and south magnetic poles
  • • Magnetic: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt
  • • Non-magnetic: wood, plastic, aluminum, glass
  • • Paper clips stick to a magnet; pennies do not
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 8

Magnets

Explore the properties of magnets and magnetic force.

Learning Objectives

Describe the poles of a magnet

Explain attraction and repulsion

Identify magnetic and non-magnetic materials

Lessons

1. Poles and Force

Every magnet has a north and south pole. Opposite poles attract; same poles repel.

Examples:

  • • N + S = attract (pull together)
  • • N + N = repel (push apart)
  • • Earth is like a giant magnet with north and south magnetic poles

2. Magnetic Materials

Magnets attract some materials but not others.

Examples:

  • • Magnetic: iron, steel, nickel, cobalt
  • • Non-magnetic: wood, plastic, aluminum, glass
  • • Paper clips stick to a magnet; pennies do not

lessons.title: The Solar System
lessons.content:
The Solar System

Learning Objectives

  • • 8 planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
  • • My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos (mnemonic)
  • • Planets closer to the sun are usually warmer
  • • Jupiter: largest planet, has a giant storm (Great Red Spot)
  • • Saturn: famous for its beautiful rings made of ice and rock
  • • Mars: the Red Planet, has the tallest volcano in the solar system
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 9

The Solar System

Explore the planets, sun, and moon in our solar system.

Learning Objectives

Name the 8 planets in order

Describe the role of the sun

Compare the sizes and features of planets

Lessons

1. Our Solar System

The solar system includes the sun and everything that orbits it.

Examples:

  • • 8 planets: Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
  • • My Very Educated Mother Just Served Us Nachos (mnemonic)
  • • Planets closer to the sun are usually warmer

2. Comparing Planets

Each planet has unique features.

Examples:

  • • Jupiter: largest planet, has a giant storm (Great Red Spot)
  • • Saturn: famous for its beautiful rings made of ice and rock
  • • Mars: the Red Planet, has the tallest volcano in the solar system

lessons.title: Scientists and Science Tools
lessons.content:
Scientists and Science Tools

Learning Objectives

  • • 1. Ask a question
  • • 2. Make a hypothesis (prediction)
  • • 3. Experiment/Observe
  • • 4. Record data
  • • 5. Draw a conclusion
  • • Magnifying glass: see small details
  • • Ruler/measuring tape: measure length
  • • Thermometer: measure temperature
  • • Balance scale: measure mass
  • • Beaker/graduated cylinder: measure liquid volume
2nd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 10

Scientists and Science Tools

Learn about the science process and the tools scientists use.

Learning Objectives

Describe the steps of the scientific method

Identify common science tools and their uses

Design a simple experiment

Lessons

1. The Scientific Method

Scientists follow a process to answer questions.

Examples:

  • • 1. Ask a question
  • • 2. Make a hypothesis (prediction)
  • • 3. Experiment/Observe
  • • 4. Record data
  • • 5. Draw a conclusion

2. Science Tools

Scientists use tools to observe and measure.

Examples:

  • • Magnifying glass: see small details
  • • Ruler/measuring tape: measure length
  • • Thermometer: measure temperature
  • • Balance scale: measure mass
  • • Beaker/graduated cylinder: measure liquid volume

courses.title: Science — 3rd Grade
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 3rd Grade.

lessons.title: Adaptations and Natural Selection
lessons.content:
Adaptations and Natural Selection

Learning Objectives

  • • Polar bear: thick fur and fat for insulation in the Arctic
  • • Cactus: thick stem stores water in the desert
  • • Duck: waterproof feathers keep it dry while swimming
  • • Migration: monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles to stay warm
  • • Hibernation: bears sleep through winter when food is scarce
  • • Camouflage: stick insects look like twigs to avoid predators
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 1

Adaptations and Natural Selection

Explore how organisms adapt to their environments over generations.

Learning Objectives

Define adaptation

Give examples of structural and behavioral adaptations

Explain how adaptations help survival

Lessons

1. Structural Adaptations

Physical features that help an organism survive in its environment.

Examples:

  • • Polar bear: thick fur and fat for insulation in the Arctic
  • • Cactus: thick stem stores water in the desert
  • • Duck: waterproof feathers keep it dry while swimming

2. Behavioral Adaptations

Actions that help an organism survive.

Examples:

  • • Migration: monarch butterflies travel thousands of miles to stay warm
  • • Hibernation: bears sleep through winter when food is scarce
  • • Camouflage: stick insects look like twigs to avoid predators

lessons.title: Ecosystems and Biodiversity
lessons.content:
Ecosystems and Biodiversity

Learning Objectives

  • • A rainforest has millions of species of plants, animals, and insects
  • • A monoculture farm (one crop only) has very low biodiversity
  • • Higher biodiversity = healthier, more resilient ecosystem
  • • Coral reef: warm, shallow ocean water; home to fish, coral, turtles
  • • Temperate forest: four seasons; home to deer, squirrels, woodpeckers, oaks
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 2

Ecosystems and Biodiversity

Examine the diversity of life in different ecosystems and the importance of biodiversity.

Learning Objectives

Define biodiversity and explain why it matters

Compare and contrast two ecosystems

Describe the impact of losing species from an ecosystem

Lessons

1. What is Biodiversity?

Biodiversity refers to the variety of life in a particular area.

Examples:

  • • A rainforest has millions of species of plants, animals, and insects
  • • A monoculture farm (one crop only) has very low biodiversity
  • • Higher biodiversity = healthier, more resilient ecosystem

2. Ecosystem Comparison

Different ecosystems support different communities of life.

Examples:

  • • Coral reef: warm, shallow ocean water; home to fish, coral, turtles
  • • Temperate forest: four seasons; home to deer, squirrels, woodpeckers, oaks

lessons.title: The Rock Cycle
lessons.content:
The Rock Cycle

Learning Objectives

  • • Igneous: cooled magma — granite, basalt, obsidian
  • • Sedimentary: layers of compressed sediment — sandstone, limestone, shale
  • • Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure — marble, slate, quartzite
  • • Magma cools → igneous → weathering/erosion → sediment → pressure → sedimentary → heat/pressure → metamorphic → melt → magma
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 3

The Rock Cycle

Explore the three types of rocks and how they form and change.

Learning Objectives

Identify igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic rocks

Explain how each type forms

Describe the rock cycle

Lessons

1. Three Types of Rocks

Rocks form in different ways and can change from one type to another.

Examples:

  • • Igneous: cooled magma — granite, basalt, obsidian
  • • Sedimentary: layers of compressed sediment — sandstone, limestone, shale
  • • Metamorphic: changed by heat and pressure — marble, slate, quartzite

2. The Rock Cycle

Rocks continuously change from one type to another over millions of years.

Examples:

  • • Magma cools → igneous → weathering/erosion → sediment → pressure → sedimentary → heat/pressure → metamorphic → melt → magma

lessons.title: Weather, Water Cycle, and Climate
lessons.content:
Weather, Water Cycle, and Climate

Learning Objectives

  • • Evaporation: sun heats water → rises as vapor
  • • Transpiration: plants release water vapor
  • • Condensation: vapor cools → forms clouds
  • • Precipitation: rain, snow, sleet, hail falls
  • • Tropical (near equator): hot and humid all year
  • • Temperate (mid latitudes): four distinct seasons
  • • Polar (near poles): cold most of the year
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 4

Weather, Water Cycle, and Climate

Deepen understanding of the water cycle and its role in weather and climate.

Learning Objectives

Explain all four stages of the water cycle in detail

Describe how the water cycle affects weather

Define climate zones

Lessons

1. Water Cycle in Depth

The water cycle continuously moves water between Earth's surface and atmosphere.

Examples:

  • • Evaporation: sun heats water → rises as vapor
  • • Transpiration: plants release water vapor
  • • Condensation: vapor cools → forms clouds
  • • Precipitation: rain, snow, sleet, hail falls

2. Climate Zones

Earth has different climate zones based on distance from the equator.

Examples:

  • • Tropical (near equator): hot and humid all year
  • • Temperate (mid latitudes): four distinct seasons
  • • Polar (near poles): cold most of the year

lessons.title: Energy: Forms and Transformations
lessons.content:
Energy: Forms and Transformations

Learning Objectives

  • • Thermal: heat from a fire or the sun
  • • Light: sunlight or a lamp
  • • Sound: music, thunder, talking
  • • Electrical: powers lights and electronics
  • • Mechanical: movement of a ball or bicycle
  • • Toaster: electrical → thermal (heat)
  • • Solar panel: light → electrical
  • • Drumming: mechanical → sound
  • • Plants: light → chemical energy (photosynthesis)
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 5

Energy: Forms and Transformations

Identify forms of energy and explore how energy transforms from one form to another.

Learning Objectives

Name forms of energy: thermal, light, sound, electrical, mechanical

Explain energy transformation with examples

Describe how we generate and use energy

Lessons

1. Forms of Energy

Energy exists in many forms and makes things happen.

Examples:

  • • Thermal: heat from a fire or the sun
  • • Light: sunlight or a lamp
  • • Sound: music, thunder, talking
  • • Electrical: powers lights and electronics
  • • Mechanical: movement of a ball or bicycle

2. Energy Transformations

Energy changes from one form to another.

Examples:

  • • Toaster: electrical → thermal (heat)
  • • Solar panel: light → electrical
  • • Drumming: mechanical → sound
  • • Plants: light → chemical energy (photosynthesis)

lessons.title: Forces and Newton's Laws (Intro)
lessons.content:
Forces and Newton's Laws (Intro)

Learning Objectives

  • • Tug of war — equal teams = balanced (no movement)
  • • One team stronger = unbalanced (rope moves their way)
  • • A book on a table: gravity pulls down, table pushes up — balanced!
  • • Jump off a diving board — you push the board, the board pushes you up
  • • A rocket expels gas downward — the gas pushes the rocket upward
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 6

Forces and Newton's Laws (Intro)

Explore balanced and unbalanced forces and introduce Newton's first and third laws.

Learning Objectives

Explain balanced and unbalanced forces

Describe Newton's 1st Law (inertia)

Describe Newton's 3rd Law (action-reaction)

Lessons

1. Balanced and Unbalanced Forces

When forces are balanced, objects stay still or keep moving. When unbalanced, motion changes.

Examples:

  • • Tug of war — equal teams = balanced (no movement)
  • • One team stronger = unbalanced (rope moves their way)
  • • A book on a table: gravity pulls down, table pushes up — balanced!

2. Action-Reaction

For every action, there is an equal and opposite reaction.

Examples:

  • • Jump off a diving board — you push the board, the board pushes you up
  • • A rocket expels gas downward — the gas pushes the rocket upward

lessons.title: Human Body: Organs and Systems
lessons.content:
Human Body: Organs and Systems

Learning Objectives

  • • Brain: controls thinking, movement, and senses
  • • Heart: pumps blood throughout the body
  • • Lungs: take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide
  • • Stomach: breaks down food
  • • Circulatory system: heart + blood vessels + blood
  • • Digestive system: mouth → esophagus → stomach → intestines
  • • Respiratory system: nose/mouth → trachea → lungs
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 7

Human Body: Organs and Systems

Identify major organs and explore how body systems work together.

Learning Objectives

Name and locate major organs

Describe the function of key body systems

Explain how systems interact

Lessons

1. Major Organs

Organs are structures in the body that do specific jobs.

Examples:

  • • Brain: controls thinking, movement, and senses
  • • Heart: pumps blood throughout the body
  • • Lungs: take in oxygen and release carbon dioxide
  • • Stomach: breaks down food

2. Body Systems

Organs work together in systems.

Examples:

  • • Circulatory system: heart + blood vessels + blood
  • • Digestive system: mouth → esophagus → stomach → intestines
  • • Respiratory system: nose/mouth → trachea → lungs

lessons.title: Soil, Erosion, and Landforms
lessons.content:
Soil, Erosion, and Landforms

Learning Objectives

  • • A river erodes its banks over time, carving canyons
  • • The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years
  • • River delta: sediment deposited where river meets sea
  • • Planting trees: roots hold soil in place
  • • Terracing: step-like farming on hillsides
  • • Seawalls: protect coastlines from wave erosion
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 8

Soil, Erosion, and Landforms

Investigate how water and wind shape Earth's surface through erosion and deposition.

Learning Objectives

Define erosion and deposition

Explain how rivers carve canyons and form deltas

Describe how humans prevent erosion

Lessons

1. Erosion and Deposition

Weathering breaks rocks apart. Erosion moves them. Deposition drops them somewhere new.

Examples:

  • • A river erodes its banks over time, carving canyons
  • • The Colorado River carved the Grand Canyon over millions of years
  • • River delta: sediment deposited where river meets sea

2. Preventing Erosion

Humans can slow erosion to protect farmland and coastlines.

Examples:

  • • Planting trees: roots hold soil in place
  • • Terracing: step-like farming on hillsides
  • • Seawalls: protect coastlines from wave erosion

lessons.title: Electricity and Circuits
lessons.content:
Electricity and Circuits

Learning Objectives

  • • Rub a balloon on your hair — it sticks to the wall
  • • Lightning is a giant static electricity discharge
  • • Socks sticking together from the dryer
  • • Complete circuit: battery → wire → light bulb → wire → battery (light turns on)
  • • Broken circuit: gap in the wire = light stays off
  • • Conductors: copper, iron, water
  • • Insulators: plastic, rubber, wood
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 9

Electricity and Circuits

Explore static electricity, current electricity, and simple circuits.

Learning Objectives

Explain static electricity

Describe a complete circuit

Distinguish conductors from insulators

Lessons

1. Static Electricity

Static electricity is a buildup of electric charge on a surface.

Examples:

  • • Rub a balloon on your hair — it sticks to the wall
  • • Lightning is a giant static electricity discharge
  • • Socks sticking together from the dryer

2. Circuits

A circuit is a closed path through which electricity flows.

Examples:

  • • Complete circuit: battery → wire → light bulb → wire → battery (light turns on)
  • • Broken circuit: gap in the wire = light stays off
  • • Conductors: copper, iron, water
  • • Insulators: plastic, rubber, wood

lessons.title: Science and Engineering Design
lessons.content:
Science and Engineering Design

Learning Objectives

  • • 1. Define the problem
  • • 2. Research and brainstorm solutions
  • • 3. Design your solution (sketch it)
  • • 4. Build a prototype
  • • 5. Test and evaluate
  • • 6. Improve and redesign
  • • Problem: bridges need to hold weight → engineers design suspension bridges
  • • Problem: need clean water → engineers design filtration systems
  • • Problem: need to communicate far away → engineers design satellites
3rd Grade
🔬 Science
Module 10

Science and Engineering Design

Apply the engineering design process to solve real-world problems.

Learning Objectives

Describe the engineering design process

Identify a problem and design a solution

Test, evaluate, and improve a design

Lessons

1. Engineering Design Process

Engineers follow a process when designing solutions.

Examples:

  • • 1. Define the problem
  • • 2. Research and brainstorm solutions
  • • 3. Design your solution (sketch it)
  • • 4. Build a prototype
  • • 5. Test and evaluate
  • • 6. Improve and redesign

2. Real-World Engineering

Engineers solve problems all around us.

Examples:

  • • Problem: bridges need to hold weight → engineers design suspension bridges
  • • Problem: need clean water → engineers design filtration systems
  • • Problem: need to communicate far away → engineers design satellites

courses.title: Science — 4th Grade
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 4th Grade.
