lessons.title: Structures of Life: Cells
lessons.content:
Structures of Life: Cells

Learning Objectives

  • • A single bacterium is made of just one cell
  • • The human body is made of about 37 trillion cells
  • • Cells are too small to see without a microscope
  • • Shared: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane
  • • Plant only: cell wall (rigid support), chloroplasts (capture light), large central vacuole
  • • Animal only: centrioles (help with cell division)
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 1

Structures of Life: Cells

Introduce cells as the basic unit of life and explore plant vs. animal cells.

Learning Objectives

Explain that all living things are made of cells

Identify key parts of a cell (cell membrane, nucleus, cytoplasm)

Compare plant and animal cells

Lessons

1. The Cell: Basic Unit of Life

Cells are the tiny building blocks of all living things.

Examples:

  • • A single bacterium is made of just one cell
  • • The human body is made of about 37 trillion cells
  • • Cells are too small to see without a microscope

2. Plant vs. Animal Cells

Both cell types share some structures, but plant cells have extra features.

Examples:

  • • Shared: nucleus, cytoplasm, cell membrane
  • • Plant only: cell wall (rigid support), chloroplasts (capture light), large central vacuole
  • • Animal only: centrioles (help with cell division)

lessons.title: Ecosystems: Energy Flow and Food Webs
lessons.content:
Ecosystems: Energy Flow and Food Webs

Learning Objectives

  • • Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next
  • • Bottom level (plants) has the most energy; top predators have the least
  • • This is why there are fewer tigers than deer
  • • Sea otters eat sea urchins; without otters, urchins overgraze kelp forests
  • • Wolves in Yellowstone control deer populations, which allows trees to regrow
  • • Remove a keystone species → ecosystem dramatically changes
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 2

Ecosystems: Energy Flow and Food Webs

Analyze complex food webs and the flow of energy through ecosystems.

Learning Objectives

Explain energy flow from sun to producers to consumers

Build and analyze a food web

Predict the impact of adding or removing a species

Lessons

1. Energy Pyramids

Energy decreases as it moves up the food chain.

Examples:

  • • Only about 10% of energy passes from one level to the next
  • • Bottom level (plants) has the most energy; top predators have the least
  • • This is why there are fewer tigers than deer

2. Keystone Species

Some species have an outsized effect on their ecosystem.

Examples:

  • • Sea otters eat sea urchins; without otters, urchins overgraze kelp forests
  • • Wolves in Yellowstone control deer populations, which allows trees to regrow
  • • Remove a keystone species → ecosystem dramatically changes

lessons.title: Weather, Climate Change, and Human Impact
lessons.content:
Weather, Climate Change, and Human Impact

Learning Objectives

  • • Natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life
  • • Too many greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane) trap extra heat
  • • This causes global average temperatures to rise
  • • Burning fossil fuels for energy and transportation releases CO₂
  • • Solutions: renewable energy (solar, wind), electric vehicles, planting forests
  • • You can help: reduce energy use, eat less meat, walk or bike
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 3

Weather, Climate Change, and Human Impact

Explore how human activities affect climate and what we can do.

Learning Objectives

Explain the greenhouse effect

Describe how human activities contribute to climate change

Identify solutions and personal actions to reduce impact

Lessons

1. The Greenhouse Effect

Greenhouse gases trap heat in Earth's atmosphere, like a blanket.

Examples:

  • • Natural greenhouse effect keeps Earth warm enough for life
  • • Too many greenhouse gases (CO₂, methane) trap extra heat
  • • This causes global average temperatures to rise

2. Human Impact and Solutions

Human activities release greenhouse gases, but we can make changes.

Examples:

  • • Burning fossil fuels for energy and transportation releases CO₂
  • • Solutions: renewable energy (solar, wind), electric vehicles, planting forests
  • • You can help: reduce energy use, eat less meat, walk or bike

lessons.title: Waves: Light and Sound
lessons.content:
Waves: Light and Sound

Learning Objectives

  • • Wavelength: distance from one peak to the next
  • • Amplitude: height of the wave (higher = louder sound or brighter light)
  • • Frequency: how many waves pass per second (higher = higher pitch)
  • • Reflection: mirror bounces light back
  • • Refraction: light bends when passing through water or glass — this is why a straw looks bent in a cup
  • • Absorption: dark surfaces absorb light; light surfaces reflect it
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 4

Waves: Light and Sound

Investigate properties of waves and how light and sound travel.

Learning Objectives

Describe wavelength, amplitude, and frequency

Explain how light is reflected, refracted, and absorbed

Explain how the ear detects sound waves

Lessons

1. Wave Properties

Waves carry energy and have measurable properties.

Examples:

  • • Wavelength: distance from one peak to the next
  • • Amplitude: height of the wave (higher = louder sound or brighter light)
  • • Frequency: how many waves pass per second (higher = higher pitch)

2. Light: Reflection and Refraction

Light behaves differently when it hits different surfaces.

Examples:

  • • Reflection: mirror bounces light back
  • • Refraction: light bends when passing through water or glass — this is why a straw looks bent in a cup
  • • Absorption: dark surfaces absorb light; light surfaces reflect it

lessons.title: Electricity and Magnetism
lessons.content:
Electricity and Magnetism

Learning Objectives

  • • Wrap wire around a nail, connect to a battery → nail becomes magnetic
  • • Turn off the current → magnetism disappears
  • • Strength increases with more wire coils or stronger battery
  • • Series: one path — if one bulb goes out, all go out (old Christmas lights)
  • • Parallel: multiple paths — if one bulb goes out, others stay on (home wiring)
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 5

Electricity and Magnetism

Investigate the relationship between electricity and magnetism, including electromagnets.

Learning Objectives

Explain how an electromagnet works

Describe series and parallel circuits

Explore real-world uses of electromagnets

Lessons

1. Electromagnets

Running electricity through a wire coil creates a magnetic field.

Examples:

  • • Wrap wire around a nail, connect to a battery → nail becomes magnetic
  • • Turn off the current → magnetism disappears
  • • Strength increases with more wire coils or stronger battery

2. Series and Parallel Circuits

Circuits can be arranged in two ways.

Examples:

  • • Series: one path — if one bulb goes out, all go out (old Christmas lights)
  • • Parallel: multiple paths — if one bulb goes out, others stay on (home wiring)

lessons.title: Earth's History and Geologic Time
lessons.content:
Earth's History and Geologic Time

Learning Objectives

  • • If Earth's history were compressed into 24 hours, humans would appear in the last 2 seconds
  • • First life (simple cells): ~3.8 billion years ago
  • • Dinosaurs: 230–65 million years ago
  • • Ammonite fossils found in mountains prove these areas were once underwater
  • • Fossilized footprints show how dinosaurs moved
  • • Scientists use the age of surrounding rock to date fossils
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 6

Earth's History and Geologic Time

Explore the age of Earth, major geologic events, and evidence from fossils.

Learning Objectives

Describe Earth's formation approximately 4.6 billion years ago

Explain how fossils provide evidence of ancient life

Describe major events in Earth's history

Lessons

1. Earth's Timeline

Earth has existed for about 4.6 billion years — an almost unimaginable amount of time.

Examples:

  • • If Earth's history were compressed into 24 hours, humans would appear in the last 2 seconds
  • • First life (simple cells): ~3.8 billion years ago
  • • Dinosaurs: 230–65 million years ago

2. Fossils as Evidence

Fossils preserve clues about life that existed millions of years ago.

Examples:

  • • Ammonite fossils found in mountains prove these areas were once underwater
  • • Fossilized footprints show how dinosaurs moved
  • • Scientists use the age of surrounding rock to date fossils

lessons.title: Newton's Laws of Motion
lessons.content:
Newton's Laws of Motion

Learning Objectives

  • • Law 1 (Inertia): An object at rest stays at rest; an object in motion stays in motion unless a force acts on it.
  • • Law 2 (F = ma): More force = more acceleration; heavier objects need more force to move.
  • • Law 3 (Action-Reaction): For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.
  • • Law 1: You lurch forward when a car brakes suddenly (your body wants to keep moving)
  • • Law 2: Pushing a shopping cart vs. a car — same force, different acceleration
  • • Law 3: A swimmer pushes water back, water pushes the swimmer forward
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 7

Newton's Laws of Motion

Understand all three of Newton's Laws and apply them to real-world situations.

Learning Objectives

State and explain Newton's 3 Laws

Apply each law to everyday examples

Calculate force using F = m × a (conceptually)

Lessons

1. Newton's Three Laws

Three laws describe how objects move.

Examples:

  • • Law 1 (Inertia): An object at rest stays at rest; an object in motion stays in motion unless a force acts on it.
  • • Law 2 (F = ma): More force = more acceleration; heavier objects need more force to move.
  • • Law 3 (Action-Reaction): For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction.

2. Laws in Real Life

Newton's Laws explain everyday movement.

Examples:

  • • Law 1: You lurch forward when a car brakes suddenly (your body wants to keep moving)
  • • Law 2: Pushing a shopping cart vs. a car — same force, different acceleration
  • • Law 3: A swimmer pushes water back, water pushes the swimmer forward

lessons.title: The Solar System and Space Exploration
lessons.content:
The Solar System and Space Exploration

Learning Objectives

  • • Inner planets (rocky): Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
  • • Outer planets (gas giants): Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
  • • Asteroid belt: between Mars and Jupiter
  • • Comets: icy bodies with tails of gas and dust
  • • 1957: Sputnik — first satellite in orbit
  • • 1969: Apollo 11 — first humans on the Moon
  • • 2004–present: Mars rovers (Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance)
  • • James Webb Space Telescope: sees farther than ever before
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 8

The Solar System and Space Exploration

Explore the solar system in depth and learn about space exploration milestones.

Learning Objectives

Describe the sun, planets, asteroids, and comets

Explain gravity's role in keeping planets in orbit

Describe key milestones in space exploration

Lessons

1. Solar System in Depth

The solar system is held together by the sun's gravity.

Examples:

  • • Inner planets (rocky): Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars
  • • Outer planets (gas giants): Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune
  • • Asteroid belt: between Mars and Jupiter
  • • Comets: icy bodies with tails of gas and dust

2. Space Exploration

Humans have explored space with rockets, satellites, and rovers.

Examples:

  • • 1957: Sputnik — first satellite in orbit
  • • 1969: Apollo 11 — first humans on the Moon
  • • 2004–present: Mars rovers (Spirit, Opportunity, Curiosity, Perseverance)
  • • James Webb Space Telescope: sees farther than ever before

lessons.title: Human Body: Nutrition and Health
lessons.content:
Human Body: Nutrition and Health

Learning Objectives

  • • Carbohydrates: main energy source (bread, rice, fruit)
  • • Proteins: build and repair tissue (meat, beans, eggs)
  • • Fats: store energy and protect organs (nuts, oils, avocado)
  • • Vitamins: support body processes (C, D, B12...)
  • • Minerals: build bones and carry oxygen (calcium, iron, potassium)
  • • Water: makes up ~60% of the body and supports every process
  • • Exercise strengthens the heart and muscles
  • • Sleep allows the brain to consolidate memories and the body to repair
  • • Fruits and vegetables provide vitamins, minerals, and fiber
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 9

Human Body: Nutrition and Health

Explore how the body uses nutrients and how lifestyle choices affect health.

Learning Objectives

Identify the six classes of nutrients

Explain the role of each nutrient in the body

Evaluate the health benefits of food and activity choices

Lessons

1. Six Nutrients

The body needs six types of nutrients to function.

Examples:

  • • Carbohydrates: main energy source (bread, rice, fruit)
  • • Proteins: build and repair tissue (meat, beans, eggs)
  • • Fats: store energy and protect organs (nuts, oils, avocado)
  • • Vitamins: support body processes (C, D, B12...)
  • • Minerals: build bones and carry oxygen (calcium, iron, potassium)
  • • Water: makes up ~60% of the body and supports every process

2. Healthy Habits

Food choices and physical activity affect long-term health.

Examples:

  • • Exercise strengthens the heart and muscles
  • • Sleep allows the brain to consolidate memories and the body to repair
  • • Fruits and vegetables provide vitamins, minerals, and fiber

lessons.title: Engineering Design and Innovation
lessons.content:
Engineering Design and Innovation

Learning Objectives

  • • Bridge challenge: must hold 500g (criteria); can only use 20 popsicle sticks and tape (constraints)
  • • Real-world: a car must be safe and affordable; engineers can't use unlimited materials or time
  • • Test your bridge with increasing weights and record when it fails
  • • Graph the data: which design held the most weight?
  • • Present: explain your design, what worked, what you'd change
4th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 10

Engineering Design and Innovation

Apply advanced engineering design principles to tackle complex real-world challenges.

Learning Objectives

Refine the engineering design process with criteria and constraints

Compare and test multiple design solutions

Communicate and present design findings

Lessons

1. Criteria and Constraints

Every engineering challenge has criteria (what the design must do) and constraints (limits).

Examples:

  • • Bridge challenge: must hold 500g (criteria); can only use 20 popsicle sticks and tape (constraints)
  • • Real-world: a car must be safe and affordable; engineers can't use unlimited materials or time

2. Testing and Presenting Solutions

Engineers test designs, collect data, and communicate results.

Examples:

  • • Test your bridge with increasing weights and record when it fails
  • • Graph the data: which design held the most weight?
  • • Present: explain your design, what worked, what you'd change

courses.title: Science — 5th Grade
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 5th Grade.

lessons.title: Matter — Properties and Changes
lessons.content:
Matter — Properties and Changes

Learning Objectives

  • • Physical: color, density, melting point, conductivity
  • • Chemical: flammability, reactivity with acid, tendency to rust
  • • Physical: ice melting, tearing paper, dissolving salt
  • • Chemical: burning wood, rusting iron, baking a cake
  • • Evidence of chemical change: color change, gas production, heat/light, precipitate
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 1

Matter — Properties and Changes

Explore physical and chemical properties of matter and how matter changes.

Learning Objectives

Distinguish physical from chemical properties

Identify physical and chemical changes

Understand conservation of mass

Lessons

1. Properties of Matter

Matter has physical properties (observable without changing the substance) and chemical properties (how it reacts).

Examples:

  • • Physical: color, density, melting point, conductivity
  • • Chemical: flammability, reactivity with acid, tendency to rust

2. Physical vs. Chemical Changes

Physical changes don't create new substances; chemical changes do.

Examples:

  • • Physical: ice melting, tearing paper, dissolving salt
  • • Chemical: burning wood, rusting iron, baking a cake
  • • Evidence of chemical change: color change, gas production, heat/light, precipitate

lessons.title: Mixtures and Solutions
lessons.content:
Mixtures and Solutions

Learning Objectives

  • • Heterogeneous mixture: trail mix, salad, soil
  • • Homogeneous mixture (solution): salt water, lemonade, air
  • • Filtration: separates solids from liquids
  • • Evaporation: removes water to leave dissolved solids
  • • Magnetism: separate iron filings from sand
  • • Distillation: separate liquids with different boiling points
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 2

Mixtures and Solutions

Understand mixtures, solutions, and methods of separation.

Learning Objectives

Distinguish heterogeneous from homogeneous mixtures

Understand what affects solubility

Identify separation methods

Lessons

1. Mixtures vs. Solutions

A mixture combines substances physically; a solution is a uniform mixture.

Examples:

  • • Heterogeneous mixture: trail mix, salad, soil
  • • Homogeneous mixture (solution): salt water, lemonade, air

2. Separation Methods

Mixtures can be separated using physical methods.

Examples:

  • • Filtration: separates solids from liquids
  • • Evaporation: removes water to leave dissolved solids
  • • Magnetism: separate iron filings from sand
  • • Distillation: separate liquids with different boiling points

lessons.title: Force and Motion
lessons.content:
Force and Motion

Learning Objectives

  • • Contact forces: friction, tension, normal force
  • • Non-contact forces: gravity, magnetism, electrostatic force
  • • First Law: Objects in motion stay in motion unless acted on by a net force (inertia)
  • • Second Law: F = ma (force = mass × acceleration)
  • • Third Law: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 3

Force and Motion

Investigate forces and their effects on motion.

Learning Objectives

Define force and describe its types

Explain Newton's First and Second Laws

Calculate force, mass, and acceleration

Lessons

1. Types of Forces

Forces are pushes or pulls that can change an object's motion.

Examples:

  • • Contact forces: friction, tension, normal force
  • • Non-contact forces: gravity, magnetism, electrostatic force

2. Newton's Laws

Newton's laws describe how forces affect motion.

Examples:

  • • First Law: Objects in motion stay in motion unless acted on by a net force (inertia)
  • • Second Law: F = ma (force = mass × acceleration)
  • • Third Law: For every action there is an equal and opposite reaction

lessons.title: Ecosystems and Food Webs
lessons.content:
Ecosystems and Food Webs

Learning Objectives

  • • Grass → rabbit → fox → decomposer
  • • Producers make their own food (photosynthesis); consumers eat others
  • • Apex predators are at the top of the food chain
  • • Wolf reintroduction in Yellowstone: changed deer behavior → restored plants → changed rivers
  • • Invasive species: cane toads in Australia wiped out native predators
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 4

Ecosystems and Food Webs

Explore ecosystems, energy flow, and the impact of humans on ecosystems.

Learning Objectives

Explain energy flow through trophic levels

Distinguish predator-prey relationships

Describe human impact on ecosystems

Lessons

1. Food Chains and Webs

Energy flows from producers to consumers in a food chain; food webs show complex relationships.

Examples:

  • • Grass → rabbit → fox → decomposer
  • • Producers make their own food (photosynthesis); consumers eat others
  • • Apex predators are at the top of the food chain

2. Ecosystem Disruption

Removing or adding species can cascade through the whole ecosystem.

Examples:

  • • Wolf reintroduction in Yellowstone: changed deer behavior → restored plants → changed rivers
  • • Invasive species: cane toads in Australia wiped out native predators

lessons.title: Earth's Systems — Water Cycle
lessons.content:
Earth's Systems — Water Cycle

Learning Objectives

  • • Evaporation: liquid water becomes water vapor
  • • Condensation: water vapor becomes liquid (clouds)
  • • Precipitation: water falls as rain, snow, sleet, or hail
  • • Transpiration: plants release water vapor through leaves
  • • Only ~3% of Earth's water is fresh; most is frozen
  • • Groundwater replenishment depends on precipitation infiltrating the soil
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 5

Earth's Systems — Water Cycle

Trace water through the hydrological cycle and explain its importance.

Learning Objectives

Describe each stage of the water cycle

Explain how the water cycle distributes fresh water

Connect the water cycle to weather patterns

Lessons

1. The Water Cycle

Water continuously moves between Earth's surface and atmosphere.

Examples:

  • • Evaporation: liquid water becomes water vapor
  • • Condensation: water vapor becomes liquid (clouds)
  • • Precipitation: water falls as rain, snow, sleet, or hail
  • • Transpiration: plants release water vapor through leaves

2. Freshwater Distribution

Most of Earth's water is unusable; the water cycle is vital for freshwater supply.

Examples:

  • • Only ~3% of Earth's water is fresh; most is frozen
  • • Groundwater replenishment depends on precipitation infiltrating the soil

lessons.title: Earth's Layers and Plate Tectonics
lessons.content:
Earth's Layers and Plate Tectonics

Learning Objectives

  • • Crust: thin outer layer of rock (5–70 km)
  • • Mantle: thick layer of semi-solid rock (~2,900 km)
  • • Outer core: liquid iron and nickel
  • • Inner core: solid iron and nickel (temperatures ~5,400°C)
  • • Convergent: plates collide → mountains or subduction zones
  • • Divergent: plates separate → rift valleys or mid-ocean ridges
  • • Transform: plates slide past → earthquakes (San Andreas Fault)
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 6

Earth's Layers and Plate Tectonics

Describe Earth's interior structure and the theory of plate tectonics.

Learning Objectives

Name and describe Earth's layers

Explain plate movement and its consequences

Identify evidence for plate tectonics

Lessons

1. Earth's Layers

Earth has four main layers with different compositions and properties.

Examples:

  • • Crust: thin outer layer of rock (5–70 km)
  • • Mantle: thick layer of semi-solid rock (~2,900 km)
  • • Outer core: liquid iron and nickel
  • • Inner core: solid iron and nickel (temperatures ~5,400°C)

2. Plate Tectonics

Earth's crust is divided into moving plates that interact at boundaries.

Examples:

  • • Convergent: plates collide → mountains or subduction zones
  • • Divergent: plates separate → rift valleys or mid-ocean ridges
  • • Transform: plates slide past → earthquakes (San Andreas Fault)

lessons.title: Energy Transformations
lessons.content:
Energy Transformations

Learning Objectives

  • • Kinetic: energy of motion
  • • Potential: stored energy (gravitational, elastic, chemical)
  • • Thermal, electromagnetic, nuclear, sound energy
  • • Light bulb: electrical → light + thermal
  • • Car: chemical (fuel) → mechanical (motion) + thermal
  • • Solar panel: light → electrical
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 7

Energy Transformations

Identify types of energy and how energy transforms from one form to another.

Learning Objectives

Identify kinetic and potential energy

Trace energy transformations

Apply conservation of energy

Lessons

1. Types of Energy

Energy exists in many forms and can transfer between them.

Examples:

  • • Kinetic: energy of motion
  • • Potential: stored energy (gravitational, elastic, chemical)
  • • Thermal, electromagnetic, nuclear, sound energy

2. Energy Transformations

Energy changes form but is never created or destroyed.

Examples:

  • • Light bulb: electrical → light + thermal
  • • Car: chemical (fuel) → mechanical (motion) + thermal
  • • Solar panel: light → electrical

lessons.title: Human Body Systems
lessons.content:
Human Body Systems

Learning Objectives

  • • Circulatory: heart, blood vessels, blood — transports nutrients and oxygen
  • • Respiratory: lungs — oxygen/CO2 exchange
  • • Digestive: breaks down food into nutrients
  • • Nervous: brain, spinal cord, nerves — control and communication
  • • Running: respiratory (more O2), circulatory (faster heart), muscular, nervous, skeletal — all involved simultaneously
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 8

Human Body Systems

Explore the major human body systems and how they interact.

Learning Objectives

Name and describe major body systems

Explain how systems work together

Connect lifestyle choices to body system health

Lessons

1. Body Systems

The body has 11 organ systems that work together.

Examples:

  • • Circulatory: heart, blood vessels, blood — transports nutrients and oxygen
  • • Respiratory: lungs — oxygen/CO2 exchange
  • • Digestive: breaks down food into nutrients
  • • Nervous: brain, spinal cord, nerves — control and communication

2. System Interactions

No system works alone; they are all interdependent.

Examples:

  • • Running: respiratory (more O2), circulatory (faster heart), muscular, nervous, skeletal — all involved simultaneously

lessons.title: Genetics — Traits and Heredity
lessons.content:
Genetics — Traits and Heredity

Learning Objectives

  • • DNA is organized into chromosomes; humans have 46 (23 pairs)
  • • A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a trait
  • • You inherit one copy of each gene from each parent
  • • Brown eyes (B) dominant over blue eyes (b)
  • • BB or Bb → brown eyes; bb → blue eyes
  • • Punnett square: cross Bb × Bb → 25% BB, 50% Bb, 25% bb
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 9

Genetics — Traits and Heredity

Understand how traits are inherited from parents to offspring.

Learning Objectives

Define gene, chromosome, DNA, and trait

Distinguish dominant from recessive traits

Predict offspring traits using a Punnett square

Lessons

1. DNA and Genes

DNA is the molecule that carries genetic information in every living cell.

Examples:

  • • DNA is organized into chromosomes; humans have 46 (23 pairs)
  • • A gene is a section of DNA that codes for a trait
  • • You inherit one copy of each gene from each parent

2. Dominant and Recessive Traits

Some alleles are dominant (always expressed if present); others are recessive (only expressed when two copies are present).

Examples:

  • • Brown eyes (B) dominant over blue eyes (b)
  • • BB or Bb → brown eyes; bb → blue eyes
  • • Punnett square: cross Bb × Bb → 25% BB, 50% Bb, 25% bb

lessons.title: Environmental Science — Sustainability
lessons.content:
Environmental Science — Sustainability

Learning Objectives

  • • Deforestation: loss of biodiversity, carbon release, disrupted water cycle
  • • Ocean plastic: over 8 million tonnes enter oceans each year
  • • Climate change: warming temperatures, extreme weather, sea level rise
  • • Renewable energy: solar, wind, hydroelectric replaces fossil fuels
  • • Circular economy: design products to be reused/recycled
  • • Rewilding: restoring natural ecosystems
5th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 10

Environmental Science — Sustainability

Explore sustainability, environmental challenges, and solutions.

Learning Objectives

Define sustainability

Describe major environmental challenges

Identify solutions and evaluate trade-offs

Lessons

1. Environmental Challenges

Human activity has created major environmental problems.

Examples:

  • • Deforestation: loss of biodiversity, carbon release, disrupted water cycle
  • • Ocean plastic: over 8 million tonnes enter oceans each year
  • • Climate change: warming temperatures, extreme weather, sea level rise

2. Sustainable Solutions

Sustainability means meeting today's needs without compromising the future.

Examples:

  • • Renewable energy: solar, wind, hydroelectric replaces fossil fuels
  • • Circular economy: design products to be reused/recycled
  • • Rewilding: restoring natural ecosystems

courses.title: Science — 6th Grade
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 6th Grade.

lessons.title: Scientific Method and Lab Skills
lessons.content:
Scientific Method and Lab Skills

Learning Objectives

  • • Observation → Question → Hypothesis → Experiment → Data → Conclusion
  • • Hypothesis format: 'If [independent variable], then [dependent variable], because [reasoning]'
  • • Control group: receives no treatment; used for comparison
  • • Independent variable: what you change
  • • Dependent variable: what you measure
  • • Controlled variables: everything else kept the same
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 1

Scientific Method and Lab Skills

Master the scientific method and essential laboratory skills.

Learning Objectives

Write a testable hypothesis

Design a controlled experiment

Analyze data and draw conclusions

Lessons

1. The Scientific Method

Science follows a systematic process to test ideas.

Examples:

  • • Observation → Question → Hypothesis → Experiment → Data → Conclusion
  • • Hypothesis format: 'If [independent variable], then [dependent variable], because [reasoning]'
  • • Control group: receives no treatment; used for comparison

2. Variables

Identify and control variables for a fair test.

Examples:

  • • Independent variable: what you change
  • • Dependent variable: what you measure
  • • Controlled variables: everything else kept the same

lessons.title: Cells — Structure and Function
lessons.content:
Cells — Structure and Function

Learning Objectives

  • • Nucleus: control center (contains DNA)
  • • Mitochondria: powerhouse (produces ATP via cellular respiration)
  • • Chloroplast: site of photosynthesis (plant cells only)
  • • Cell membrane: controls what enters/exits
  • • Ribosome: makes proteins
  • • Prokaryotes: bacteria, archaea
  • • Eukaryotes: animals, plants, fungi, protists
  • • All organisms on Earth are one or the other
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 2

Cells — Structure and Function

Study cell organelles and the differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

Learning Objectives

Identify cell organelles and their functions

Distinguish plant from animal cells

Compare prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells

Lessons

1. Cell Organelles

Each organelle has a specific function, like organs in a body.

Examples:

  • • Nucleus: control center (contains DNA)
  • • Mitochondria: powerhouse (produces ATP via cellular respiration)
  • • Chloroplast: site of photosynthesis (plant cells only)
  • • Cell membrane: controls what enters/exits
  • • Ribosome: makes proteins

2. Prokaryotes vs. Eukaryotes

Prokaryotes lack a nucleus; eukaryotes have a membrane-bound nucleus.

Examples:

  • • Prokaryotes: bacteria, archaea
  • • Eukaryotes: animals, plants, fungi, protists
  • • All organisms on Earth are one or the other

lessons.title: Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration
lessons.content:
Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration

Learning Objectives

  • • 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
  • • Takes place in chloroplasts
  • • Glucose stores the energy from sunlight as chemical energy
  • • C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP
  • • Aerobic (with O₂): most efficient — 36-38 ATP per glucose
  • • Anaerobic: lactic acid fermentation in muscles; yeast produces CO₂ + alcohol
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 3

Photosynthesis and Cellular Respiration

Understand how plants produce food and how all cells release energy.

Learning Objectives

Write and explain the equation for photosynthesis

Write and explain cellular respiration

Explain how they are complementary processes

Lessons

1. Photosynthesis

Plants use light energy to convert CO₂ and water into glucose and oxygen.

Examples:

  • • 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂
  • • Takes place in chloroplasts
  • • Glucose stores the energy from sunlight as chemical energy

2. Cellular Respiration

All living cells break down glucose to release usable energy (ATP).

Examples:

  • • C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP
  • • Aerobic (with O₂): most efficient — 36-38 ATP per glucose
  • • Anaerobic: lactic acid fermentation in muscles; yeast produces CO₂ + alcohol

lessons.title: Atoms and Elements
lessons.content:
Atoms and Elements

Learning Objectives

  • • Protons: positive charge, in nucleus; number defines the element
  • • Neutrons: no charge, in nucleus; affect atomic mass
  • • Electrons: negative charge, orbit in shells
  • • Rows (periods): elements with same number of electron shells
  • • Columns (groups): elements with similar chemical properties
  • • Metals, nonmetals, and metalloids have characteristic properties
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 4

Atoms and Elements

Explore atomic structure, elements, and the periodic table.

Learning Objectives

Describe the structure of an atom

Use the periodic table to find element information

Understand atomic number and atomic mass

Lessons

1. Atomic Structure

Atoms are made of protons, neutrons, and electrons.

Examples:

  • • Protons: positive charge, in nucleus; number defines the element
  • • Neutrons: no charge, in nucleus; affect atomic mass
  • • Electrons: negative charge, orbit in shells

2. The Periodic Table

Elements are organized by atomic number in the periodic table.

Examples:

  • • Rows (periods): elements with same number of electron shells
  • • Columns (groups): elements with similar chemical properties
  • • Metals, nonmetals, and metalloids have characteristic properties

lessons.title: Weather and Climate Science
lessons.content:
Weather and Climate Science

Learning Objectives

  • • Uneven heating: equator receives more solar energy than poles → wind and ocean currents
  • • Convection cells: Hadley, Ferrel, and Polar cells move heat around the globe
  • • Coriolis effect: Earth's rotation deflects winds to the right in northern hemisphere
  • • Latitude: closer to equator = warmer
  • • Altitude: higher = colder (temp drops ~6.5°C per 1,000 m)
  • • Ocean currents: Gulf Stream warms Europe
  • • Rain shadow: leeward side of mountains is drier
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 5

Weather and Climate Science

Investigate atmospheric science, weather patterns, and climate.

Learning Objectives

Explain how the sun drives weather

Describe factors that influence climate

Interpret weather maps and data

Lessons

1. Atmospheric Energy

The sun drives atmospheric circulation, which creates weather.

Examples:

  • • Uneven heating: equator receives more solar energy than poles → wind and ocean currents
  • • Convection cells: Hadley, Ferrel, and Polar cells move heat around the globe
  • • Coriolis effect: Earth's rotation deflects winds to the right in northern hemisphere

2. Climate Factors

Multiple factors determine a region's climate.

Examples:

  • • Latitude: closer to equator = warmer
  • • Altitude: higher = colder (temp drops ~6.5°C per 1,000 m)
  • • Ocean currents: Gulf Stream warms Europe
  • • Rain shadow: leeward side of mountains is drier

lessons.title: Waves — Light and Sound
lessons.content:
Waves — Light and Sound

Learning Objectives

  • • Wavelength: distance between crests
  • • Frequency: number of waves per second (Hertz)
  • • Amplitude: height of wave (related to energy)
  • • v = fλ (wave speed = frequency × wavelength)
  • • Sound: longitudinal wave — travels through air, water, solids; ~343 m/s in air
  • • Light: transverse electromagnetic wave — travels through vacuum at 3×10⁸ m/s
  • • Electromagnetic spectrum: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma ray
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 6

Waves — Light and Sound

Understand wave properties and the behavior of light and sound.

Learning Objectives

Identify wave properties: wavelength, frequency, amplitude

Explain how sound travels

Describe the electromagnetic spectrum

Lessons

1. Wave Properties

Waves transfer energy without transferring matter.

Examples:

  • • Wavelength: distance between crests
  • • Frequency: number of waves per second (Hertz)
  • • Amplitude: height of wave (related to energy)
  • • v = fλ (wave speed = frequency × wavelength)

2. Light and Sound

Sound needs a medium; light does not.

Examples:

  • • Sound: longitudinal wave — travels through air, water, solids; ~343 m/s in air
  • • Light: transverse electromagnetic wave — travels through vacuum at 3×10⁸ m/s
  • • Electromagnetic spectrum: radio, microwave, infrared, visible, UV, X-ray, gamma ray

lessons.title: Heredity and Evolution
lessons.content:
Heredity and Evolution

Learning Objectives

  • • Darwin's finches: different beak shapes evolved for different food sources
  • • Antibiotic resistance: bacteria with resistance genes survive → reproduce → resistance spreads
  • • 4 requirements: variation, inheritance, differential survival, time
  • • Fossil record: shows change over time
  • • Comparative anatomy: homologous structures (human arm, bat wing, whale flipper)
  • • DNA evidence: humans share ~98.8% of DNA with chimpanzees
  • • Biogeography: related species on nearby islands
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 7

Heredity and Evolution

Connect genetics to evolution and natural selection.

Learning Objectives

Explain natural selection

Describe evidence for evolution

Connect genetic variation to evolution

Lessons

1. Natural Selection

Traits that improve survival and reproduction become more common over time.

Examples:

  • • Darwin's finches: different beak shapes evolved for different food sources
  • • Antibiotic resistance: bacteria with resistance genes survive → reproduce → resistance spreads
  • • 4 requirements: variation, inheritance, differential survival, time

2. Evidence for Evolution

Multiple independent lines of evidence support evolution.

Examples:

  • • Fossil record: shows change over time
  • • Comparative anatomy: homologous structures (human arm, bat wing, whale flipper)
  • • DNA evidence: humans share ~98.8% of DNA with chimpanzees
  • • Biogeography: related species on nearby islands

lessons.title: Space Science — Solar System
lessons.content:
Space Science — Solar System

Learning Objectives

  • • Nebular hypothesis: cloud of gas collapsed under gravity → sun formed at center
  • • Remaining material clumped together to form planets
  • • Terrestrial planets (rocky): Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — inner solar system
  • • Gas giants: Jupiter, Saturn; Ice giants: Uranus, Neptune — outer solar system
  • • Planets closer to the sun move faster and have shorter years
  • • Earth orbits the sun at ~29.8 km/s
  • • Kepler's 3rd law: the farther from the sun, the longer the orbital period
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 8

Space Science — Solar System

Explore the solar system, its formation, and the planets within it.

Learning Objectives

Describe how the solar system formed

Compare the planets

Explain orbital mechanics and gravity

Lessons

1. Solar System Formation

The solar system formed ~4.6 billion years ago from a spinning disk of gas and dust.

Examples:

  • • Nebular hypothesis: cloud of gas collapsed under gravity → sun formed at center
  • • Remaining material clumped together to form planets
  • • Terrestrial planets (rocky): Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars — inner solar system
  • • Gas giants: Jupiter, Saturn; Ice giants: Uranus, Neptune — outer solar system

2. Orbital Mechanics

Gravity keeps planets in orbit; Kepler's laws describe how.

Examples:

  • • Planets closer to the sun move faster and have shorter years
  • • Earth orbits the sun at ~29.8 km/s
  • • Kepler's 3rd law: the farther from the sun, the longer the orbital period

lessons.title: Human Impact on Earth
lessons.content:
Human Impact on Earth

Learning Objectives

  • • CO₂, methane, and water vapor trap heat in atmosphere
  • • Since 1880, global average temperature has risen ~1.1°C
  • • Effects: more frequent extreme weather, glacier melt, sea level rise, ocean acidification
  • • Habitat destruction is the #1 cause of species loss
  • • Invasive species, pollution, overhunting, and climate change also contribute
  • • 1 million species are threatened with extinction (IPBES, 2019)
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 9

Human Impact on Earth

Analyze how human activity affects Earth's systems and what can be done.

Learning Objectives

Explain the greenhouse effect and climate change

Describe impacts on biodiversity

Evaluate solutions

Lessons

1. Climate Change Mechanisms

The greenhouse effect is natural; humans are intensifying it.

Examples:

  • • CO₂, methane, and water vapor trap heat in atmosphere
  • • Since 1880, global average temperature has risen ~1.1°C
  • • Effects: more frequent extreme weather, glacier melt, sea level rise, ocean acidification

2. Biodiversity Loss

Current extinction rates are 100-1,000× background rates — a mass extinction.

Examples:

  • • Habitat destruction is the #1 cause of species loss
  • • Invasive species, pollution, overhunting, and climate change also contribute
  • • 1 million species are threatened with extinction (IPBES, 2019)

lessons.title: Engineering Design Process
lessons.content:
Engineering Design Process

Learning Objectives

  • • Define: What is the problem? What are the criteria (what it must do) and constraints (limits)?
  • • Brainstorm: Generate many possible solutions
  • • Prototype: Build a testable model
  • • Test: Evaluate against criteria
  • • Improve: Use test results to refine the design
6th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 10

Engineering Design Process

Apply the engineering design process to solve a real-world problem.

Learning Objectives

Define a problem and establish criteria and constraints

Generate, test, and evaluate solutions

Communicate design decisions

Lessons

1. The EDP

Engineers follow an iterative design process.

Examples:

  • • Define: What is the problem? What are the criteria (what it must do) and constraints (limits)?
  • • Brainstorm: Generate many possible solutions
  • • Prototype: Build a testable model
  • • Test: Evaluate against criteria
  • • Improve: Use test results to refine the design

courses.title: Science — 7th Grade
courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 7th Grade.

lessons.title: Life Science — Cells to Organisms
lessons.content:
Life Science — Cells to Organisms

Learning Objectives

  • • Muscle cells → muscle tissue → muscular system → organism
  • • Unicellular: does all life functions in one cell (amoeba, bacteria)
  • • Multicellular: division of labor — cells specialize for efficiency
  • • Mitosis: produces 2 identical daughter cells (growth, repair)
  • • Meiosis: produces 4 genetically unique cells (reproduction)
  • • Uncontrolled cell division = cancer
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 1

Life Science — Cells to Organisms

Explore levels of biological organization from cells to ecosystems.

Learning Objectives

Describe levels of organization: cell → tissue → organ → system → organism

Explain how cell specialization enables multicellular life

Compare unicellular and multicellular organisms

Lessons

1. Levels of Organization

In multicellular organisms, cells specialize and work together.

Examples:

  • • Muscle cells → muscle tissue → muscular system → organism
  • • Unicellular: does all life functions in one cell (amoeba, bacteria)
  • • Multicellular: division of labor — cells specialize for efficiency

2. Cell Division

Cells reproduce by dividing to allow growth and repair.

Examples:

  • • Mitosis: produces 2 identical daughter cells (growth, repair)
  • • Meiosis: produces 4 genetically unique cells (reproduction)
  • • Uncontrolled cell division = cancer

lessons.title: Ecosystems — Cycling of Matter
lessons.content:
Ecosystems — Cycling of Matter

Learning Objectives

  • • Photosynthesis: CO₂ → organic carbon (in plants)
  • • Respiration and decomposition: organic carbon → CO₂
  • • Fossil fuels: ancient carbon released back to atmosphere by burning — disrupts the cycle
  • • Nitrogen fixation: bacteria convert N₂ to ammonia (NH₃)
  • • Nitrification: bacteria convert ammonia to nitrates
  • • Denitrification: bacteria return N₂ to atmosphere
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 2

Ecosystems — Cycling of Matter

Study how matter cycles through ecosystems via biogeochemical cycles.

Learning Objectives

Trace carbon through the carbon cycle

Describe the nitrogen cycle

Explain how matter cycling differs from energy flow

Lessons

1. Carbon Cycle

Carbon cycles between the atmosphere, organisms, and Earth's crust.

Examples:

  • • Photosynthesis: CO₂ → organic carbon (in plants)
  • • Respiration and decomposition: organic carbon → CO₂
  • • Fossil fuels: ancient carbon released back to atmosphere by burning — disrupts the cycle

2. Nitrogen Cycle

Nitrogen makes up 78% of air but most organisms can't use it directly.

Examples:

  • • Nitrogen fixation: bacteria convert N₂ to ammonia (NH₃)
  • • Nitrification: bacteria convert ammonia to nitrates
  • • Denitrification: bacteria return N₂ to atmosphere

lessons.title: Chemical Reactions
lessons.content:
Chemical Reactions

Learning Objectives

  • • 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (synthesis)
  • • CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (decomposition)
  • • CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (combustion)
  • • H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (unbalanced) → 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (balanced)
  • • Count each element on both sides; add coefficients to balance
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 3

Chemical Reactions

Understand chemical reactions, balancing equations, and reaction types.

Learning Objectives

Recognize evidence of chemical reactions

Balance simple chemical equations

Identify synthesis, decomposition, and combustion reactions

Lessons

1. Chemical Equations

Chemical equations show reactants → products, with atoms balanced on both sides.

Examples:

  • • 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (synthesis)
  • • CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (decomposition)
  • • CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O (combustion)

2. Balancing Equations

Matter is conserved — atoms must balance on both sides.

Examples:

  • • H₂ + O₂ → H₂O (unbalanced) → 2H₂ + O₂ → 2H₂O (balanced)
  • • Count each element on both sides; add coefficients to balance

lessons.title: Forces and Newton's Laws
lessons.content:
Forces and Newton's Laws

Learning Objectives

  • • 1st Law: A soccer ball stays put until kicked; a sliding puck keeps sliding until friction stops it
  • • 2nd Law: F=ma. A 10 kg object accelerated at 3 m/s² requires 30 N
  • • 3rd Law: Rocket propulsion; walking (push ground back, ground pushes you forward)
  • • p = mv: a 60 kg person running at 5 m/s has momentum = 300 kg·m/s
  • • Impulse (force × time) changes momentum: airbags increase collision time to reduce force
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 4

Forces and Newton's Laws

Apply Newton's three laws to real-world situations involving motion and forces.

Learning Objectives

Apply Newton's three laws to scenarios

Calculate net force, acceleration, and momentum

Explain friction, gravity, and air resistance

Lessons

1. Newton's Three Laws

Newton's laws govern all motion we observe in everyday life.

Examples:

  • • 1st Law: A soccer ball stays put until kicked; a sliding puck keeps sliding until friction stops it
  • • 2nd Law: F=ma. A 10 kg object accelerated at 3 m/s² requires 30 N
  • • 3rd Law: Rocket propulsion; walking (push ground back, ground pushes you forward)

2. Friction and Momentum

Friction opposes motion; momentum is mass × velocity.

Examples:

  • • p = mv: a 60 kg person running at 5 m/s has momentum = 300 kg·m/s
  • • Impulse (force × time) changes momentum: airbags increase collision time to reduce force

lessons.title: Electricity and Circuits
lessons.content:
Electricity and Circuits

Learning Objectives

  • • Rubbing a balloon: electrons transfer to balloon (negative charge)
  • • Opposite charges attract; like charges repel
  • • Lightning: charge buildup between clouds and ground discharges dramatically
  • • V=12V, R=4Ω → I=3A
  • • Series circuit: one path; one bulb out = all out
  • • Parallel circuit: multiple paths; one bulb out = others stay on
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 5

Electricity and Circuits

Understand electric charge, current, and how circuits work.

Learning Objectives

Explain static electricity and charge transfer

Describe current, voltage, and resistance (Ohm's Law)

Analyze series and parallel circuits

Lessons

1. Static Electricity

Charge builds up when electrons transfer between objects.

Examples:

  • • Rubbing a balloon: electrons transfer to balloon (negative charge)
  • • Opposite charges attract; like charges repel
  • • Lightning: charge buildup between clouds and ground discharges dramatically

2. Circuits and Ohm's Law

V = IR: voltage = current × resistance.

Examples:

  • • V=12V, R=4Ω → I=3A
  • • Series circuit: one path; one bulb out = all out
  • • Parallel circuit: multiple paths; one bulb out = others stay on

lessons.title: Astronomy — Stars and Galaxies
lessons.content:
Astronomy — Stars and Galaxies

Learning Objectives

  • • Low-mass star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
  • • High-mass star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
  • • Our sun is a middle-aged, medium-mass star ~halfway through its 10-billion-year life
  • • Milky Way: ~200-400 billion stars; barred spiral galaxy; ~100,000 light-years across
  • • Three types: spiral, elliptical, irregular
  • • Observable universe: ~2 trillion galaxies
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 6

Astronomy — Stars and Galaxies

Study the life cycle of stars, types of galaxies, and the scale of the universe.

Learning Objectives

Describe the stellar life cycle

Classify stars using the H-R Diagram

Describe the structure of galaxies and the universe

Lessons

1. Stellar Life Cycle

Stars are born from nebulae and end in dramatically different ways depending on mass.

Examples:

  • • Low-mass star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red giant → planetary nebula → white dwarf
  • • High-mass star: nebula → protostar → main sequence → red supergiant → supernova → neutron star or black hole
  • • Our sun is a middle-aged, medium-mass star ~halfway through its 10-billion-year life

2. Galaxies

Galaxies are vast systems of stars, gas, and dark matter.

Examples:

  • • Milky Way: ~200-400 billion stars; barred spiral galaxy; ~100,000 light-years across
  • • Three types: spiral, elliptical, irregular
  • • Observable universe: ~2 trillion galaxies

lessons.title: Climate Change Science
lessons.content:
Climate Change Science

Learning Objectives

  • • Pre-industrial CO₂: ~280 ppm; today: ~420 ppm — highest in 800,000 years
  • • Feedback loops: warming → melting ice → less reflection → more warming
  • • Ocean acidification: CO₂ dissolves in seawater → carbonic acid → threatens marine life
  • • Mitigation: renewable energy, electric vehicles, reforestation, carbon capture
  • • Adaptation: sea walls, drought-resistant crops, early warning systems
  • • Net-zero: balancing emissions with carbon removal
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 7

Climate Change Science

Deepen understanding of the scientific mechanisms and evidence for climate change.

Learning Objectives

Explain the enhanced greenhouse effect

Analyze climate data and trends

Evaluate mitigation and adaptation strategies

Lessons

1. Enhanced Greenhouse Effect

Human CO₂ emissions are intensifying the natural greenhouse effect.

Examples:

  • • Pre-industrial CO₂: ~280 ppm; today: ~420 ppm — highest in 800,000 years
  • • Feedback loops: warming → melting ice → less reflection → more warming
  • • Ocean acidification: CO₂ dissolves in seawater → carbonic acid → threatens marine life

2. Mitigation and Adaptation

Both reducing emissions and adapting to changes are necessary.

Examples:

  • • Mitigation: renewable energy, electric vehicles, reforestation, carbon capture
  • • Adaptation: sea walls, drought-resistant crops, early warning systems
  • • Net-zero: balancing emissions with carbon removal

lessons.title: Biotechnology and Genetics
lessons.content:
Biotechnology and Genetics

Learning Objectives

  • • PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): rapidly copies DNA — used in COVID tests, forensics
  • • DNA sequencing: reading the order of base pairs — cost dropped from billions to ~$100
  • • GMOs: organisms with modified DNA for desired traits (Bt corn, golden rice)
  • • Can insert, delete, or modify specific genes
  • • Medical potential: curing sickle cell disease, potentially preventing hereditary cancers
  • • Ethical concerns: 'designer babies', germline editing, inequality in access
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 8

Biotechnology and Genetics

Explore modern genetic technologies and their scientific, ethical, and social dimensions.

Learning Objectives

Explain how DNA is used in biotechnology

Describe CRISPR gene editing

Evaluate ethical issues in biotechnology

Lessons

1. DNA Technology

Scientists can now read, copy, and edit DNA.

Examples:

  • • PCR (Polymerase Chain Reaction): rapidly copies DNA — used in COVID tests, forensics
  • • DNA sequencing: reading the order of base pairs — cost dropped from billions to ~$100
  • • GMOs: organisms with modified DNA for desired traits (Bt corn, golden rice)

2. CRISPR

CRISPR-Cas9 allows precise gene editing.

Examples:

  • • Can insert, delete, or modify specific genes
  • • Medical potential: curing sickle cell disease, potentially preventing hereditary cancers
  • • Ethical concerns: 'designer babies', germline editing, inequality in access

lessons.title: Earth History and Geologic Time
lessons.content:
Earth History and Geologic Time

Learning Objectives

  • • Relative dating: Law of Superposition — older layers are on the bottom
  • • Absolute dating: radioactive decay — half-life allows calculation of age
  • • Carbon-14: effective for up to ~50,000 years; uranium-lead: billions of years
  • • Hadean (4.6–4.0 Ga): Earth forms; molten, no atmosphere
  • • Archean (4.0–2.5 Ga): first life (single-celled)
  • • Cambrian explosion (~541 Ma): sudden diversification of multicellular life
  • • Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction (66 Ma): asteroid wipes out non-avian dinosaurs
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 9

Earth History and Geologic Time

Read the fossil record and understand geologic time scales.

Learning Objectives

Describe methods of dating rocks and fossils

Explain major events in Earth's history

Interpret a geologic time scale

Lessons

1. Dating Rocks and Fossils

Scientists use relative and absolute dating to determine ages.

Examples:

  • • Relative dating: Law of Superposition — older layers are on the bottom
  • • Absolute dating: radioactive decay — half-life allows calculation of age
  • • Carbon-14: effective for up to ~50,000 years; uranium-lead: billions of years

2. Geologic Time

Earth is ~4.6 billion years old; life has been evolving for ~3.8 billion years.

Examples:

  • • Hadean (4.6–4.0 Ga): Earth forms; molten, no atmosphere
  • • Archean (4.0–2.5 Ga): first life (single-celled)
  • • Cambrian explosion (~541 Ma): sudden diversification of multicellular life
  • • Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction (66 Ma): asteroid wipes out non-avian dinosaurs

lessons.title: Physics — Energy, Work, and Machines
lessons.content:
Physics — Energy, Work, and Machines

Learning Objectives

  • • Lifting a 20 N box 3 m: W = 60 J
  • • Doing 300 J of work in 10 seconds: P = 30 W
  • • No movement = no work (in physics), even if you're pushing hard!
  • • Lever: crowbar (MA = load arm ÷ effort arm)
  • • Pulley: flagpole, crane (each additional pulley reduces force needed)
  • • Inclined plane: ramp (longer ramp = less force but more distance)
  • • Wheel/axle, wedge, screw are the other three
7th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 10

Physics — Energy, Work, and Machines

Understand work, power, simple machines, and mechanical advantage.

Learning Objectives

Calculate work and power

Identify six types of simple machines

Calculate mechanical advantage

Lessons

1. Work and Power

Work = Force × Distance; Power = Work / Time.

Examples:

  • • Lifting a 20 N box 3 m: W = 60 J
  • • Doing 300 J of work in 10 seconds: P = 30 W
  • • No movement = no work (in physics), even if you're pushing hard!

2. Simple Machines

Simple machines multiply force or change its direction.

Examples:

  • • Lever: crowbar (MA = load arm ÷ effort arm)
  • • Pulley: flagpole, crane (each additional pulley reduces force needed)
  • • Inclined plane: ramp (longer ramp = less force but more distance)
  • • Wheel/axle, wedge, screw are the other three

courses.description: Life, earth, physical science & more. Grade level: 8th Grade.

lessons.title: Physical Science — Structure of Matter
lessons.content:
Physical Science — Structure of Matter

Learning Objectives

  • • Bohr model (1913): electrons in fixed orbits — useful but simplified
  • • Electron cloud model: electrons exist in regions of probability
  • • Electron configuration determines chemical behavior
  • • Ionic bond: electron transfer between metal and non-metal (NaCl: Na⁺ and Cl⁻)
  • • Covalent bond: electron sharing between non-metals (H₂O: O shares electrons with 2 H)
  • • Metallic bond: sea of electrons shared among metal atoms → conducts electricity
8th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 1

Physical Science — Structure of Matter

Study atomic structure, the periodic table, and chemical bonding.

Learning Objectives

Describe atomic models historically and currently

Read the periodic table (periods, groups, blocks)

Explain ionic and covalent bonding

Lessons

1. Modern Atomic Model

The modern quantum model describes electrons in probability clouds called orbitals.

Examples:

  • • Bohr model (1913): electrons in fixed orbits — useful but simplified
  • • Electron cloud model: electrons exist in regions of probability
  • • Electron configuration determines chemical behavior

2. Chemical Bonding

Atoms bond to achieve stable electron configurations.

Examples:

  • • Ionic bond: electron transfer between metal and non-metal (NaCl: Na⁺ and Cl⁻)
  • • Covalent bond: electron sharing between non-metals (H₂O: O shares electrons with 2 H)
  • • Metallic bond: sea of electrons shared among metal atoms → conducts electricity

lessons.content: Acids, Bases, and pH

lessons.title: Motion and Forces — Advanced
lessons.content: Motion and Forces — Advanced

lessons.title: Energy — Heat and Thermodynamics
lessons.content:
Energy — Heat and Thermodynamics

Learning Objectives

  • • Conduction: direct contact (metal spoon in hot soup)
  • • Convection: fluid movement (hot air rises, cool air sinks)
  • • Radiation: electromagnetic waves (sun heats Earth across vacuum)
  • • 1st Law: energy cannot be created or destroyed; ΔU = Q − W
  • • 2nd Law: heat flows naturally from hot to cold; disorder (entropy) increases
  • • Why machines can't be 100% efficient: some energy always lost to heat
8th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 4

Energy — Heat and Thermodynamics

Study heat transfer, thermal energy, and the laws of thermodynamics.

Learning Objectives

Distinguish temperature from thermal energy

Describe heat transfer mechanisms

Apply the first and second laws of thermodynamics

Lessons

1. Heat Transfer

Thermal energy moves from hot to cold by three mechanisms.

Examples:

  • • Conduction: direct contact (metal spoon in hot soup)
  • • Convection: fluid movement (hot air rises, cool air sinks)
  • • Radiation: electromagnetic waves (sun heats Earth across vacuum)

2. Laws of Thermodynamics

Energy is conserved; entropy always increases.

Examples:

  • • 1st Law: energy cannot be created or destroyed; ΔU = Q − W
  • • 2nd Law: heat flows naturally from hot to cold; disorder (entropy) increases
  • • Why machines can't be 100% efficient: some energy always lost to heat

lessons.title: Electromagnetism
lessons.content:
Electromagnetism

Learning Objectives

  • • Earth acts like a giant magnet — magnetic north is near geographic north
  • • Oersted (1820): discovered that current-carrying wire deflects a compass
  • • Solenoid: coil of wire carrying current creates a strong magnetic field (electromagnet)
  • • Faraday's Law of Induction (1831): moving a magnet through a coil generates electricity
  • • Generator: converts mechanical energy to electrical energy (rotating magnet in coil)
  • • Motor: converts electrical energy to mechanical (current in magnetic field creates force)
8th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 5

Electromagnetism

Explore the relationship between electricity and magnetism.

Learning Objectives

Describe magnetic fields and poles

Explain electromagnetic induction

Understand how motors and generators work

Lessons

1. Magnetic Fields

Every magnet creates a magnetic field; electric currents also create magnetic fields.

Examples:

  • • Earth acts like a giant magnet — magnetic north is near geographic north
  • • Oersted (1820): discovered that current-carrying wire deflects a compass
  • • Solenoid: coil of wire carrying current creates a strong magnetic field (electromagnet)

2. Induction and Devices

A changing magnetic field induces an electric current.

Examples:

  • • Faraday's Law of Induction (1831): moving a magnet through a coil generates electricity
  • • Generator: converts mechanical energy to electrical energy (rotating magnet in coil)
  • • Motor: converts electrical energy to mechanical (current in magnetic field creates force)

lessons.title: Geology — Earth's History
lessons.content:
Geology — Earth's History

Learning Objectives

  • • Igneous: cooled magma/lava (granite, basalt)
  • • Sedimentary: compacted sediment (sandstone, limestone) — contains fossils
  • • Metamorphic: transformed by heat/pressure (marble from limestone, quartzite from sandstone)
  • • Precambrian: 88% of Earth's history; single-celled life
  • • Paleozoic: Cambrian explosion, first vertebrates, mass extinctions
  • • Mesozoic: age of dinosaurs; ~66 Ma ended by asteroid impact
  • • Cenozoic: mammals dominate; last 65.5 million years; humans appear in last 0.3 Ma
8th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 6

Geology — Earth's History

Read the rock record, understand geological processes, and Earth's changing surface.

Learning Objectives

Apply principles of stratigraphy

Explain geological processes: weathering, erosion, deposition

Describe major geological eras and events

Lessons

1. Rock Types and Cycles

Rocks form through igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic processes in a continuous cycle.

Examples:

  • • Igneous: cooled magma/lava (granite, basalt)
  • • Sedimentary: compacted sediment (sandstone, limestone) — contains fossils
  • • Metamorphic: transformed by heat/pressure (marble from limestone, quartzite from sandstone)

2. Geological Time

Earth's 4.6-billion-year history is divided into eons, eras, periods, and epochs.

Examples:

  • • Precambrian: 88% of Earth's history; single-celled life
  • • Paleozoic: Cambrian explosion, first vertebrates, mass extinctions
  • • Mesozoic: age of dinosaurs; ~66 Ma ended by asteroid impact
  • • Cenozoic: mammals dominate; last 65.5 million years; humans appear in last 0.3 Ma

lessons.title: Ecology — Population Dynamics
lessons.content:
Ecology — Population Dynamics

Learning Objectives

  • • J-curve: exponential growth (no resource limits) — bacteria in ideal conditions
  • • S-curve: logistic growth (real-world carrying capacity)
  • • Carrying capacity (K): maximum population an environment can support
  • • Density-dependent: disease, competition, predation — effects increase with population density
  • • Density-independent: natural disasters, extreme weather — affect populations regardless of size
  • • Predator-prey oscillations: Lotka-Volterra model; lynx-hare cycles
8th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 7

Ecology — Population Dynamics

Analyze how populations change over time and interact within ecosystems.

Learning Objectives

Describe factors that limit population growth

Explain predator-prey dynamics

Analyze human population growth and its implications

Lessons

1. Population Growth Models

Populations grow exponentially when unlimited but logistically when resources are limited.

Examples:

  • • J-curve: exponential growth (no resource limits) — bacteria in ideal conditions
  • • S-curve: logistic growth (real-world carrying capacity)
  • • Carrying capacity (K): maximum population an environment can support

2. Limiting Factors

Biotic and abiotic factors limit population size.

Examples:

  • • Density-dependent: disease, competition, predation — effects increase with population density
  • • Density-independent: natural disasters, extreme weather — affect populations regardless of size
  • • Predator-prey oscillations: Lotka-Volterra model; lynx-hare cycles

lessons.title: Nuclear Physics — Introduction
lessons.content:
Nuclear Physics — Introduction

Learning Objectives

  • • Alpha decay: releases α particle (2p + 2n) — least penetrating
  • • Beta decay: releases β particle (electron) — from neutron → proton
  • • Gamma decay: releases high-energy photon — most penetrating
  • • Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron → two smaller nuclei + energy) — used in nuclear power plants and bombs
  • • Fusion: two light nuclei combine (H + H → He + energy) — powers the sun; experimental fusion reactors (ITER) aim for commercial power by 2040s
  • • Fusion produces ~4× more energy than fission per kg; no long-lived radioactive waste
8th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 8

Nuclear Physics — Introduction

Introduce nuclear reactions, radioactivity, and nuclear energy.

Learning Objectives

Describe types of radioactive decay

Explain fission and fusion

Evaluate nuclear energy's role in the future

Lessons

1. Radioactive Decay

Unstable nuclei release radiation to become more stable.

Examples:

  • • Alpha decay: releases α particle (2p + 2n) — least penetrating
  • • Beta decay: releases β particle (electron) — from neutron → proton
  • • Gamma decay: releases high-energy photon — most penetrating

2. Fission and Fusion

Both nuclear reactions release enormous energy via E = mc².

Examples:

  • • Fission: heavy nucleus splits (U-235 + neutron → two smaller nuclei + energy) — used in nuclear power plants and bombs
  • • Fusion: two light nuclei combine (H + H → He + energy) — powers the sun; experimental fusion reactors (ITER) aim for commercial power by 2040s
  • • Fusion produces ~4× more energy than fission per kg; no long-lived radioactive waste

lessons.title: Biomedical Science
lessons.content:
Biomedical Science

Learning Objectives

  • • Innate: skin, fever, inflammation — first line of defense (non-specific)
  • • Adaptive: B-cells (antibodies) and T-cells (kill infected cells) — specific response, develops memory
  • • Autoimmune disorders: immune system attacks own cells (lupus, MS, type 1 diabetes)
  • • Vaccines: introduce antigen (weakened pathogen or mRNA) → immune memory formed → fast response if exposed to real pathogen
  • • mRNA vaccines (COVID-19): instruct cells to make spike protein — new platform for many diseases
  • • Antibiotics: kill bacteria by disrupting cell walls or protein synthesis; antibiotic resistance is a growing crisis
8th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 9

Biomedical Science

Explore how biology and medicine intersect through disease, immunity, and modern treatments.

Learning Objectives

Describe how the immune system works

Explain how vaccines work

Analyze modern medical technologies

Lessons

1. The Immune System

The immune system defends the body through innate and adaptive immunity.

Examples:

  • • Innate: skin, fever, inflammation — first line of defense (non-specific)
  • • Adaptive: B-cells (antibodies) and T-cells (kill infected cells) — specific response, develops memory
  • • Autoimmune disorders: immune system attacks own cells (lupus, MS, type 1 diabetes)

2. Vaccines and Modern Medicine

Vaccines train the immune system; modern medicine has revolutionized health.

Examples:

  • • Vaccines: introduce antigen (weakened pathogen or mRNA) → immune memory formed → fast response if exposed to real pathogen
  • • mRNA vaccines (COVID-19): instruct cells to make spike protein — new platform for many diseases
  • • Antibiotics: kill bacteria by disrupting cell walls or protein synthesis; antibiotic resistance is a growing crisis

lessons.title: Physics — Waves and Modern Technology
lessons.content:
Physics — Waves and Modern Technology

Learning Objectives

  • • Reflection: waves bounce off surfaces (mirrors, echo)
  • • Refraction: waves bend when entering a new medium (lens, prism)
  • • Diffraction: waves bend around obstacles (sound around corners)
  • • Interference: waves add (constructive) or cancel (destructive)
  • • MRI: uses radio waves and magnetic fields to image soft tissue
  • • Ultrasound: high-frequency sound waves create images of internal organs (pregnancy imaging, heart scans)
  • • Fiber optics: total internal reflection carries data as light pulses at the speed of light
  • • Wi-Fi and 5G: radio waves carry digital data; different frequencies for different uses
8th Grade
🔬 Science
Module 10

Physics — Waves and Modern Technology

Explore wave behavior and how wave physics underpins modern technology.

Learning Objectives

Describe wave behaviors: reflection, refraction, diffraction, interference

Explain how digital technology uses waves

Connect wave physics to medical and communication technology

Lessons

1. Wave Behaviors

Waves interact with matter and each other in predictable ways.

Examples:

  • • Reflection: waves bounce off surfaces (mirrors, echo)
  • • Refraction: waves bend when entering a new medium (lens, prism)
  • • Diffraction: waves bend around obstacles (sound around corners)
  • • Interference: waves add (constructive) or cancel (destructive)

2. Wave Technology

Wave physics underlies nearly all modern communication and medical technology.

Examples:

  • • MRI: uses radio waves and magnetic fields to image soft tissue
  • • Ultrasound: high-frequency sound waves create images of internal organs (pregnancy imaging, heart scans)
  • • Fiber optics: total internal reflection carries data as light pulses at the speed of light
  • • Wi-Fi and 5G: radio waves carry digital data; different frequencies for different uses

courses.title: History — Kindergarten
courses.description: World & American history across the ages. Grade level: Kindergarten.

lessons.title: My Family History
lessons.content:
My Family History

Learning Objectives

  • • Some families have two parents, some have one
  • • Some children live with grandparents or aunts and uncles
  • • Families can have many kids or just one
  • • Holiday celebrations and foods
  • • Bedtime stories or weekend rituals
  • • Cultural dances, songs, or clothing
Kindergarten
🏛️ History
Module 1

My Family History

Explore family history, traditions, and how families are alike and different.

Learning Objectives

Describe their own family

Compare families across cultures

Understand that families have histories and traditions

Lessons

1. All Kinds of Families

Families come in many shapes and sizes, but all families care for one another.

Examples:

  • • Some families have two parents, some have one
  • • Some children live with grandparents or aunts and uncles
  • • Families can have many kids or just one

2. Family Traditions

Traditions are special things families do together, often passed down through generations.

Examples:

  • • Holiday celebrations and foods
  • • Bedtime stories or weekend rituals
  • • Cultural dances, songs, or clothing

lessons.title: Classroom and School Community
lessons.content:
Classroom and School Community

Learning Objectives

  • • The classroom is a small community
  • • Rules help everyone feel safe and respected
  • • Everyone has a job: student, teacher, principal, custodian
  • • Right: to be heard; Responsibility: to listen to others
  • • Right: to learn; Responsibility: to follow classroom rules
Kindergarten
🏛️ History
Module 2

Classroom and School Community

Learn how classrooms and schools are communities with rules and responsibilities.

Learning Objectives

Define community

Identify classroom rules and why they exist

Explain the roles of people in a school

Lessons

1. Our Classroom Community

A community is a group of people who live or work together and help each other.

Examples:

  • • The classroom is a small community
  • • Rules help everyone feel safe and respected
  • • Everyone has a job: student, teacher, principal, custodian

2. Rights and Responsibilities

In a community, everyone has rights (what they deserve) and responsibilities (what they must do).

Examples:

  • • Right: to be heard; Responsibility: to listen to others
  • • Right: to learn; Responsibility: to follow classroom rules

lessons.title: Holidays and Celebrations
lessons.content:
Holidays and Celebrations

Learning Objectives

  • • Independence Day: celebrates when the U.S. declared independence
  • • Thanksgiving: a time to be grateful and share with others
  • • Martin Luther King Jr. Day: honors a leader who fought for equality
  • • Lunar New Year celebrated in many Asian cultures
  • • Diwali: the Hindu festival of lights
  • • Hanukkah: Jewish festival of lights
Kindergarten
🏛️ History
Module 3

Holidays and Celebrations

Explore national and cultural holidays and why communities celebrate them.

Learning Objectives

Name important national holidays

Explain why holidays are celebrated

Connect holidays to community values

Lessons

1. National Holidays

National holidays honor important events and people in a country's history.

Examples:

  • • Independence Day: celebrates when the U.S. declared independence
  • • Thanksgiving: a time to be grateful and share with others
  • • Martin Luther King Jr. Day: honors a leader who fought for equality

2. Cultural Celebrations

Different cultures have their own celebrations that bring communities together.

Examples:

  • • Lunar New Year celebrated in many Asian cultures
  • • Diwali: the Hindu festival of lights
  • • Hanukkah: Jewish festival of lights

lessons.title: People Who Help Us — Community Heroes
lessons.content:
People Who Help Us — Community Heroes

Learning Objectives

  • • Firefighters put out fires and rescue people
  • • Doctors and nurses keep people healthy
  • • Teachers help children learn
  • • Harriet Tubman helped enslaved people escape to freedom
  • • Florence Nightingale improved hospital care for soldiers
  • • Fred Rogers made children feel valued and loved
Kindergarten
🏛️ History
Module 4

People Who Help Us — Community Heroes

Recognize and appreciate community helpers and their roles in history and today.

Learning Objectives

Identify community helpers (firefighters, doctors, teachers)

Explain how helpers make communities safer

Name historical figures who helped others

Lessons

1. Community Helpers Today

Community helpers keep neighborhoods safe, healthy, and running smoothly.

Examples:

  • • Firefighters put out fires and rescue people
  • • Doctors and nurses keep people healthy
  • • Teachers help children learn

2. Heroes from History

Throughout history, people have done brave things to help others.

Examples:

  • • Harriet Tubman helped enslaved people escape to freedom
  • • Florence Nightingale improved hospital care for soldiers
  • • Fred Rogers made children feel valued and loved

lessons.title: Then and Now — How Things Change
lessons.content:
Then and Now — How Things Change

Learning Objectives

  • • Then: horse and buggy, steam trains
  • • Now: cars, airplanes, high-speed trains
  • • Future: electric vehicles, possibly flying cars
  • • Then: letters delivered by hand, town criers
  • • Later: telegraph, telephone
  • • Now: texting, video calls, social media
Kindergarten
🏛️ History
Module 5

Then and Now — How Things Change

Compare life in the past to life today across transportation, communication, and home life.

Learning Objectives

Compare old and new versions of everyday items

Use vocabulary: past, present, change

Understand that history shows how things change over time

Lessons

1. Transportation Then and Now

The ways people travel have changed greatly over time.

Examples:

  • • Then: horse and buggy, steam trains
  • • Now: cars, airplanes, high-speed trains
  • • Future: electric vehicles, possibly flying cars

2. Communication Then and Now

How people share information has transformed over centuries.

Examples:

  • • Then: letters delivered by hand, town criers
  • • Later: telegraph, telephone
  • • Now: texting, video calls, social media

lessons.title: American Symbols and Landmarks
lessons.content:
American Symbols and Landmarks

Learning Objectives

  • • The American flag: 50 stars (states) and 13 stripes (original colonies)
  • • The Bald Eagle: national bird symbolizing freedom and strength
  • • The Liberty Bell: symbol of independence and freedom
  • • Statue of Liberty: gift from France, welcomes immigrants
  • • Mount Rushmore: carved faces of four presidents
  • • The White House: where the President lives and works
Kindergarten
🏛️ History
Module 6

American Symbols and Landmarks

Identify key American symbols and explain what they represent.

Learning Objectives

Name major American symbols

Explain what the flag and Pledge represent

Identify famous national landmarks

Lessons

1. American Symbols

Symbols represent ideas that are important to a nation.

Examples:

  • • The American flag: 50 stars (states) and 13 stripes (original colonies)
  • • The Bald Eagle: national bird symbolizing freedom and strength
  • • The Liberty Bell: symbol of independence and freedom

2. Famous Landmarks

Landmarks are important places that represent the nation's history.

Examples:

  • • Statue of Liberty: gift from France, welcomes immigrants
  • • Mount Rushmore: carved faces of four presidents
  • • The White House: where the President lives and works

lessons.title: Leaders and Government — A First Look
lessons.content:
Leaders and Government — A First Look

Learning Objectives

  • • A class president organizes school events
  • • A mayor makes decisions for a city
  • • The President leads the whole country
  • • School rule: walk in the hallways
  • • City law: stop at a red light
  • • National law: everyone deserves to be treated equally
Kindergarten
🏛️ History
Module 7

Leaders and Government — A First Look

Introduce the concept of leadership and simple ideas about government.

Learning Objectives

Explain why communities need leaders

Identify roles of a mayor, governor, and president (simply)

Understand that rules and laws help communities

Lessons

1. Why We Need Leaders

Leaders help communities make decisions and stay organized.

Examples:

  • • A class president organizes school events
  • • A mayor makes decisions for a city
  • • The President leads the whole country

2. Rules and Laws

Rules in school are like laws in a country — they help keep everyone safe and fair.

Examples:

  • • School rule: walk in the hallways
  • • City law: stop at a red light
  • • National law: everyone deserves to be treated equally

lessons.title: Native Americans — First Peoples
lessons.content:
Native Americans — First Peoples

Learning Objectives

  • • Lakota Sioux: Plains hunters, lived in tipis
  • • Pueblo peoples: Southwest farmers, built adobe homes
  • • Iroquois: Northeast forest people, built longhouses
  • • Planted the Three Sisters: corn, beans, and squash together
  • • Used every part of the buffalo: food, clothing, shelter
  • • Passed down knowledge through oral storytelling
Kindergarten
🏛️ History
Module 8

Native Americans — First Peoples

Introduce Native American cultures, their relationship with the land, and their history.

Learning Objectives

Name a few Native American tribes
