  • • John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry (1859): terrified the South
5th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 7

Slavery and the Road to Civil War

Trace the deepening sectional crisis over slavery from 1820–1860.

Learning Objectives

Explain the Missouri Compromise and Compromise of 1850

Describe the abolitionist movement

Analyze events that pushed the nation toward civil war

Lessons

1. Compromises and Crises

A series of compromises delayed but could not prevent civil war.

Examples:

  • • Missouri Compromise (1820): drew a line dividing free/slave territory
  • • Compromise of 1850: California enters free; Fugitive Slave Act enrages northerners
  • • Kansas-Nebraska Act (1854): 'popular sovereignty' → 'Bleeding Kansas' violence
  • • Dred Scott decision (1857): enslaved people have no rights; unconstitutional to restrict slavery in territories

2. Abolitionist Movement

A growing movement demanded the immediate end of slavery.

Examples:

  • • Frederick Douglass: escaped enslaved man; powerful orator and writer
  • • Harriet Tubman: Underground Railroad conductor; freed ~70 people
  • • Harriet Beecher Stowe: Uncle Tom's Cabin (1852) turned millions against slavery
  • • John Brown's raid on Harpers Ferry (1859): terrified the South

lessons.title: Reconstruction and Its Aftermath
lessons.content:
Reconstruction and Its Aftermath

Learning Objectives

  • • 13th Amendment (1865): abolished slavery
  • • 14th Amendment (1868): equal citizenship; due process; equal protection
  • • 15th Amendment (1870): Black men's right to vote
  • • Freedmen's Bureau: education, healthcare, legal aid for 4 million formerly enslaved people
  • • KKK and White League: terrorized Black voters and officials
  • • Compromise of 1877: federal troops withdrawn; Republicans give up Reconstruction for the presidency
  • • Jim Crow laws (1877–1965): legal segregation in Southern states — 'separate but equal'
  • • Plessy v. Ferguson (1896): Supreme Court upheld segregation
5th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 8

Reconstruction and Its Aftermath

Evaluate the achievements and failures of Reconstruction, and the rise of Jim Crow.

Learning Objectives

Describe Reconstruction's goals and achievements

Explain how Reconstruction ended and why

Trace the rise of Jim Crow laws and their impact

Lessons

1. Reconstruction Achievements

Reconstruction (1865–1877) brought important constitutional changes.

Examples:

  • • 13th Amendment (1865): abolished slavery
  • • 14th Amendment (1868): equal citizenship; due process; equal protection
  • • 15th Amendment (1870): Black men's right to vote
  • • Freedmen's Bureau: education, healthcare, legal aid for 4 million formerly enslaved people

2. End of Reconstruction and Jim Crow

Reconstruction was undermined by violence, politics, and white supremacy.

Examples:

  • • KKK and White League: terrorized Black voters and officials
  • • Compromise of 1877: federal troops withdrawn; Republicans give up Reconstruction for the presidency
  • • Jim Crow laws (1877–1965): legal segregation in Southern states — 'separate but equal'
  • • Plessy v. Ferguson (1896): Supreme Court upheld segregation

lessons.title: The Industrial Age and Progressive Era
lessons.content:
The Industrial Age and Progressive Era

Learning Objectives

  • • Transcontinental Railroad (1869): connected the nation; built largely by Chinese and Irish immigrants
  • • Standard Oil (Rockefeller) and Carnegie Steel: massive monopolies
  • • By 1900, the U.S. produced more steel than Britain and Germany combined
  • • Muckrakers: Upton Sinclair's 'The Jungle' exposed meatpacking conditions → Pure Food and Drug Act (1906)
  • • Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire (1911): 146 workers died; led to fire safety and labor laws
  • • Child labor laws: keyed to 'Progressive' movement; children under 14 banned from factories (1916 Keating-Owen Act)
5th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 9

The Industrial Age and Progressive Era

Explore industrialization's transformation of America and the Progressive response.

Learning Objectives

Describe the transformation of American industry 1865–1900

Identify problems of the Gilded Age

Explain Progressive reforms

Lessons

1. Industrial Transformation

After the Civil War, the U.S. became the world's largest industrial economy.

Examples:

  • • Transcontinental Railroad (1869): connected the nation; built largely by Chinese and Irish immigrants
  • • Standard Oil (Rockefeller) and Carnegie Steel: massive monopolies
  • • By 1900, the U.S. produced more steel than Britain and Germany combined

2. Progressive Reforms

Reformers used investigative journalism and legislation to address industrial abuses.

Examples:

  • • Muckrakers: Upton Sinclair's 'The Jungle' exposed meatpacking conditions → Pure Food and Drug Act (1906)
  • • Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire (1911): 146 workers died; led to fire safety and labor laws
  • • Child labor laws: keyed to 'Progressive' movement; children under 14 banned from factories (1916 Keating-Owen Act)

lessons.title: America in the 20th Century — Overview
lessons.content:
America in the 20th Century — Overview

Learning Objectives

  • • WWI (1917 entry): Zimmermann Telegram and unrestricted submarine warfare brought U.S. in; decisive tipping of balance
  • • Great Depression: WWI's aftermath, Prohibition, speculation bubble → crash of 1929
  • • WWII: Pearl Harbor → total mobilization; 16 million served; Hiroshima and Nagasaki ended the Pacific war
  • • Truman Doctrine (1947): U.S. would resist Soviet expansion anywhere
  • • Marshall Plan: $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe → keeps it out of Soviet orbit
  • • NATO (1949): military alliance; Soviet atomic bomb test that year changed everything
5th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 10

America in the 20th Century — Overview

Survey major events in 20th-century American history from WWI to the Cold War.

Learning Objectives

Trace U.S. involvement in WWI and WWII

Describe the New Deal

Explain the beginning of the Cold War

Lessons

1. World Wars

America played decisive roles in both World Wars.

Examples:

  • • WWI (1917 entry): Zimmermann Telegram and unrestricted submarine warfare brought U.S. in; decisive tipping of balance
  • • Great Depression: WWI's aftermath, Prohibition, speculation bubble → crash of 1929
  • • WWII: Pearl Harbor → total mobilization; 16 million served; Hiroshima and Nagasaki ended the Pacific war

2. Cold War Beginnings

After WWII, the U.S. and USSR became competing superpowers.

Examples:

  • • Truman Doctrine (1947): U.S. would resist Soviet expansion anywhere
  • • Marshall Plan: $13 billion to rebuild Western Europe → keeps it out of Soviet orbit
  • • NATO (1949): military alliance; Soviet atomic bomb test that year changed everything

courses.title: History — 6th Grade
courses.description: World & American history across the ages. Grade level: 6th Grade.

lessons.title: Ancient Civilizations Compared
lessons.content:
Ancient Civilizations Compared

Learning Objectives

  • • Surplus agriculture → specialized labor → social hierarchy → government → writing → monumental architecture
  • • River valley civilizations: all arose near major rivers for water, fertile soil, and transportation
  • • Cultural diffusion: ideas spread between civilizations through trade and conquest
  • • Greece: democracy, philosophy, Olympic Games, scientific method
  • • Rome: law, engineering, Latin language, Christian church structure
  • • China: paper, printing, compass, gunpowder, civil service examinations
  • • Mesopotamia: first writing (cuneiform), first law code (Hammurabi)
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 1

Ancient Civilizations Compared

Compare the major ancient civilizations of Egypt, Mesopotamia, Greece, Rome, China, and India.

Learning Objectives

Identify common features across ancient civilizations

Analyze how geography shaped each civilization

Evaluate lasting contributions to the modern world

Lessons

1. What Makes a Civilization?

Historians define a civilization by specific characteristics.

Examples:

  • • Surplus agriculture → specialized labor → social hierarchy → government → writing → monumental architecture
  • • River valley civilizations: all arose near major rivers for water, fertile soil, and transportation
  • • Cultural diffusion: ideas spread between civilizations through trade and conquest

2. Legacy Comparison

Ancient civilizations left enduring marks on modern society.

Examples:

  • • Greece: democracy, philosophy, Olympic Games, scientific method
  • • Rome: law, engineering, Latin language, Christian church structure
  • • China: paper, printing, compass, gunpowder, civil service examinations
  • • Mesopotamia: first writing (cuneiform), first law code (Hammurabi)

lessons.title: Medieval World
lessons.content:
Medieval World

Learning Objectives

  • • Feudalism: king → lords → knights → serfs — land for military service
  • • The Church unified European culture; Pope wielded enormous power
  • • Crusades (1096–1291): Christian military campaigns to control Jerusalem; mixed results
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 2

Medieval World

Explore medieval Europe, the Islamic world, and East Asia from 500–1400 CE.

Learning Objectives

Describe feudalism and manorialism

Explain the significance of the Islamic Golden Age

Compare medieval Europe to contemporaneous civilizations

Lessons

1. Medieval Europe

After Rome's fall, Europe fragmented into feudal kingdoms.

Examples:

  • • Feudalism: king → lords → knights → serfs — land for military service
  • • The Church unified European culture; Pope wielded enormous power
  • • Crusades (1096–1291): Christian military campaigns to control Jerusalem; mixed results

lessons.title: The Renaissance and Reformation
lessons.content:
The Renaissance and Reformation

Learning Objectives

  • • Civic humanism: being a good, engaged citizen is the highest virtue
  • • Leonardo da Vinci: embodiment of the 'Renaissance man' — artist, scientist, engineer
  • • Machiavelli's The Prince: analyzed political power realistically, not morally
  • • 95 Theses (1517): criticized indulgences — the Church selling forgiveness
  • • Council of Trent (1545–63): Catholic Counter-Reformation cleaned up abuses
  • • Religious wars devastated Europe for a century (Thirty Years' War 1618–48)
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 3

The Renaissance and Reformation

Study the Renaissance and Protestant Reformation as transformative intellectual movements.

Learning Objectives

Explain Renaissance humanism

Describe the Protestant Reformation's causes and impact

Analyze how the printing press changed history

Lessons

1. Renaissance Humanism

Humanism put human achievement and potential at the center, rather than theology.

Examples:

  • • Civic humanism: being a good, engaged citizen is the highest virtue
  • • Leonardo da Vinci: embodiment of the 'Renaissance man' — artist, scientist, engineer
  • • Machiavelli's The Prince: analyzed political power realistically, not morally

2. The Reformation

Martin Luther's challenge to the Church split Christianity permanently.

Examples:

  • • 95 Theses (1517): criticized indulgences — the Church selling forgiveness
  • • Council of Trent (1545–63): Catholic Counter-Reformation cleaned up abuses
  • • Religious wars devastated Europe for a century (Thirty Years' War 1618–48)

lessons.title: Atlantic World — Trade, Slavery, and Colonialism
lessons.content:
Atlantic World — Trade, Slavery, and Colonialism

Learning Objectives

  • • Europe → Africa: guns, textiles, manufactured goods
  • • Africa → Americas: 12.5 million enslaved Africans (over 300 years)
  • • Americas → Europe: sugar, tobacco, cotton, silver
  • • African states were destabilized; coastal kingdoms grew powerful through slave-trading
  • • Enslavement built the wealth of Britain, France, the Netherlands, and the American colonies
  • • Reparations debates today reflect the unresolved legacy of this history
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 4

Atlantic World — Trade, Slavery, and Colonialism

Analyze the Atlantic economy built on colonialism and the slave trade.

Learning Objectives

Describe the Triangular Trade

Analyze the impact of the slave trade on Africa

Evaluate the long-term legacy of Atlantic colonialism

Lessons

1. Triangular Trade

The Atlantic economy linked Europe, Africa, and the Americas in a brutal system.

Examples:

  • • Europe → Africa: guns, textiles, manufactured goods
  • • Africa → Americas: 12.5 million enslaved Africans (over 300 years)
  • • Americas → Europe: sugar, tobacco, cotton, silver

2. Impact and Legacy

The Atlantic slave trade reshaped Africa and built European and American wealth.

Examples:

  • • African states were destabilized; coastal kingdoms grew powerful through slave-trading
  • • Enslavement built the wealth of Britain, France, the Netherlands, and the American colonies
  • • Reparations debates today reflect the unresolved legacy of this history

lessons.title: Revolutions — American, French, Haitian
lessons.content:
Revolutions — American, French, Haitian

Learning Objectives

  • • Locke: natural rights (life, liberty, property); government by consent
  • • Rousseau: the social contract; popular sovereignty
  • • Voltaire: freedom of speech; separation of church and state
  • • Haiti (Saint-Domingue) was France's most profitable colony; brutal enslaved conditions
  • • Toussaint Louverture led enslaved people to defeat France, Britain, and Spain
  • • Haiti declared independence Jan. 1, 1804 — forced to pay France reparations until 1947
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 5

Revolutions — American, French, Haitian

Compare the American, French, and Haitian Revolutions and their shared and different outcomes.

Learning Objectives

Identify Enlightenment ideas driving all three revolutions

Compare causes, processes, and outcomes

Evaluate which revolution was most radical

Lessons

1. Enlightenment Foundations

All three revolutions drew on Enlightenment ideas about natural rights.

Examples:

  • • Locke: natural rights (life, liberty, property); government by consent
  • • Rousseau: the social contract; popular sovereignty
  • • Voltaire: freedom of speech; separation of church and state

2. The Haitian Revolution (1791–1804)

The Haitian Revolution was the only successful slave revolt in history — creating the first Black republic.

Examples:

  • • Haiti (Saint-Domingue) was France's most profitable colony; brutal enslaved conditions
  • • Toussaint Louverture led enslaved people to defeat France, Britain, and Spain
  • • Haiti declared independence Jan. 1, 1804 — forced to pay France reparations until 1947

lessons.title: Industrialization and Global Change
lessons.content:
Industrialization and Global Change

Learning Objectives

  • • Coal and iron deposits, navigable rivers, strong navy, colonial markets, patent law protecting inventors
  • • Enclosure movement: drove rural poor into cities as factory workers
  • • Child labor: children as young as 5 worked 14-hour days in mines and mills
  • • By 1914, European powers controlled 84% of the world's land surface
  • • 'Scramble for Africa' (1880–1914): Africa divided by European powers
  • • Economic imperialism in China: opium wars forced China to accept British trade terms
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 6

Industrialization and Global Change

Examine industrialization's transformation of work, society, and global power.

Learning Objectives

Explain why industrialization began in Britain

Describe social impacts of industrialization

Analyze how industrialization drove imperialism

Lessons

1. Industrial Revolution

Britain industrialized first due to a unique combination of factors.

Examples:

  • • Coal and iron deposits, navigable rivers, strong navy, colonial markets, patent law protecting inventors
  • • Enclosure movement: drove rural poor into cities as factory workers
  • • Child labor: children as young as 5 worked 14-hour days in mines and mills

2. Industrialization and Imperialism

Industrial nations sought colonies for raw materials and markets.

Examples:

  • • By 1914, European powers controlled 84% of the world's land surface
  • • 'Scramble for Africa' (1880–1914): Africa divided by European powers
  • • Economic imperialism in China: opium wars forced China to accept British trade terms

lessons.title: WWI — Causes and Consequences
lessons.content:
WWI — Causes and Consequences

Learning Objectives

  • • Militarism: European powers had built massive armies and navies for decades
  • • Alliances: Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) vs. Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain)
  • • Imperialism: competition for colonies created tensions
  • • Nationalism: desire for self-determination; ethnic minorities in Austria-Hungary wanted independence
  • • War guilt clause: Germany solely blamed → $33 billion in reparations
  • • Germany lost 13% of territory and all colonies
  • • Redrew maps of Europe and Middle East creating new, often unstable nations
  • • Hitler would later exploit German resentment of the treaty
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 7

WWI — Causes and Consequences

Examine the causes, course, and consequences of World War I.

Learning Objectives

Explain MAIN causes: Militarism, Alliances, Imperialism, Nationalism

Describe the experience of trench warfare

Evaluate the Treaty of Versailles and its consequences

Lessons

1. MAIN Causes

WWI had deep structural causes underlying the assassination trigger.

Examples:

  • • Militarism: European powers had built massive armies and navies for decades
  • • Alliances: Triple Alliance (Germany, Austria-Hungary, Italy) vs. Triple Entente (France, Russia, Britain)
  • • Imperialism: competition for colonies created tensions
  • • Nationalism: desire for self-determination; ethnic minorities in Austria-Hungary wanted independence

2. Treaty of Versailles

The peace settlement humiliated Germany and set the stage for WWII.

Examples:

  • • War guilt clause: Germany solely blamed → $33 billion in reparations
  • • Germany lost 13% of territory and all colonies
  • • Redrew maps of Europe and Middle East creating new, often unstable nations
  • • Hitler would later exploit German resentment of the treaty

lessons.title: WWII — Global Conflict
lessons.content:
WWII — Global Conflict

Learning Objectives

  • • Hitler's rise: economic depression + German resentment + propaganda = Nazi takeover (1933)
  • • Mussolini's fascist Italy (1922); Franco's Spain (1939); Stalin's Soviet Union
  • • Japan's militarist government expanded aggressively into China and Southeast Asia
  • • 1933–1939: legal persecution, stripping of rights (Nuremberg Laws)
  • • 1941–1945: 'Final Solution' — systematic extermination via death camps
  • • Auschwitz-Birkenau: largest camp; over 1 million killed
  • • Nuremberg Trials (1945–46): established legal precedent for crimes against humanity
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 8

WWII — Global Conflict

Study the causes, major theaters, and outcome of World War II.

Learning Objectives

Explain the rise of totalitarian regimes

Describe the Holocaust and its causes

Evaluate WWII's consequences for global order

Lessons

1. Rise of Totalitarianism

WWI's aftermath produced totalitarian regimes in Europe and Asia.

Examples:

  • • Hitler's rise: economic depression + German resentment + propaganda = Nazi takeover (1933)
  • • Mussolini's fascist Italy (1922); Franco's Spain (1939); Stalin's Soviet Union
  • • Japan's militarist government expanded aggressively into China and Southeast Asia

2. The Holocaust

The Holocaust was the systematic, state-sponsored murder of 6 million Jews and millions of others.

Examples:

  • • 1933–1939: legal persecution, stripping of rights (Nuremberg Laws)
  • • 1941–1945: 'Final Solution' — systematic extermination via death camps
  • • Auschwitz-Birkenau: largest camp; over 1 million killed
  • • Nuremberg Trials (1945–46): established legal precedent for crimes against humanity

lessons.title: The Cold War
lessons.content:
The Cold War

Learning Objectives

  • • Korean War (1950–53): first hot war of Cold War; divided Korea remains today
  • • Cuban Missile Crisis (1962): closest the world came to nuclear war; Kennedy and Khrushchev's 13-day standoff
  • • Vietnam War (1955–75): U.S. failed to prevent communist unification; 58,000 Americans and 3 million Vietnamese died
  • • Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika (1985): openness and economic reform
  • • Fall of the Berlin Wall (November 9, 1989)
  • • Soviet Union dissolved December 25, 1991 → 15 independent republics
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 9

The Cold War

Examine the Cold War ideological conflict, major crises, and its global impact.

Learning Objectives

Explain the ideological divide between capitalism and communism

Analyze the Korean War, Cuban Missile Crisis, and Vietnam War

Describe how the Cold War ended

Lessons

1. Cold War Crises

The Cold War nearly turned hot several times.

Examples:

  • • Korean War (1950–53): first hot war of Cold War; divided Korea remains today
  • • Cuban Missile Crisis (1962): closest the world came to nuclear war; Kennedy and Khrushchev's 13-day standoff
  • • Vietnam War (1955–75): U.S. failed to prevent communist unification; 58,000 Americans and 3 million Vietnamese died

2. End of the Cold War

The Soviet Union collapsed due to economic failure, nationalism, and reform.

Examples:

  • • Gorbachev's glasnost and perestroika (1985): openness and economic reform
  • • Fall of the Berlin Wall (November 9, 1989)
  • • Soviet Union dissolved December 25, 1991 → 15 independent republics

lessons.title: The World Since 1991
lessons.content:
The World Since 1991

Learning Objectives

  • • Globalization accelerated: trade, immigration, internet connected the world
  • • Yugoslav Wars (1991–2001): ethnic conflict after communism; genocide in Bosnia and Kosovo
  • • Rwandan Genocide (1994): 800,000 Tutsi killed in 100 days; world's failure to act
  • • 9/11 (2001): 2,977 killed; U.S. invaded Afghanistan and Iraq
  • • Arab Spring (2010–12): pro-democracy uprisings across Middle East; mixed outcomes
  • • Climate crisis: increasing urgency; Paris Agreement (2015) set targets
  • • COVID-19 (2020): 7+ million deaths globally; exposed inequality in healthcare systems
6th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 10

The World Since 1991

Survey major world events from 1991 to the present.

Learning Objectives

Describe the post-Cold War world order

Analyze the September 11 attacks and the 'War on Terror'

Identify major global challenges today

Lessons

1. Post-Cold War World

The U.S. emerged as the world's sole superpower — but the world remained complex.

Examples:

  • • Globalization accelerated: trade, immigration, internet connected the world
  • • Yugoslav Wars (1991–2001): ethnic conflict after communism; genocide in Bosnia and Kosovo
  • • Rwandan Genocide (1994): 800,000 Tutsi killed in 100 days; world's failure to act

2. 21st Century Challenges

The 21st century brought new and ongoing challenges.

Examples:

  • • 9/11 (2001): 2,977 killed; U.S. invaded Afghanistan and Iraq
  • • Arab Spring (2010–12): pro-democracy uprisings across Middle East; mixed outcomes
  • • Climate crisis: increasing urgency; Paris Agreement (2015) set targets
  • • COVID-19 (2020): 7+ million deaths globally; exposed inequality in healthcare systems

courses.title: History — 7th Grade
courses.description: World & American history across the ages. Grade level: 7th Grade.

lessons.title: Prehistory to Early Civilizations
lessons.content:
Prehistory to Early Civilizations

Learning Objectives

  • • 'Out of Africa' model: all modern humans descend from African ancestors
  • • By 12,000 BCE, humans had reached all continents except Antarctica
  • • Megafauna extinction: humans likely drove mammoths, giant sloths, and other large animals extinct
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 1

Prehistory to Early Civilizations

Trace human history from early hominids through the first civilizations.

Learning Objectives

Describe human evolution and migration out of Africa

Explain the Neolithic Revolution's significance

Compare the first four river valley civilizations

Lessons

1. Human Origins and Migration

Homo sapiens evolved in Africa ~300,000 years ago and spread across the globe.

Examples:

  • • 'Out of Africa' model: all modern humans descend from African ancestors
  • • By 12,000 BCE, humans had reached all continents except Antarctica
  • • Megafauna extinction: humans likely drove mammoths, giant sloths, and other large animals extinct

lessons.title: Classical Civilizations
lessons.content:
Classical Civilizations

Learning Objectives

  • • Athens: direct democracy (limited to male citizens)
  • • Rome: republic → empire; concept of citizenship
  • • Han China: centralized empire governed by Confucian bureaucrats
  • • Maurya Empire (India): centralized state; Ashoka adopted Buddhist ethics
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 2

Classical Civilizations

Analyze the classical civilizations of Greece, Rome, China, India, and the Americas.

Learning Objectives

Compare political systems of classical civilizations

Explain the Silk Road's role in cultural diffusion

Analyze causes of classical civilization collapse

Lessons

1. Classical Political Systems

Classical civilizations developed a variety of governance models.

Examples:

  • • Athens: direct democracy (limited to male citizens)
  • • Rome: republic → empire; concept of citizenship
  • • Han China: centralized empire governed by Confucian bureaucrats
  • • Maurya Empire (India): centralized state; Ashoka adopted Buddhist ethics

lessons.title: Medieval and Early Modern World
lessons.content:
Medieval and Early Modern World

Learning Objectives

  • • Muhammad received revelations from 610 CE; died 632 CE; had unified most of Arabia
  • • Within 100 years of Muhammad's death, Muslim armies controlled from Spain to Central Asia
  • • Five Pillars of Islam: Shahada, Salat, Zakat, Sawm, Hajj
  • • Spread along trade routes from Central Asia to Europe via Mongol trade networks
  • • Killed ~25 million Europeans; labor shortage → peasants gained bargaining power
  • • Undermined confidence in the Church; contributed to Renaissance questioning of tradition
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 3

Medieval and Early Modern World

Study the medieval world and the transitions to the early modern era.

Learning Objectives

Describe the rise and spread of Islam

Compare Medieval Europe with the Islamic world

Explain the significance of the Black Death

Lessons

1. Rise of Islam

Islam arose in the Arabian Peninsula in the 7th century and spread rapidly.

Examples:

  • • Muhammad received revelations from 610 CE; died 632 CE; had unified most of Arabia
  • • Within 100 years of Muhammad's death, Muslim armies controlled from Spain to Central Asia
  • • Five Pillars of Islam: Shahada, Salat, Zakat, Sawm, Hajj

2. The Black Death

The bubonic plague killed ~1/3 of Europe's population (1347–1353) — transforming medieval society.

Examples:

  • • Spread along trade routes from Central Asia to Europe via Mongol trade networks
  • • Killed ~25 million Europeans; labor shortage → peasants gained bargaining power
  • • Undermined confidence in the Church; contributed to Renaissance questioning of tradition

lessons.title: Age of Exploration and Its Consequences
lessons.content:
Age of Exploration and Its Consequences

Learning Objectives

  • • Portugal: sought sea route to Asia to cut out Muslim middlemen; Vasco da Gama succeeded (1498)
  • • Spain: Columbus (1492); Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided world between Spain and Portugal
  • • England and France: sought northwest passage to Asia; colonized North America instead
  • • Estimates vary: 50–90% of Indigenous American populations died within a century of contact
  • • Disease (smallpox, measles, influenza) was the primary killer
  • • Population of central Mexico fell from ~25 million in 1500 to ~1 million by 1600
  • • This depopulation made large-scale African enslavement seem economically 'necessary' to colonizers
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 4

Age of Exploration and Its Consequences

Analyze European exploration and its transformative — and often devastating — consequences.

Learning Objectives

Map major exploration routes

Analyze the Columbian Exchange in depth

Evaluate the demographic and cultural impact on the Americas

Lessons

1. Exploration and Trade Routes

European exploration was driven by economic and religious motivations.

Examples:

  • • Portugal: sought sea route to Asia to cut out Muslim middlemen; Vasco da Gama succeeded (1498)
  • • Spain: Columbus (1492); Treaty of Tordesillas (1494) divided world between Spain and Portugal
  • • England and France: sought northwest passage to Asia; colonized North America instead

2. Demographic Catastrophe

European contact caused the greatest demographic collapse in human history.

Examples:

  • • Estimates vary: 50–90% of Indigenous American populations died within a century of contact
  • • Disease (smallpox, measles, influenza) was the primary killer
  • • Population of central Mexico fell from ~25 million in 1500 to ~1 million by 1600
  • • This depopulation made large-scale African enslavement seem economically 'necessary' to colonizers

lessons.title: Revolutions — Political and Industrial
lessons.content:
Revolutions — Political and Industrial

Learning Objectives

  • • American Revolution (1776): first successful revolution based on Enlightenment principles
  • • French Revolution (1789–1799): more radical; challenged religion, aristocracy, and monarchy; ended in Napoleon
  • • Haitian Revolution (1791–1804): most radical of all — enslaved people won their freedom
  • • Bourgeoisie (middle class): factory owners, professionals — gained power
  • • Proletariat (working class): factory workers — long hours, dangerous conditions, low wages
  • • Marx and Engels: The Communist Manifesto (1848) — predicted workers' revolution
  • • Labor movement: strikes and unions → 8-hour workday, minimum wage, weekends
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 5

Revolutions — Political and Industrial

Examine the age of revolutions and how they reshaped political and economic life.

Learning Objectives

Analyze the intellectual origins of political revolution

Compare the American and French Revolutions

Explain the social impacts of industrialization

Lessons

1. Political Revolutions

Enlightenment ideas challenged absolute monarchy and hereditary privilege.

Examples:

  • • American Revolution (1776): first successful revolution based on Enlightenment principles
  • • French Revolution (1789–1799): more radical; challenged religion, aristocracy, and monarchy; ended in Napoleon
  • • Haitian Revolution (1791–1804): most radical of all — enslaved people won their freedom

2. Industrial Revolution's Social Impact

Industrialization created new social classes and enormous inequalities.

Examples:

  • • Bourgeoisie (middle class): factory owners, professionals — gained power
  • • Proletariat (working class): factory workers — long hours, dangerous conditions, low wages
  • • Marx and Engels: The Communist Manifesto (1848) — predicted workers' revolution
  • • Labor movement: strikes and unions → 8-hour workday, minimum wage, weekends

lessons.title: Imperialism and Nationalism
lessons.content:
Imperialism and Nationalism

Learning Objectives

  • • By 1914: Britain controlled 25% of Earth's land surface; France 9%
  • • 'White man's burden': racist ideology that justified colonialism as 'civilizing'
  • • Resistance: Zulu Wars, Sepoy Mutiny, Boxer Rebellion — colonized peoples fought back
  • • Italian unification (Risorgimento, 1861): Garibaldi and Cavour unified fragmented peninsula
  • • German unification (1871): Bismarck used 'blood and iron' — wars and diplomacy
  • • Nationalism in Austria-Hungary: multiple ethnic groups (Czechs, Slovaks, Serbs) wanted independence — leading to WWI
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 6

Imperialism and Nationalism

Study 19th-century imperialism and the rise of nationalism.

Learning Objectives

Explain economic and social motivations for imperialism

Describe nationalist movements

Analyze imperialism's legacy in the contemporary world

Lessons

1. European Imperialism

European powers colonized most of the world in the 19th century.

Examples:

  • • By 1914: Britain controlled 25% of Earth's land surface; France 9%
  • • 'White man's burden': racist ideology that justified colonialism as 'civilizing'
  • • Resistance: Zulu Wars, Sepoy Mutiny, Boxer Rebellion — colonized peoples fought back

2. Nationalism

Nationalism — loyalty to a shared language/culture — both unified and destabilized nations.

Examples:

  • • Italian unification (Risorgimento, 1861): Garibaldi and Cavour unified fragmented peninsula
  • • German unification (1871): Bismarck used 'blood and iron' — wars and diplomacy
  • • Nationalism in Austria-Hungary: multiple ethnic groups (Czechs, Slovaks, Serbs) wanted independence — leading to WWI

lessons.title: WWI and the Interwar Period
lessons.content:
WWI and the Interwar Period

Learning Objectives

  • • Wilson's 14 Points: self-determination, League of Nations, no punitive peace — largely ignored
  • • New nations created: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Iraq, Palestine (as British mandate)
  • • Middle East mandate system: Britain and France divided Arab lands, ignoring promises made during the war
  • • Benito Mussolini: used black-shirted thugs to gain power in Italy (1922); glorified violence and the state
  • • Adolf Hitler: blamed Germany's problems on Jews, communists, and 'foreign powers'; Hitler Youth indoctrination
  • • Both regimes used propaganda, censorship, and terror to suppress opposition
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 7

WWI and the Interwar Period

Examine WWI and the unstable interwar period that led to WWII.

Learning Objectives

Analyze WWI's causes in depth

Evaluate the Paris Peace Conference

Describe the rise of fascism

Lessons

1. Paris Peace Conference

The 1919 Paris Peace Conference reshaped the world map but created new problems.

Examples:

  • • Wilson's 14 Points: self-determination, League of Nations, no punitive peace — largely ignored
  • • New nations created: Poland, Czechoslovakia, Yugoslavia, Iraq, Palestine (as British mandate)
  • • Middle East mandate system: Britain and France divided Arab lands, ignoring promises made during the war

2. Rise of Fascism

Economic crisis and political instability produced fascist movements in Italy and Germany.

Examples:

  • • Benito Mussolini: used black-shirted thugs to gain power in Italy (1922); glorified violence and the state
  • • Adolf Hitler: blamed Germany's problems on Jews, communists, and 'foreign powers'; Hitler Youth indoctrination
  • • Both regimes used propaganda, censorship, and terror to suppress opposition

lessons.title: WWII and the Holocaust
lessons.content:
WWII and the Holocaust

Learning Objectives

  • • 1933–1938: legal discrimination; Jews stripped of citizenship (Nuremberg Laws, 1935)
  • • 1938: Kristallnacht ('Night of Broken Glass') — pogroms against Jewish homes and businesses
  • • 1941: mobile killing units (Einsatzgruppen) killed ~1 million Jews in Soviet territories
  • • 1942: Wannsee Conference — systematic plan for 'Final Solution' finalized
  • • Nuremberg Trials (1945–46): 24 Nazi leaders tried for crimes against humanity — established international law precedent
  • • Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948): proclaimed fundamental rights for all
  • • State of Israel established (1948); United Nations created (1945)
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 8

WWII and the Holocaust

Study WWII in depth with special focus on the Holocaust and human rights.

Learning Objectives

Analyze WWII as a continuation of WWI's unresolved issues

Document the steps of the Holocaust

Evaluate post-war attempts at justice and human rights

Lessons

1. Holocaust — Steps of Persecution

The Holocaust didn't begin with death camps — it was a step-by-step process.

Examples:

  • • 1933–1938: legal discrimination; Jews stripped of citizenship (Nuremberg Laws, 1935)
  • • 1938: Kristallnacht ('Night of Broken Glass') — pogroms against Jewish homes and businesses
  • • 1941: mobile killing units (Einsatzgruppen) killed ~1 million Jews in Soviet territories
  • • 1942: Wannsee Conference — systematic plan for 'Final Solution' finalized

2. Post-War Justice

The world responded to the Holocaust with new institutions and legal frameworks.

Examples:

  • • Nuremberg Trials (1945–46): 24 Nazi leaders tried for crimes against humanity — established international law precedent
  • • Universal Declaration of Human Rights (1948): proclaimed fundamental rights for all
  • • State of Israel established (1948); United Nations created (1945)

lessons.title: Decolonization and Independence Movements
lessons.content:
Decolonization and Independence Movements

Learning Objectives

  • • Gandhi: satyagraha (nonviolent resistance); Salt March (1930) — walked 240 miles to protest British salt tax
  • • WWII exhausted Britain economically and morally — empire became unsustainable
  • • Independence (August 15, 1947): accompanied by Partition — India and Pakistan; ~15 million displaced; ~2 million died in violence
  • • Ghana (1957): first sub-Saharan African nation to gain independence; led by Kwame Nkrumah
  • • Kenya: Mau Mau uprising (1952–60) combined with political pressure forced British withdrawal
  • • Apartheid South Africa: remained white-minority ruled until Nelson Mandela's election (1994)
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 9

Decolonization and Independence Movements

Examine the global wave of decolonization after WWII.

Learning Objectives

Explain why decolonization accelerated after WWII

Describe independence movements in India, Africa, and Southeast Asia

Evaluate the challenges of post-colonial nations

Lessons

1. India's Independence

Gandhi's nonviolent independence movement inspired the world.

Examples:

  • • Gandhi: satyagraha (nonviolent resistance); Salt March (1930) — walked 240 miles to protest British salt tax
  • • WWII exhausted Britain economically and morally — empire became unsustainable
  • • Independence (August 15, 1947): accompanied by Partition — India and Pakistan; ~15 million displaced; ~2 million died in violence

2. African Decolonization

Most of Africa gained independence between 1957 and 1975.

Examples:

  • • Ghana (1957): first sub-Saharan African nation to gain independence; led by Kwame Nkrumah
  • • Kenya: Mau Mau uprising (1952–60) combined with political pressure forced British withdrawal
  • • Apartheid South Africa: remained white-minority ruled until Nelson Mandela's election (1994)

lessons.title: The Contemporary World
lessons.content:
The Contemporary World

Learning Objectives

  • • WTO, NAFTA, EU single market: reduced trade barriers
  • • Global supply chains: your iPhone involves components from 43 countries
  • • Cultural globalization: American films, K-pop, Bollywood reach global audiences
  • • Climate crisis: existential threat requiring global cooperation
  • • Inequality: 1% of the world owns more than half of all wealth
  • • Democracy under threat: authoritarian movements growing in many countries
  • • Pandemic preparedness: COVID-19 revealed global vulnerabilities
7th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 10

The Contemporary World

Analyze major developments shaping the contemporary world.

Learning Objectives

Describe the post-Cold War world

Analyze globalization and its effects

Evaluate major ongoing global challenges

Lessons

1. Globalization

After 1991, the world became increasingly economically and culturally integrated.

Examples:

  • • WTO, NAFTA, EU single market: reduced trade barriers
  • • Global supply chains: your iPhone involves components from 43 countries
  • • Cultural globalization: American films, K-pop, Bollywood reach global audiences

2. Current Global Challenges

The 21st century is defined by interconnected global challenges.

Examples:

  • • Climate crisis: existential threat requiring global cooperation
  • • Inequality: 1% of the world owns more than half of all wealth
  • • Democracy under threat: authoritarian movements growing in many countries
  • • Pandemic preparedness: COVID-19 revealed global vulnerabilities

courses.title: History — 8th Grade
courses.description: World & American history across the ages. Grade level: 8th Grade.

lessons.title: Origins of Democracy and Republic
lessons.content:
Origins of Democracy and Republic

Learning Objectives

  • • Athens (Cleisthenes, ~508 BCE): direct democracy; 30,000 male citizens could vote; excluded women, slaves, foreigners
  • • Pericles' Funeral Oration: 'power in the hands of the many, not the few'
  • • Roman Republic: SPQR (Senatus Populusque Romanus); Senate, consuls, tribunes; model for the U.S. Constitution
  • • Magna Carta (1215): 'no taxation without representation' principle; habeas corpus
  • • English Civil War and Glorious Revolution (1688): Parliamentary supremacy established
  • • Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau: Enlightenment thinkers who directly influenced the American Founders
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 1

Origins of Democracy and Republic

Trace democratic ideas from Athens and Rome through the Enlightenment to modern democracy.

Learning Objectives

Analyze Athenian democracy's strengths and limits

Trace the development of republican government

Connect historical governance to today's systems

Lessons

1. Athens and Rome

Ancient Athens and Rome created enduring models of self-governance.

Examples:

  • • Athens (Cleisthenes, ~508 BCE): direct democracy; 30,000 male citizens could vote; excluded women, slaves, foreigners
  • • Pericles' Funeral Oration: 'power in the hands of the many, not the few'
  • • Roman Republic: SPQR (Senatus Populusque Romanus); Senate, consuls, tribunes; model for the U.S. Constitution

2. Magna Carta to Enlightenment

English constitutional tradition slowly expanded rights and limited royal power.

Examples:

  • • Magna Carta (1215): 'no taxation without representation' principle; habeas corpus
  • • English Civil War and Glorious Revolution (1688): Parliamentary supremacy established
  • • Locke, Montesquieu, Rousseau: Enlightenment thinkers who directly influenced the American Founders

lessons.title: U.S. History — The Gilded Age to WWI
lessons.content:
U.S. History — The Gilded Age to WWI

Learning Objectives

  • • Cornelius Vanderbilt (railroads), Andrew Carnegie (steel), John D. Rockefeller (oil): built monopolies worth hundreds of billions in today's dollars
  • • Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): first attempt to regulate monopolies — largely unenforced
  • • Workers formed unions: Knights of Labor, AFL; Homestead Strike (1892) and Pullman Strike (1894) crushed by force
  • • Spanish-American War (1898): U.S. gained Guam, Puerto Rico, Philippines
  • • Panama Canal (1904–1914): U.S. backed Panamanian independence from Colombia to secure canal rights
  • • Yellow journalism (Hearst, Pulitzer): sensationalist coverage inflamed public opinion toward war
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 2

U.S. History — The Gilded Age to WWI

Examine America's rise to world power from Reconstruction's end through WWI.

Learning Objectives

Describe the Gilded Age economy and its contradictions

Analyze American imperialism in Cuba, Philippines, and Panama

Explain U.S. entry into WWI

Lessons

1. Gilded Age and Robber Barons

The Gilded Age (1870–1900) saw explosive economic growth alongside staggering inequality.

Examples:

  • • Cornelius Vanderbilt (railroads), Andrew Carnegie (steel), John D. Rockefeller (oil): built monopolies worth hundreds of billions in today's dollars
  • • Sherman Antitrust Act (1890): first attempt to regulate monopolies — largely unenforced
  • • Workers formed unions: Knights of Labor, AFL; Homestead Strike (1892) and Pullman Strike (1894) crushed by force

2. American Imperialism

At the turn of the 20th century, the U.S. became an imperial power.

Examples:

  • • Spanish-American War (1898): U.S. gained Guam, Puerto Rico, Philippines
  • • Panama Canal (1904–1914): U.S. backed Panamanian independence from Colombia to secure canal rights
  • • Yellow journalism (Hearst, Pulitzer): sensationalist coverage inflamed public opinion toward war

lessons.title: U.S. History — WWII Through Cold War
lessons.content:
U.S. History — WWII Through Cold War

Learning Objectives

  • • War Production Board: converted factories from consumer goods to weapons virtually overnight
  • • 6 million women entered the workforce ('Rosie the Riveter')
  • • Japanese American internment: Executive Order 9066; 120,000 Japanese Americans sent to camps; later ruled unconstitutional
  • • African American 'Double V' campaign: victory against fascism abroad AND Jim Crow at home
  • • Truman's decision: estimated 500,000–1 million U.S. casualties to invade Japan; actual deaths from bombs ~200,000
  • • USSR tests atomic bomb (1949) → nuclear arms race
  • • McCarthyism (1950–54): Senator McCarthy accused hundreds of communism with little evidence; damaged civil liberties
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 3

U.S. History — WWII Through Cold War

Examine the United States from WWII mobilization through the Cold War era.

Learning Objectives

Describe total war mobilization on the home front

Evaluate the decision to use atomic bombs

Analyze the domestic Cold War: McCarthyism and civil defense

Lessons

1. WWII Home Front

WWII required the mobilization of the entire American economy and society.

Examples:

  • • War Production Board: converted factories from consumer goods to weapons virtually overnight
  • • 6 million women entered the workforce ('Rosie the Riveter')
  • • Japanese American internment: Executive Order 9066; 120,000 Japanese Americans sent to camps; later ruled unconstitutional
  • • African American 'Double V' campaign: victory against fascism abroad AND Jim Crow at home

2. Atomic Bomb and Cold War

The atomic bomb ended WWII but began a new era of existential threat.

Examples:

  • • Truman's decision: estimated 500,000–1 million U.S. casualties to invade Japan; actual deaths from bombs ~200,000
  • • USSR tests atomic bomb (1949) → nuclear arms race
  • • McCarthyism (1950–54): Senator McCarthy accused hundreds of communism with little evidence; damaged civil liberties

lessons.title: The Civil Rights Movement — Depth Study
lessons.content:
The Civil Rights Movement — Depth Study

Learning Objectives

  • • Thurgood Marshall argued 32 cases before the Supreme Court; won 29
  • • Brown v. Board of Education (1954): overturned Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
  • • Strategy: challenge the 'separate but equal' doctrine by proving separate was inherently unequal
  • • Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56): 381 days; MIA organized carpools; Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional
  • • Birmingham Campaign (1963): Bull Connor's fire hoses and police dogs broadcast nationally → shocked the nation
  • • March on Washington (August 28, 1963): 250,000 attended; MLK's 'I Have a Dream' speech
  • • Selma to Montgomery March (1965) → Voting Rights Act (1965)
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 4

The Civil Rights Movement — Depth Study

Examine the Civil Rights Movement in depth, from its roots to its legislative victories.

Learning Objectives

Trace the legal and political strategy of the NAACP

Analyze key events and turning points

Evaluate the unfinished work of the movement

Lessons

1. Legal Strategy — NAACP

The NAACP systematically challenged segregation through the courts.

Examples:

  • • Thurgood Marshall argued 32 cases before the Supreme Court; won 29
  • • Brown v. Board of Education (1954): overturned Plessy v. Ferguson (1896)
  • • Strategy: challenge the 'separate but equal' doctrine by proving separate was inherently unequal

2. Street-Level Activism

Mass direct action combined with legal strategy to win legislative victories.

Examples:

  • • Montgomery Bus Boycott (1955–56): 381 days; MIA organized carpools; Supreme Court ruled bus segregation unconstitutional
  • • Birmingham Campaign (1963): Bull Connor's fire hoses and police dogs broadcast nationally → shocked the nation
  • • March on Washington (August 28, 1963): 250,000 attended; MLK's 'I Have a Dream' speech
  • • Selma to Montgomery March (1965) → Voting Rights Act (1965)

lessons.title: Social Movements of the 1960s–70s
lessons.content:
Social Movements of the 1960s–70s

Learning Objectives

  • • Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963): gave voice to educated women's dissatisfaction
  • • NOW (National Organization for Women, 1966): lobbied for legal equality
  • • Title IX (1972): banned sex discrimination in education → transformed women's athletics
  • • Roe v. Wade (1973): abortion rights; remained law until overturned by Dobbs (2022)
  • • Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962): documented pesticide dangers; sparked the environmental movement
  • • Cuyahoga River fire (1969): burning river in Cleveland shocked the nation
  • • Earth Day (April 22, 1970): 20 million Americans participated
  • • EPA established (1970); Clean Air Act (1970); Clean Water Act (1972)
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 5

Social Movements of the 1960s–70s

Examine the major social movements that transformed American society in the 1960s–70s.

Learning Objectives

Describe the women's liberation movement

Analyze the environmental movement's origins

Evaluate the legacy of these movements

Lessons

1. Women's Liberation Movement

Second-wave feminism challenged gender discrimination in law and culture.

Examples:

  • • Betty Friedan's The Feminine Mystique (1963): gave voice to educated women's dissatisfaction
  • • NOW (National Organization for Women, 1966): lobbied for legal equality
  • • Title IX (1972): banned sex discrimination in education → transformed women's athletics
  • • Roe v. Wade (1973): abortion rights; remained law until overturned by Dobbs (2022)

2. Environmental Movement

The environmental movement transformed American law and consciousness.

Examples:

  • • Rachel Carson's Silent Spring (1962): documented pesticide dangers; sparked the environmental movement
  • • Cuyahoga River fire (1969): burning river in Cleveland shocked the nation
  • • Earth Day (April 22, 1970): 20 million Americans participated
  • • EPA established (1970); Clean Air Act (1970); Clean Water Act (1972)

lessons.title: America from Reagan to Obama
lessons.content:
America from Reagan to Obama

Learning Objectives

  • • Supply-side economics ('Reaganomics'): cut taxes especially for wealthy; deregulate business
  • • 'Evil Empire' speech: escalated Cold War rhetoric against USSR; Soviet economy couldn't keep up
  • • Iran-Contra affair: administration secretly sold arms to Iran, used proceeds to fund Nicaraguan Contras (illegal)
  • • 1st Gulf War (1991): U.S. led coalition expelled Iraq from Kuwait
  • • Clinton era: longest peacetime expansion; NAFTA; welfare reform; scandal and impeachment
  • • 9/11 and 'War on Terror': transformed foreign policy, civil liberties, and national psychology
  • • Obama (2008): first Black president; ACA ('Obamacare'); 2009 Nobel Peace Prize; economy recovery from Great Recession
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 6

America from Reagan to Obama

Survey American history from the Reagan Revolution through the Obama era.

Learning Objectives

Explain Reagan's political and economic philosophy

Describe post-Cold War American foreign policy

Analyze the significance of Obama's election

Lessons

1. The Reagan Revolution

Ronald Reagan's presidency (1981–1989) shifted American politics rightward.

Examples:

  • • Supply-side economics ('Reaganomics'): cut taxes especially for wealthy; deregulate business
  • • 'Evil Empire' speech: escalated Cold War rhetoric against USSR; Soviet economy couldn't keep up
  • • Iran-Contra affair: administration secretly sold arms to Iran, used proceeds to fund Nicaraguan Contras (illegal)

2. Post-Cold War to Obama

Post-Cold War America faced new challenges and historic milestones.

Examples:

  • • 1st Gulf War (1991): U.S. led coalition expelled Iraq from Kuwait
  • • Clinton era: longest peacetime expansion; NAFTA; welfare reform; scandal and impeachment
  • • 9/11 and 'War on Terror': transformed foreign policy, civil liberties, and national psychology
  • • Obama (2008): first Black president; ACA ('Obamacare'); 2009 Nobel Peace Prize; economy recovery from Great Recession

lessons.title: Global History — 20th Century Atrocities
lessons.content:
Global History — 20th Century Atrocities

Learning Objectives

  • • Coined by Raphael Lemkin (1944) who lost 49 family members in the Holocaust
  • • UN Genocide Convention (1948): first international law defining and prohibiting genocide
  • • 'Never Again': promise made after the Holocaust — but genocide has continued
  • • Colonial Belgium had institutionalized Hutu-Tutsi distinction, exacerbating tensions
  • • Radio broadcasts (RTLM) called Tutsi 'cockroaches' and incited killing
  • • U.S. and UN explicitly avoided using the word 'genocide' to avoid obligation to intervene
  • • International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda: held perpetrators accountable; established precedents for international justice
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 7

Global History — 20th Century Atrocities

Study 20th-century genocides and crimes against humanity and the international response.

Learning Objectives

Study the Armenian Genocide as a forerunner of the Holocaust

Analyze the Rwandan Genocide

Evaluate the effectiveness of 'Never Again'

Lessons

1. Defining Genocide

Genocide is the deliberate destruction of a national, ethnic, racial, or religious group.

Examples:

  • • Coined by Raphael Lemkin (1944) who lost 49 family members in the Holocaust
  • • UN Genocide Convention (1948): first international law defining and prohibiting genocide
  • • 'Never Again': promise made after the Holocaust — but genocide has continued

2. Rwandan Genocide (1994)

800,000 Tutsi were killed in 100 days while the world watched.

Examples:

  • • Colonial Belgium had institutionalized Hutu-Tutsi distinction, exacerbating tensions
  • • Radio broadcasts (RTLM) called Tutsi 'cockroaches' and incited killing
  • • U.S. and UN explicitly avoided using the word 'genocide' to avoid obligation to intervene
  • • International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda: held perpetrators accountable; established precedents for international justice

lessons.title: Globalization and its Discontents
lessons.content:
Globalization and its Discontents

Learning Objectives

  • • World trade tripled between 1990 and 2020
  • • Global extreme poverty dropped from ~36% (1990) to ~10% (2015) — largely due to China's growth
  • • Multinational corporations: Apple, Amazon, and Walmart each have revenues larger than most countries' GDPs
  • • Deindustrialization: manufacturing jobs moved to low-wage countries → rust belt economies in U.S., UK, France
  • • 'Race to the bottom': competition for jobs leads countries to weaken labor and environmental standards
  • • Brexit (2016), Trump (2016), nationalism in France, Hungary: political backlash against globalization
  • • Inequality within countries has grown even as inequality between countries shrinks
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 8

Globalization and its Discontents

Analyze globalization — its economic benefits, cultural impacts, and growing backlash.

Learning Objectives

Define economic globalization

Evaluate who benefits and who loses

Analyze the backlash to globalization

Lessons

1. Economic Globalization

Since 1991, economic integration has accelerated dramatically.

Examples:

  • • World trade tripled between 1990 and 2020
  • • Global extreme poverty dropped from ~36% (1990) to ~10% (2015) — largely due to China's growth
  • • Multinational corporations: Apple, Amazon, and Walmart each have revenues larger than most countries' GDPs

2. Globalization's Discontents

Globalization has created winners and losers — and fueled political backlash.

Examples:

  • • Deindustrialization: manufacturing jobs moved to low-wage countries → rust belt economies in U.S., UK, France
  • • 'Race to the bottom': competition for jobs leads countries to weaken labor and environmental standards
  • • Brexit (2016), Trump (2016), nationalism in France, Hungary: political backlash against globalization
  • • Inequality within countries has grown even as inequality between countries shrinks

lessons.title: Technology and History
lessons.content:
Technology and History

Learning Objectives

  • • Printing press (1440): enabled Reformation, Scientific Revolution, American Revolution — made ideas unstoppable
  • • Steam engine (1769): Industrial Revolution; transformed work, cities, and global power
  • • Internet (1991, public): democratized information; connected the world; enabled social media and disinformation
  • • AI revolution: automation threatens white-collar as well as blue-collar jobs
  • • Social media: Arab Spring; Cambridge Analytica; social isolation; democracy under pressure
  • • Big data and surveillance: governments and corporations can track behavior at unprecedented scale
  • • The choices made in the next decade about AI and digital rights will shape the 21st century
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 9

Technology and History

Analyze how transformative technologies have shaped historical change.

Learning Objectives

Identify key technologies that changed history

Analyze the printing press, industrial machinery, and the internet

Evaluate the current digital revolution

Lessons

1. Technologies That Changed History

Certain inventions fundamentally altered the course of human history.

Examples:

  • • Printing press (1440): enabled Reformation, Scientific Revolution, American Revolution — made ideas unstoppable
  • • Steam engine (1769): Industrial Revolution; transformed work, cities, and global power
  • • Internet (1991, public): democratized information; connected the world; enabled social media and disinformation

2. The Digital Revolution

We are living through a transformation as significant as the Industrial Revolution.

Examples:

  • • AI revolution: automation threatens white-collar as well as blue-collar jobs
  • • Social media: Arab Spring; Cambridge Analytica; social isolation; democracy under pressure
  • • Big data and surveillance: governments and corporations can track behavior at unprecedented scale
  • • The choices made in the next decade about AI and digital rights will shape the 21st century

lessons.title: Historiography — How We Know History
lessons.content:
Historiography — How We Know History

Learning Objectives

  • • The same event can be interpreted very differently by different historians
  • • 'History is written by the victors' — whose perspective is missing?
  • • Revisionist history: when new evidence or perspectives change the accepted narrative (not a bad thing — it's how history improves)
  • • HAPP analysis: Historical context, Audience, Purpose, Perspective
  • • Primary source: letter from a Civil War soldier — invaluable but represents one person's limited view
  • • The Diary of Anne Frank: extraordinary primary source, but unrepresentative of most Holocaust victims' experience
  • • 'Silences' in the archive: whose voices are missing? Why? What does that tell us?
8th Grade
🏛️ History
Module 10

Historiography — How We Know History

Study how history is written, interpreted, and contested.

Learning Objectives

Define historiography

Analyze how interpretations of history change over time

Evaluate primary sources for bias and context

Lessons

1. What is Historiography?

Historiography is the study of how history is written and how interpretations change.

Examples:

  • • The same event can be interpreted very differently by different historians
  • • 'History is written by the victors' — whose perspective is missing?
  • • Revisionist history: when new evidence or perspectives change the accepted narrative (not a bad thing — it's how history improves)

2. Evaluating Sources

All historical sources have a perspective, audience, and purpose.

Examples:

  • • HAPP analysis: Historical context, Audience, Purpose, Perspective
  • • Primary source: letter from a Civil War soldier — invaluable but represents one person's limited view
  • • The Diary of Anne Frank: extraordinary primary source, but unrepresentative of most Holocaust victims' experience
  • • 'Silences' in the archive: whose voices are missing? Why? What does that tell us?

courses.title: Geography — Kindergarten
courses.description: Maps, regions, landforms & world cultures. Grade level: Kindergarten.

lessons.title: Me on the Map
lessons.content:
Me on the Map

Learning Objectives

  • • Draw your bedroom from a bird's-eye view
  • • Draw your classroom from above
  • • A map of your neighborhood would show streets, parks, and buildings
  • • Earth has more water (oceans) than land
  • • You can spin a globe to see all parts of Earth
  • • A flat map stretches the round Earth, but a globe shows true shapes
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 1

Me on the Map

Learn how maps represent the world at different scales, from a bedroom to the globe.

Learning Objectives

Draw a simple map of a familiar place

Understand that maps show places from above

Identify a globe as a model of Earth

Lessons

1. What is a Map?

A map is a drawing of a place as if you were looking at it from above.

Examples:

  • • Draw your bedroom from a bird's-eye view
  • • Draw your classroom from above
  • • A map of your neighborhood would show streets, parks, and buildings

2. Globes and Earth

A globe is a round model of Earth that shows all the land and water.

Examples:

  • • Earth has more water (oceans) than land
  • • You can spin a globe to see all parts of Earth
  • • A flat map stretches the round Earth, but a globe shows true shapes

lessons.title: Land and Water
lessons.content:
Land and Water

Learning Objectives

  • • Mountain: tall, rocky land
  • • Hill: smaller than a mountain, rounded at the top
  • • Valley: low land between hills or mountains
  • • Plain: flat, wide stretch of land
  • • Island: land completely surrounded by water
  • • Ocean: the largest body of salt water
  • • River: fresh water flowing across land
  • • Lake: body of fresh water surrounded by land
  • • Pond: small, shallow body of fresh water
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 2

Land and Water

Identify and describe basic landforms and bodies of water.

Learning Objectives

Name basic landforms: mountain, hill, valley, plain, island

Name bodies of water: ocean, river, lake, pond

Locate land and water on a simple map

Lessons

1. Landforms

The surface of the Earth has many different shapes.

Examples:

  • • Mountain: tall, rocky land
  • • Hill: smaller than a mountain, rounded at the top
  • • Valley: low land between hills or mountains
  • • Plain: flat, wide stretch of land
  • • Island: land completely surrounded by water

2. Bodies of Water

Water covers most of Earth's surface in different forms.

Examples:

  • • Ocean: the largest body of salt water
  • • River: fresh water flowing across land
  • • Lake: body of fresh water surrounded by land
  • • Pond: small, shallow body of fresh water

lessons.title: Our Neighborhood and Community
lessons.content:
Our Neighborhood and Community

Learning Objectives

  • • School, park, grocery store, post office, fire station
  • • Neighborhoods can be urban (city), suburban (near a city), or rural (countryside)
  • • Library: free books and learning for everyone
  • • Hospital: medical care for sick or injured people
  • • Fire station: firefighters protect the community from fires
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 3

Our Neighborhood and Community

Explore the concept of neighborhood and community, identifying key local places.

Learning Objectives

Define neighborhood and community

Identify key places: school, park, library, store

Draw a simple map of the neighborhood

Lessons

1. What's in My Neighborhood?

A neighborhood is the area around where you live, full of places and people.

Examples:

  • • School, park, grocery store, post office, fire station
  • • Neighborhoods can be urban (city), suburban (near a city), or rural (countryside)

2. Community Helpers and Places

Certain buildings serve the whole community.

Examples:

  • • Library: free books and learning for everyone
  • • Hospital: medical care for sick or injured people
  • • Fire station: firefighters protect the community from fires

lessons.title: Cardinal Directions
lessons.content:
Cardinal Directions

Learning Objectives

  • • The sun rises in the East and sets in the West
  • • On a map, North is usually at the top
  • • 'Never Eat Shredded Wheat' — a way to remember N, E, S, W going clockwise
  • • The library is north of the school
  • • The park is east of the grocery store
  • • Turn left (West) at the corner to reach the post office
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 4

Cardinal Directions

Learn and use the four cardinal directions: North, South, East, West.

Learning Objectives

Name the four cardinal directions

Use cardinal directions to describe location

Apply directions to a simple map

Lessons

1. North, South, East, West

The four cardinal directions help us describe where things are located.

Examples:

  • • The sun rises in the East and sets in the West
  • • On a map, North is usually at the top
  • • 'Never Eat Shredded Wheat' — a way to remember N, E, S, W going clockwise

2. Using Directions on a Map

We use a compass rose on maps to show directions.

Examples:

  • • The library is north of the school
  • • The park is east of the grocery store
  • • Turn left (West) at the corner to reach the post office

lessons.title: Our Country — The United States
lessons.content:
Our Country — The United States

Learning Objectives

  • • 50 states, each with its own capital city
  • • Washington D.C. is the national capital
  • • Bordered by Canada to the north, Mexico to the south, Pacific Ocean to the west, Atlantic Ocean to the east
  • • Rocky Mountains in the West
  • • Great Plains in the Midwest
  • • Appalachian Mountains in the East
  • • Everglades wetlands in Florida
  • • Desert Southwest (Arizona, Nevada)
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 5

Our Country — The United States

Introduce the United States — its size, location, and diversity.

Learning Objectives

Locate the U.S. on a world map

Name a few states and their capitals

Describe geographic diversity of the U.S.

Lessons

1. The United States

The United States is a large country in North America made up of 50 states.

Examples:

  • • 50 states, each with its own capital city
  • • Washington D.C. is the national capital
  • • Bordered by Canada to the north, Mexico to the south, Pacific Ocean to the west, Atlantic Ocean to the east

2. Geographic Diversity

The U.S. has many different landforms and climates.

Examples:

  • • Rocky Mountains in the West
  • • Great Plains in the Midwest
  • • Appalachian Mountains in the East
  • • Everglades wetlands in Florida
  • • Desert Southwest (Arizona, Nevada)

lessons.title: The Seven Continents
lessons.content:
The Seven Continents

Learning Objectives

  • • North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Antarctica
  • • Asia is the largest continent; Australia is the smallest
  • • Antarctica has no permanent human population — only scientists visit
  • • Pacific (largest), Atlantic, Indian, Arctic
  • • The Pacific Ocean is larger than all land on Earth combined
  • • Oceans connect all continents and are vital for weather and climate
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 6

The Seven Continents

Name and locate the seven continents and four major oceans.

Learning Objectives

Name all seven continents

Locate continents on a world map

Name the four major oceans

Lessons

1. Seven Continents

Earth's land is divided into seven large areas called continents.

Examples:

  • • North America, South America, Europe, Africa, Asia, Australia (Oceania), Antarctica
  • • Asia is the largest continent; Australia is the smallest
  • • Antarctica has no permanent human population — only scientists visit

2. Four Oceans

Earth's oceans cover about 71% of the surface.

Examples:

  • • Pacific (largest), Atlantic, Indian, Arctic
  • • The Pacific Ocean is larger than all land on Earth combined
  • • Oceans connect all continents and are vital for weather and climate

lessons.title: Weather and Climate Around the World
lessons.content:
Weather and Climate Around the World

Learning Objectives

  • • Near the equator: hot and sunny all year (tropics)
  • • Near the poles: cold and icy most of the year
  • • In between: four seasons — warm summers and cold winters
  • • Tropical: near the equator — Amazon Rainforest, Central Africa
  • • Temperate: mid-latitudes — the U.S., Europe, China
  • • Polar: near the poles — Arctic, Antarctica, northern Canada
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 7

Weather and Climate Around the World

Explore how weather and climate differ around the world and why.

Learning Objectives

Distinguish between weather and climate

Explain why different places have different climates

Match climates to regions of the world

Lessons

1. Hot, Cold, and In Between

Different parts of the world have very different climates.

Examples:

  • • Near the equator: hot and sunny all year (tropics)
  • • Near the poles: cold and icy most of the year
  • • In between: four seasons — warm summers and cold winters

2. Climate Zones

Scientists divide the world into three main climate zones.

Examples:

  • • Tropical: near the equator — Amazon Rainforest, Central Africa
  • • Temperate: mid-latitudes — the U.S., Europe, China
  • • Polar: near the poles — Arctic, Antarctica, northern Canada

lessons.title: People and Places — How We Adapt
lessons.content:
People and Places — How We Adapt

Learning Objectives

  • • Thick insulated homes; underfloor heating in Scandinavia
  • • Inuit igloos: ice traps body heat and keeps interior warm
  • • Heavy clothing, dog sleds, snowshoes
  • • Desert homes: thick walls keep interiors cool during hot days
  • • Nomadic lifestyles: following water and grazing land (Bedouin, Masai)
  • • Shade structures, light-colored clothing, water storage systems
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 8

People and Places — How We Adapt

Explore how people adapt their lives and homes to different environments.

Learning Objectives

Give examples of how people adapt to cold climates

Give examples of adapting to hot or dry climates

Explain why houses look different around the world

Lessons

1. Adapting to Cold

People in cold climates design their lives around staying warm.

Examples:

  • • Thick insulated homes; underfloor heating in Scandinavia
  • • Inuit igloos: ice traps body heat and keeps interior warm
  • • Heavy clothing, dog sleds, snowshoes

2. Adapting to Heat and Dryness

People in hot or dry climates focus on staying cool and finding water.

Examples:

  • • Desert homes: thick walls keep interiors cool during hot days
  • • Nomadic lifestyles: following water and grazing land (Bedouin, Masai)
  • • Shade structures, light-colored clothing, water storage systems

lessons.title: Maps and Map Skills
lessons.content:
Maps and Map Skills

Learning Objectives

  • • A blue line might represent a river
  • • A green area might represent a park or forest
  • • A star symbol usually marks a capital city
  • • 1 inch = 10 miles: two cities 3 inches apart are about 30 miles apart in real life
  • • A world map has a very small scale (large area, small map)
  • • A neighborhood map has a large scale (small area, big map)
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 9

Maps and Map Skills

Develop basic map reading skills including symbols, legends, and scale.

Learning Objectives

Read a map legend/key

Understand that map symbols represent real things

Use a simple scale to estimate distance

Lessons

1. Map Legends and Symbols

A map legend (or key) explains what the symbols on a map mean.

Examples:

  • • A blue line might represent a river
  • • A green area might represent a park or forest
  • • A star symbol usually marks a capital city

2. Map Scale

A map scale shows the relationship between distance on the map and real distance.

Examples:

  • • 1 inch = 10 miles: two cities 3 inches apart are about 30 miles apart in real life
  • • A world map has a very small scale (large area, small map)
  • • A neighborhood map has a large scale (small area, big map)

lessons.title: Our Planet — Caring for Earth
lessons.content:
Our Planet — Caring for Earth

Learning Objectives

  • • Forests cleared for farmland and cities
  • • Rivers dammed for electricity and water supply
  • • Wetlands drained for development (losing important habitats)
  • • Plant trees and native plants to restore habitats
  • • Reduce, reuse, recycle to cut down on pollution
  • • Use water wisely — millions of people lack clean drinking water
  • • Support national parks and conservation areas
Kindergarten
🌍 Geography
Module 10

Our Planet — Caring for Earth

Connect geography to environmental responsibility and stewardship.

Learning Objectives

Explain how human activities affect geography

Identify environmental challenges: deforestation, pollution, water scarcity

Describe actions children can take to care for Earth

Lessons

1. How Humans Change the Land

As populations grow, humans transform the natural landscape.

Examples:

  • • Forests cleared for farmland and cities
  • • Rivers dammed for electricity and water supply
  • • Wetlands drained for development (losing important habitats)

2. Being Earth Stewards

Everyone can help protect Earth's geography.

Examples:

  • • Plant trees and native plants to restore habitats
  • • Reduce, reuse, recycle to cut down on pollution
  • • Use water wisely — millions of people lack clean drinking water
  • • Support national parks and conservation areas

Read a compass rose with cardinal and intermediate directions

A compass rose shows eight directions: N, NE, E, SE, S, SW, W, NW.

lessons.title: Regions of the United States
lessons.content:
Regions of the United States

Learning Objectives

  • • Northeast: oldest settlements, dense cities (New York, Boston), Appalachian Mountains
  • • Southeast: warm climate, coastal plains, Everglades, Gulf Coast
  • • Midwest: Great Plains, farming ('breadbasket of America'), Great Lakes
  • • Southwest: desert, canyons, Hispanic/Native American cultural influence

Regions of the United States

Explore the five major regions of the U.S. and their geographic and cultural features.

Learning Objectives

Name the five U.S. regions

Describe key physical features of each

Connect regional geography to economy and culture

Lessons

1. Five Regions

The U.S. is often divided into five geographic and cultural regions.

Examples:

  • • Northeast: oldest settlements, dense cities (New York, Boston), Appalachian Mountains
  • • Southeast: warm climate, coastal plains, Everglades, Gulf Coast
  • • Midwest: Great Plains, farming ('breadbasket of America'), Great Lakes
